People who have not chosen a theme open in the new default from their next sign-in. People who have chosen one keep theirs; on **Your profile** they see the workspace's default and can choose **Use the workspace default**.

## The themes
| Theme | What it is |
|---|---|
| System | Light or Dark, as each person's device is set |
| Light | The console's own, on white |
| Dark | Neutral dark |
| Ocean | Calm blue and teal on light |
| Midnight | Deep navy with teal accents |
| High contrast | Black on white, strongest edges |

> **Tip:** High contrast helps people with low vision and on bright ward screens; suggest it rather than making it everyone's default.

## Example
Summit Valley's default theme is Light, so printed screenshots and shared screens look the same for everyone. The night-shift nurses on Ward 4B choose Midnight for themselves.

articles.title: Your models: model connections
articles.summary: Where prompts run, which model does what, local models, the two caps, and why every answer is a DRAFT.
articles.who: Workspace administrators add, change and test connections; everyone else uses them through prompts, AI steps and the AI Assistant
articles.popular: Connect a model
articles.md:
Every AI feature in the console runs on a **model connection**: a provider, its key, a default model and two caps. Prompts,
AI steps in pipelines, image descriptions, the AI Assistant, Ask your data and the reading of documents all go through one.
One connection is the workspace **default**; a prompt that names no connection runs on it.

A model's answer is always a **DRAFT for a person to check**. The console marks it so where a pipeline says so, holds it for
review where the pipeline asks for a review, and never treats it as a decision. A clinician, an analyst or a reviewer decides.

![Model connections, the workspace's local connection selected](ai-model-connections "Model connections: the list on the left; the selected connection's last test, caps, models and the last 30 days of runs")

## Add a connection
1. Open **Administration & billing › Settings › Model connections** and choose **New connection**.
2. Give it a **Name** people will recognise, such as *Local Ollama* or *OpenAI · production*.
3. Pick the **Provider**: OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama (local), Azure OpenAI, or an OpenAI-compatible server (Groq, vLLM,
   LM Studio and others).
4. Fill **API endpoint** only where the provider needs one (Azure OpenAI and OpenAI-compatible servers); the others have it
   built in. Paste the **API key** for a hosted provider. A local Ollama connection needs no key.
5. Type the **Default model**: what a prompt runs on unless it names another model.
6. Set the two caps (see below) and save.
7. Choose **Test connection**. A passing test lists the models the provider offers and confirms the key; the result shows
   under **Last test**.

> **Privacy:** A key is encrypted when it is stored and is never sent back to the browser. To change it, edit the connection
> and paste a new key; leaving the field blank keeps the stored one.

## The two caps
- **Calls in flight**: at most this many calls at once through this connection (1 to 64); the rest wait in order.
- **Daily token budget**: once the day's runs reach it, a step fails before any call is made. Blank means no cap. The
  connection's page shows how much of today's budget is used.

> **Tip:** On a local model, keep **Calls in flight** low. A small machine answers one question at a time well and several
> slowly. The showcase's *Local Ollama* connection allows one call in flight.

## Which model does what
- A prompt names its **Connection** and, if it wants, a **Model** (see [Write and test a prompt](#ai-prompts)). Blank uses
  the workspace default and that connection's default model.
- Text work (classify, extract, summarise) runs on a text model; describing an image needs a vision model, named on the
  prompt. In the showcase, text prompts run on `qwen3:8b` and the image prompts name `gemma3:4b`.
- The AI Assistant runs on the workspace default unless an administrator picks another connection at the top of its page.
- Which models may see a given kind of data is the workspace's data policy:
  see [Which models may see which data](#ai-data-levels).

## Local models
An **Ollama (local)** connection runs models on machines your organisation runs itself, so the data never goes to a hosted
provider. The **Sensitive** data level starts as *Local only*: until an administrator changes it, only local connections
may see sensitive data.

## Make a connection inactive, or the default
- **Make inactive** stops everything that runs on the connection: the AI Assistant, Ask your data, document reading,
  pipeline AI steps, image description and prompts are refused until it is made active again. If it is the default,
  everything that runs on the default is refused too.
- The **⋮** menu holds **Edit connection**, **Set as default** and **Delete connection**.
- The page shows who last made it active or inactive, and when.

## What the page tells you
| Part | What it shows |
|---|---|
| Last test | Passed, failed or never tested, with the provider's message in words |
| Endpoint | Where calls go, and whether a key is stored |
| Caps | Calls in flight, and today's tokens against the budget |
| Models | The default model and what the provider listed at the last test |
| Usage · last 30 days | Runs, tokens in and out, and the prompts that run on it |
| Recent runs | Each call: when, which prompt, model, status, time and tokens; a failure in plain words, with **Details** |

## Example
Summit Valley Health System runs only local models. Its administrator added *Local Ollama* (Ollama (local), default model
`qwen3:8b`, one call in flight, no daily budget) and set it as the default. Twenty-two prompts run on it, from *Referral
urgency* to *Discharge summary (DRAFT)*; every clinical prompt says DRAFT in its name.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Calls in flight | 1 to 64 per connection (default 4) |
| Who may add, change, test or delete | A workspace administrator |
| A connection belongs to | One workspace; only its prompts run on it |

articles.title: Write and test a prompt
articles.summary: Instructions, a message with variables, a JSON answer checked against a schema, Try it, and versions.
articles.who: Workspace administrators write, try, activate and delete prompts; anyone whose page access includes Prompts reads the list
articles.popular: Write a prompt and try it
articles.md:
A **prompt** is what a step says to a model: who the model is, the message sent each time with **variables** the pipeline
fills in, and the shape of the answer. A pipeline's **AI prompt** step runs a saved prompt row by row, so the same words are
used every time and every change is kept as a version.

![The prompt editor beside Try it](ai-prompt-editor "A prompt open in the editor: About it and Model on the left, Try it and its recent runs on the right")

## Write a prompt
1. Open **Build › Pipelines › Prompts** and choose **New prompt**.
2. **About it**: a **Name** (say what it does, and add *(DRAFT)* when the answer is a draft for a clinician), a
   **Description**, the **Data sensitivity** of what it is sent (Public, Internal or Sensitive; *Not set* is read as
   internal), and **Tags**. A file type in the tags (pdf, docx) offers the prompt in the file chat.
3. **Model**: the **Connection** (blank runs on the workspace default) and the **Model** (blank is the connection's default).
   **Temperature** 0 gives the steadiest answers; **Max tokens** caps the answer's length.
4. **What it says**: the **System instructions** (the same for every run) and the **Message template**, the text sent each
   time. Type `{{name}}` or click a variable under **Insert** to put one in.
5. **Variables**: **Add variable** for each value the pipeline fills in. Give it a **Type** (text, number, url, or
   file → text), tick **Required** if a row without it should fail, and a **Sample value** for Try it.
6. **The answer**: choose **Text** (used as it is) or **JSON object**.
7. Choose **Save draft**, or **Save & activate** to make it the version steps use.

```A message template with two variables
Synthetic wound photo for {{mrn}}: measured in code {{length_cm}} x {{width_cm}} cm. Describe the stage, tissue and exudate.
```

> **Tip:** Write the instructions so the model never invents a value, and say the answer is a draft. The showcase's
> *Wound description (DRAFT)* begins: describe only what is visible; your answer is a DRAFT, never a diagnosis.

## Ask for a JSON answer
With **Output** set to **JSON object**, an **Output schema** appears. The schema is sent to the model, and every answer is
checked against it, with one repair round. An answer that still does not fit is **held for review**, never used.

```An output schema with an allowed list
{ "properties": { "stage": { "type": "string", "enum": ["1", "2", "3", "4", "Unstageable"] }, "summary": { "type": "string" } } }
```

- Give each key a `type`; list allowed values in `enum` and no other value is accepted.
- `properties` without `required` requires them all. A blank schema accepts any JSON object.
- Keep schemas small. On a local model, a long list of allowed values or tight number limits can make each answer take
  minutes.

## Try it before anything uses it
1. Fill each variable's **Sample value**, or choose the folder button to fill it from a file in a bucket (any type the file
   chat can read).
2. Choose **Run** under **Try it**. It runs the page as it stands, saved or not, and records the run as a try.
3. Read the answer, the tokens in and out, and the time. **Show rendered input** shows exactly what was sent.
4. **Recent runs** lists the tries and the pipeline steps that ran the prompt, with their version.

> **Note:** A try spends the workspace's tokens like any other call, and is billed. A JSON answer that does not fit the
> schema shows as **Held for review**, with the answer that was held.

## Versions
Every save is a version. In the editor, **Save as v2** (the next number) keeps the change without activating it; **Save &
activate** makes it current. The list shows each prompt's version, connection and model, its variables, whether it answers
Text or JSON, how many pipelines use it, its runs and when it last ran (and whether that run failed or was held).

From a row's **⋮** menu: **Edit & try**, **Activate** or **Deactivate**, and **Delete**.

## Example
Summit Valley's *Care plan (DRAFT)* prompt takes the findings of one admission and answers a JSON object with `risk`,
`goals`, `interventions` and `follow_up`. Journey 9 runs it; when `risk` is *High*, the *Patient journey* workflow asks a
senior physician as well (see [Design an approval workflow](#apr-workflows)).

![The Prompts list](ai-prompts "Build › Pipelines › Prompts: every prompt with its connection, variables, output and use")

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Variable names | Letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter or underscore |
| Repair rounds for a JSON answer | One; then the answer is held for review |
| Who may write, try or delete | A workspace administrator (in a managed workspace, read only) |

articles.title: AI in pipelines
articles.summary: The AI prompt step: classify, extract, summarise or describe an image, row by row or a few at a time, and what happens when the model is busy.
articles.who: Workspace administrators add and change steps; anyone who may open the run reads its AI answers
articles.md:
A pipeline asks a model with an **AI prompt** step. The step runs a saved prompt once for each row it reads, fills the
prompt's variables from the row's columns, and adds the answer to the row. What the step does is up to the prompt:

- **Classify**: a referral's urgency, a denial's reason, a card transaction's spend category.
- **Extract**: fields from a note or a letter, as a JSON answer.
- **Summarise**: a visit, a care plan, a discharge summary, always as a DRAFT.
- **Describe an image**: a wound photo or an X-ray sent to a vision model with the prompt.

Documents that arrive as files (referrals, lab results, invoices) are read into fields by Document Intelligence rather
than by a prompt step; see [How documents are read](#doc-reading).

![An AI prompt step's settings](ai-step-settings "The settings of an AI prompt step: the prompt, its variables, the image to send and the answer's fields")

## Add an AI step
1. Open the pipeline under **Build › Pipelines** and go to **Steps**.
2. In **Add step from the Task Registry…**, find **AI prompt** and add it where the rows are ready.
3. Under **Task settings**, pick the **Prompt**.
4. **Variables**: name a value for a variable only when it does not come from a column of the same name, as in
   `{{record_id}}`. A required variable with no value fails that row.
5. For an image, fill **Image**: the **Bucket** and the **Image key column** that holds each row's image (png, jpg, webp or gif).
6. **Answer column** names the column the answer goes in. For a JSON answer, add **Fields**: **From the answer at** (a path
   such as `status` or `result.score`) and **As column**, so later steps and conditions read them as ordinary columns.
7. **When a row fails**: fail the step, skip the row, or keep it with the answer empty.
8. **At most rows**: the step refuses an input with more rows before it makes any call.
9. **Apply**, then **Validate** and **Save** the pipeline.

> **Tip:** Send a model only the columns it needs. Measure, count and compare in ordinary steps first and let the model
> describe: Summit Valley measures each wound against the ruler in code, and the vision model only describes the stage,
> tissue and exudate.

## Row by row, or a few at a time
**Calls at once** (1 to 8) lets the step ask several rows at the same time. 1, the default, asks one after another.
Answers keep the rows' order whatever order they finish in, and the workspace's calls together are capped as well, so one
busy pipeline cannot take every call. The model connection's **Calls in flight** still applies.

## When the model is busy
A model or provider that answers *busy* is not a failure at first. The step waits (as long as the provider asks, otherwise
1, 2, 4 and then 8 seconds), asks again up to four times, and halves its own number of calls at once while it is busy.
Only a row that is still refused after that fails, and then **When a row fails** decides what happens.

> **Warning:** A connection's **Daily token budget** is a hard stop: once the day's runs reach it, the step fails before
> any call is made. Raise the budget or wait for the next day, then retry the run from the failed step.

## Read the answers
A run of a pipeline with AI steps has an **AI answers** tab. Each answer shows the prompt and its version, whether it was
**Answered** or held, the time and the tokens; open one to read the answer itself.

![A run's AI answers](ai-run-answers "A run's AI answers tab: the wound description, a JSON answer from the vision model")

A JSON answer that does not fit the prompt's schema is held for review and never used. When the pipeline asks for a review,
its results wait in **Review** until a person approves them; see [Review a run's results](#apr-run-review). For a sign-off
on one step in the middle of a run, use an Approval step: [Approval steps inside a run](#apr-approval-steps).

## Example
Summit Valley's *Journey 7 · Wound photo: measure, describe, wound-care review* reads the photo a nurse dropped, measures
it against the 1 cm ruler, asks *Wound description (DRAFT)* on the vision model, compares the area with the last visit,
and waits for Sam Harper (Wound care) to approve the measurement before one report per photo is made.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Calls at once | 1 to 8 per step; the workspace's calls together are capped too |
| At most rows | Default 50, at most 500 |
| Fields taken from a JSON answer | 50 |
| Tries when the model is busy | 4, with waits of 1, 2, 4 and 8 seconds unless the provider says otherwise |
| Image types | png, jpg, webp, gif |

articles.title: Turn recordings into text
articles.summary: The Transcribe audio step and the Audio Transcript tool: recordings to text, with or without times, and what is billed.
articles.who: Workspace administrators add the step to a pipeline; anyone whose page access includes Tools › Audio Transcript uses the tool
articles.md:
Recordings (care calls, telehealth visits, dictated notes) become text with the platform's own transcriber, the same one
in a pipeline and on the tool page. A pipeline can then summarise the text with an [AI prompt step](#ai-steps), write a
report for each call, or search it in Ask your data.

## Transcribe one recording by hand
1. Open **See results › Tools › Audio Transcript**.
2. Choose **Upload a file** and drop an .mp3 or .m4a, or choose **From a bucket** and pick one you can see.
3. Tick **Include timestamps before each segment** if you want each stretch of speech with its time.
4. Choose **Extract transcript**. Transcription runs on the server and can take a few minutes for a long recording.
5. Read the **Transcript**: **Copy** it, **Read aloud**, or copy a timestamp to point a colleague at a moment.

![The Audio Transcript tool](ai-transcript "See results › Tools › Audio Transcript: the formats and limits above the drop zone")

## Transcribe in a pipeline
1. In the pipeline's **Steps**, add **Transcribe audio** from **Add step from the Task Registry…**.
2. Say which recordings: the files the run was started for (a recording dropped in the inbox, for example), or the rows of
   an earlier step that name a file.
3. Tick **Timestamps** to add `segments`: each stretch of speech with its start and end, as JSON.
4. **When a file fails**: fail the step, skip the row, or keep it with the transcript empty. A kept row says why in
   `transcribe_status` and `transcribe_error`.
5. **Calls at once** transcribes several files at the same time; **At most files** refuses a larger input before any file
   is read.

Each row gets `file_name`, `file_stem`, `transcript`, `language` and `duration_seconds`, and with timestamps `segments`.
Each recording is an item of the run, so the run's **Items** tab shows how each one went (see
[The Items view](#run-items)).

> **Tip:** A silent or damaged recording need not stop the others. Set **When a file fails** to keep the row: the run
> completes, and the row says why that one has no text.

## When the transcriber is busy
A busy transcriber is waited for and asked again, up to six tries, waiting at most five minutes between two tries. On the
tool page you are told it is busy; nothing is lost, and you try again in about 30 seconds.

## Example
Summit Valley Home Health drops each care call (`call-*.m4a`) into the workspace inbox. *Care-call insight, one report per
call* transcribes it, asks *Call insight (JSON)* for the reason, follow-up and concerns, and makes one report for each call.
Tamara Brooks (Home health nurses) reads the transcript beside the insight before anything is shared.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Formats in a pipeline | mp3, m4a, wav, ogg, flac, webm |
| Formats on the tool page | mp3, m4a |
| Size | Upload up to 250 MB on the tool page; a recording in a bucket up to 500 MB |
| Time on the tool page | Up to 30 minutes a recording |
| At most files in a step | Default 20 |
| Billed | By the minute of audio (see [What AI costs](#ai-costs)) |

articles.title: Design a pipeline with the AI Assistant
articles.summary: Describe a pipeline in plain words, check the flow it draws, create it; ask about runs, sources and files; what it can and cannot reach.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Prompts › AI Assistant; creating a pipeline and choosing the model are a workspace administrator's
articles.popular: Describe a pipeline to the AI Assistant
articles.md:
The **AI Assistant** turns a description in plain words into a pipeline you can check, fill in and create, and answers
questions about your runs, sources and files. It uses only the tools in the Tool Registry, acts as you, and asks before it
runs, saves or deletes anything. Nothing it designs is saved until you choose **Create pipeline**.

![The AI Assistant with a drawn flow](ai-assistant "Build › AI Assistant: conversations on the left, the chat in the middle, the drawn flow on the right")

## Design a pipeline in a conversation
1. Open **Build › AI Assistant** and choose **New chat**.
2. Say what should happen to your data, as you would to a colleague, or start from a suggestion under **Design a
   pipeline**.
3. The assistant draws the pipeline on the **Flow** tab, step by step, checked against this workspace's tasks. The flow's
   label says where it stands: **Ready to create**, *N settings to fill*, *Check N warnings* or *N errors*.
4. Select a step on the flow to see what it does and fill its settings. To change the flow, ask in the chat ("also email
   the physicians", "read only yesterday's files"); settings you filled for a step the change keeps stay filled.
5. When the label says **Ready to create**, choose **Create pipeline**. Name it, pick its topic and how it starts, and
   confirm. It is saved in this workspace as you, as the pipeline's first version.
6. Open it with **Open in step builder**, or start it with **Run now** or **Schedule**.

```A description the assistant can draw
Design a pipeline: every night read orders.csv from storage, keep the paid orders, and save them as a CSV.
```

> **Tip:** If the flow changes after you created it, the button becomes **Update pipeline**: it saves the change as a new
> version. **Create pipeline** is not offered again, so the same pipeline is never made twice.

## Ask about runs, sources and files
Questions such as *How did my last run go?*, *Which runs failed this week?* or *List the data sources in this workspace*
are answered at once from what you may open. A question about numbers in a dataset can come back as a chart on the
**Chart** tab; you can pin it to a dashboard if you may edit dashboards. **Tool calls** shows every tool the assistant
used for an answer, and how long each took.

## It asks before it acts
Anything that changes something comes back as a card, **Confirm before it runs**, naming the tool and what it will do,
with a time it expires. Nothing happens until you choose the card's button (**Run pipeline**, **Save file**, **Create PDF**,
**Delete file**) or **Cancel**. The card says it runs as you, in this workspace.

## What it can and cannot reach
The **Context** tab says exactly what applies to you here:

![The assistant's Context tab](ai-assistant-context "Context: the workspace, who it acts as, the model, the data policy and the tools allowed")

- **Workspace** and **Acting as**: it works only in this workspace, as you. It reads only what your own access opens.
- **Model**: the workspace default, unless an administrator picks another connection at the top of the page.
- **Data policy**: for each data level, which models may see it and whether the assistant's write tools may act on it.
  Sensitive data stays on local models, and the write tools do not act on it, unless your administrator changes the policy.
- **Tools allowed** and **Asks first for**: the tools it may use (from **Settings › Tool Registry**) and those that always
  need your confirmation. A blocked tool is listed with the reason.

It cannot reach another workspace, a page your access does not open, or anything outside the tools listed.

> **Note:** A local model can take a minute to plan. **Stop** ends the run on the server; whatever it said before it
> stopped stays in the conversation, and **Retry** asks the same question again.

## Your conversations
The list on the left keeps your conversations, newest first, with whether each made a pipeline (**Pipeline created**,
**Not saved**) or answered a question. Search them, filter by **Pipelines**, **Questions** or **Runs**, rename one, or delete it.

## Example
Summit Valley's administrator asks for a daily SMS reminder: read `clinic/appointments.csv` at 17:00, keep tomorrow's booked
appointments, and send them to the SMS messages API in batches of 100. The assistant draws three steps; once each setting is
filled the label reads **Ready to create**, and **Create pipeline** saves it with its schedule.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| One message | 4,000 characters |
| Who may create or update a pipeline | A workspace administrator; in a managed workspace you can still ask and draw |
| Who may pick the model | A workspace administrator |

articles.title: Ask your data, and chat with a file
articles.summary: Questions in plain words with their sources or query, answers drawn as charts and pinned to a dashboard, and asking one file.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Ask your data (and Files for the file chat); pinning needs dashboard editing; the search index is a workspace administrator's

where.label: See results › Analysis › Ask your data

articles.popular: Ask a question about your data
articles.md:
**Ask your data** answers a question in plain words from what you can open in this workspace: documents, forms,
pipeline results and datasets. Every answer shows where it came from, either its numbered sources or the query it ran,
so you can check it. The **file chat** does the same for one file.

![Ask your data](ai-ask-data "See results › Analysis › Ask your data: the question box, suggestions from your own data, examples and pinned answers")

## Ask a question
1. Open **See results › Analysis › Ask your data**.
2. Type a question, or pick one under **Try:** (made from what your workspace holds) or **Start with an example**.
   The badge at the top says what is searched, such as *Searching 3 documents, 7 pipeline results and 6 forms*.
3. Choose **Ask**. The answer comes in one of three shapes:
   - **From documents and forms**: the answer in words, with numbered citations; each source below it links to the
     document, form or file, with the passage it came from.
   - **From a dataset**: the answer, a chart, the rows behind it, and **The query, run as you** over that dataset.
     **Open in Analysis Studio** opens the query; **Download CSV** takes the rows.
   - **Not found**: it says it cannot find that in your data. Try naming a document, a schedule, a column or a value.
4. The line under each answer says which model answered, on which connection, and how long it took.

> **Note:** An answer is a DRAFT for a person to check, like any model's answer. Read the sources or the query before you
> use a number.

## Pin a chart to a dashboard
An answer drawn as a chart has **Pin to dashboard**. The pin becomes a tile that runs its query again whenever the dashboard
is opened, so it stays current. **Pinned answers** lists what you pinned from here. Pinning needs dashboard editing in your
page access; see also [Put an Ask your data answer on a board](#dash-ask-pin).

## Your recent questions
**Your recent questions** keeps what you asked in this browser; ask one again to get today's answer, or **Clear** the list.

## The search index (administrators)
With the **Search index** on, questions search your documents, forms and chosen folders by words and by meaning, so answers
keep up as they grow. Each person still finds only what they can open, and values the Data Catalog holds as sensitive are
stored masked. Pipeline results are always read live. With it off, every question reads your sources live.

## Chat with one file
1. Open **See results › Analysis › Files** and find the file.
2. From its row menu choose **Chat with this file**.
3. Pick the **Agent**: the prompts offered for this kind of file (a prompt whose **Tags** name the file type, such as
   *pdf*). Ask, or start from *Summarise this file*, *What are the key points?* or *List any dates mentioned*.
4. If the file is longer than the model can read at once, a note says how much of it the answers cover; a large file may
   be answered from the passages most relevant to each question.
5. **Close** ends the chat. The conversation is deleted and the text read from the file is dropped: nothing is kept.

## Example
Summit Valley's operations director asks *What is the average length of stay by ward this month?* The answer is drawn as a
bar chart from the ward census results, with the query beside it; Jordan Reyes pins it to the *Patient journey* dashboard.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| One question | 500 characters |
| What is searched | Only what you may open in this workspace |
| Recent questions | Kept in this browser, for you |

articles.title: Which models may see which data
articles.summary: The three data levels, the model rule for each, how a call's level is decided, and the AI Assistant's write tools.
articles.who: Workspace administrators change the data policy; every member may read it
articles.md:
The workspace's **data policy** decides, for each level of data, which models may see it, how long a run keeps its working
files, and whether the AI Assistant's write tools may act on it. A prompt, an AI step or the assistant runs only on the
models its data's level allows.

![The data policy's levels side by side](ai-data-policies "Data policies: Sensitive, Internal and Public side by side, a setting a row")

## The three levels
| Level | What it is for |
|---|---|
| **Sensitive** | Personal, health or confidential data (PHI, PII, confidential, restricted) |
| **Internal** | The workspace's everyday data. A call is internal when nothing says otherwise |
| **Public** | Data anyone may see: published figures, open datasets and APIs |

## How a call's level is decided
- A prompt declares its level with **Data sensitivity** on its editor ([Write and test a prompt](#ai-prompts)).
- A pipeline may declare one in its **Settings** (Patient data is Sensitive).
- An API collection or a data contract has a level of its own.

When nothing is set, the call is read as internal. The page's **How a call's level is decided** box says the rule in full.

## Set the model rule
1. Open **Administration & billing › Administration › Data policies**.
2. For each level choose a **Model rule**:
   - **Any model**: any of the workspace's model connections, hosted or local.
   - **BAA-signed hosted, or local**: local models, and hosted models only on a connection marked as covered by a signed
     Business Associate Agreement (marked on **Model connections**).
   - **Local only**: only models on your own machines (Ollama connections); the data never goes to a hosted provider.
3. Optionally tick **Allowed models**: none ticked allows any model the rule allows; a ticked connection allows each of its models.
4. **Keep run files**: how many days a run keeps its working copies for its next steps and downloads (1 to 3650). Blank
   is the pipeline's own: 24 hours unless it sets another.
5. **AI write tools**: whether the assistant may run pipelines, create PDFs, save or delete files and call APIs that
   change data at this level. It still asks first.
6. **Minimum-fields warning**: reminds whoever builds a step to send a model only the fields it needs.
7. Choose **Save policy**.

> **Privacy:** Until a level is saved it follows its default: public and internal data may go to any model and the write
> tools may act on it; sensitive data stays on local models and the write tools do not act on it.

> **Note:** How you configure and use these controls is your organisation's decision. The console does not by itself make a
> workspace compliant with any law or standard, and marking a connection as covered by an agreement is your statement,
> not the console's check.

## On the same page
- **Bulk review**: whether runs and documents may be approved many at once (see
  [Decide many at once](#apr-bulk)).
- **Retention**: how long each kind of record is kept, and legal holds.

## Example
Summit Valley keeps the defaults: its patient data is Sensitive and runs only on *Local Ollama*. A research prompt over
public CDC figures is marked Public, so it could run on a hosted model if the workspace added one.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Keep run files | 1 to 3650 days, or blank for the pipeline's own |
| Who may change the policy | A workspace administrator |

articles.title: What AI costs
articles.summary: Tokens, minutes of audio and pages read, where each shows in Cost & usage, and how to keep AI spending in hand.
articles.who: Workspace administrators read Cost & usage and set the model connections' caps
articles.md:
AI work is metered as it happens and priced from the workspace's rate card, like everything else the workspace uses.
**Cost & usage** shows the month as the invoice will read it; the AI lines are among the others.

## What is counted
| What | Counted as | When |
|---|---|---|
| Asking a model (prompts, AI steps, the AI Assistant, Ask your data, the file chat, Try it) | **Model tokens in** and **Model tokens out** | Every call, a try included |
| Transcription | Minutes of audio | Each recording transcribed, by a pipeline or on the tool page |
| Reading scanned pages | Pages read | Each page a Read text from pages step reads |
| Converting documents | **Documents converted** | Each file converted |

A run's own page has **What this run cost** (for administrators), and the run's summary shows its **Cost**.

![Line by line in Cost & usage](ai-costs "Cost & usage › Line by line: Model tokens in and out at the top, each line with its rate and amount")

## Read the AI lines
1. Open **Administration & billing › Billing › Cost & usage** and pick the month.
2. **By service** shows **Model calls** beside storage, pipelines, analytics and the API.
3. **AI model calls** lists the month's calls by what called the model (a prompt by name, the assistant, a pipeline), or
   every call.
4. **Cost by pipeline** shows which pipelines spend the most; pick one for its runs.
5. In **Line by line**, click a line for what is behind it, such as which prompt.

## Keep it in hand
- Set a **Daily token budget** on a model connection: once the day's runs reach it, steps fail before any call is made.
- Keep **Calls in flight** and an AI step's **Calls at once** low on shared or local models.
- Use **At most rows** on an AI step, and filter rows before the step, so a large file is never sent row by row by mistake.
- Send only the columns a prompt needs, and cap the answer with **Max tokens**.
- Retry a failed run from the step that failed: the steps before it are reused, not run again. **Run again from the start**
  runs every step again, and its work is billed again. Retry failed items retries only the items that failed.

> **Tip:** On a local model the tokens are still counted, so you can see which prompts do the most work before you move any of
> them to a hosted model.

## Example
In October, Summit Valley's month to date was mostly **Model calls**: about 1.6 million tokens in and 21,000 out across
22 prompts on *Local Ollama*. **AI model calls** shows which prompts those tokens went to.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Who reads Cost & usage | A workspace administrator |
| Prices | The workspace's rate card for the month; an issued invoice keeps the rate card that priced it |

articles.title: Review: everything waiting for you
articles.summary: All waiting, Approvals, Runs and Documents; what each row says; the badge count on the menu and on Home.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes the Task inbox or Document review; each tab shows only what you may decide
articles.popular: Find what waits for your decision
articles.md:
Everything that waits for a person is in one place: **Run & review › Review**. Approval steps and tasks of workflows, runs
whose results wait for a review, and documents with values to check are listed together, overdue first, then the longest
waiting, with one count beside **Review** in the menu.

![Review › All waiting](apr-review-all "Review › All waiting: an approval task and two documents, each with what it is, where it came from and whom it waits on")

## The four tabs
| Tab | What it lists |
|---|---|
| **All waiting** | Everything below, together, in one list |
| **Approvals** | Approval steps and tasks for you or your teams, run reviews among them, the soonest due first (see [Review a run's results](#apr-run-review)) |
| **Runs** | Runs whose results wait for a review, newest first |
| **Documents** | Documents with values to check beside the page image (see [Review a document](#doc-review)) |

Each tab has its own page access, so a reviewer sees only the kinds their profile lets them decide.

## Work through All waiting
1. Open **Run & review › Review**. **All waiting** opens first.
2. Narrow it by kind (**All**, **Approvals**, **Runs**, **Documents**, each with its count), by **Waits on** (**Anyone**,
   **You**, **Your teams**, **Not claimed**), or with **Search what, from, who**.
3. Each row says its **Type**, **What** it is (with a line under it, such as *2 of 13 values to check*), where it is
   **From** (the workflow, the pipeline, the document type), **Waiting since**, whom it **Waits on**, and **Due / age**
   (*Due in 21 h*, *Overdue · was due …*, *Waiting 3 h*).
4. Click a row to read it in the side panel: what it is, what to check, and **Approve…** or **Reject…** when you may
   decide it there; or open its own page with **Open in Approvals**, **Open the run** or **Open the document**.
5. To decide several at once, tick them and choose **Approve** or **Reject** in the bar (see
   [Decide many at once](#apr-bulk)).

> **Note:** Some rows cannot be decided from the list, and say why: your own request (someone else decides it), a run
> whose pipeline requires individual review (open it to decide), a task step (open it to do it), or a document someone
> else has claimed.

## The badge
The number beside **Review** in the menu, and Home's *N waiting for your review*, count everything in **All waiting** for
you. It is read again whenever a new notification arrives (a new task, a reminder, an escalation) and every two minutes
while the console is open, so it stays current without a refresh.

## Example
Dr. Anika Patel opens **Review** at the start of her shift. **All waiting** shows two referral documents with values to
check from the night's intake, and the care plan waiting for her approval in the *Patient journey*. She filters **Waits on**
to **You**, decides the care plan first because it is due soonest, and leaves the documents to the HIM team.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| What you see | Only what your page access and your teams let you decide |
| Your own requests | Listed, never decided by you |

articles.title: Review a run's results
articles.summary: A pipeline whose results wait for a person: approve, or reject with a reason; one by one or in bulk; runs that must be decided one at a time.
articles.who: Workspace administrators decide any run's review; members decide the runs a pipeline names them for, through their task in Review › Approvals
articles.popular: Approve or reject a run's results
articles.md:
A pipeline can hold its results until a person has looked at them. The run completes, but its status reads
**Completed · waiting for review**, and nothing downstream should treat the results as final until someone approves them.
This is how a model's draft, a triage or a reconciliation gets a person's decision.

## Turn it on for a pipeline
1. Open the pipeline under **Build › Pipelines** and go to **Settings › Review**.
2. Under **Results need review by**, tick **Our team** (and **The customer (through the API)** for a two-party review, see
   [Two-party review](#apr-two-party)).
3. Who is asked, the reminders and the due time are set in **Build › Approval workflows › Pipeline run review**.
4. Tick **Requires individual review (never approved or rejected in bulk)** when every run must be looked at on its own.

![A run review decided by the radiologist](apr-run-review-done "Review › Approvals › Done: a chest X-ray triage run reviewed by the radiologist, with what was reviewed")

## Decide a run
1. Open the run from **Review › Approvals** (a reviewer's task about the run) or **Review › Runs** (administrators), or open
   the run's page.
2. Read **What to review**: the image the run reviewed, the first fields a reviewer looks at (a model's answer is marked
   **DRAFT**: *made by a model for a person to check; not a decision*), the rest on demand, the **Report PDF** and
   **Open the run**.
3. Choose **Approve**, with an optional note of **What you checked**; or **Reject** and say why: a reason is required.
4. On a rejection you may tick **Run the schedule again**, so a new run is made once the cause is fixed.

The decision is recorded in **Review › Approvals** under your name, and the run's status becomes **Completed · approved** or
**Completed · rejected**.

> **Tip:** On the run's own page, **Next steps** at the top holds the same Approve and Reject, with whom it waits on.

## One by one, or in bulk
Runs can be approved several at once from **Review** (see [Decide many at once](#apr-bulk)), unless:
- the pipeline **Requires individual review**: it is skipped by every bulk decision and must be opened and decided on its own;
- the workspace has turned off **Allow bulk approve of runs** under **Administration › Data policies › Bulk review**.

Rejecting in bulk is always allowed.

## Who decides
- A workspace administrator may decide any run's review.
- A member decides the runs the pipeline names them for, by role or by team, through their task in **Review › Approvals**.
  They can read those runs even when the schedule is not theirs.
- No one decides their own request.

## Example
*Journey 8 · Chest X-ray triage* sends each X-ray to the vision model and holds the result for the Radiology team, with
individual review on. Dr. Lena Schmidt opens her task, looks at the image and the DRAFT finding, and approves it on its own;
a bulk approval of the day's runs skips it with *The pipeline requires individual review*.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Runs that wait for review | Completed runs only; a failed run has no results to decide |
| Rejecting | Needs a reason |
| Decisions | One per party for each run, final once recorded |

articles.title: Approval steps inside a run
articles.summary: An Approval step pauses a run at that step until its reviewers approve; what the task shows; rejecting fails the run with your reason.
articles.who: Workspace administrators add the step; the reviewers it names decide it in Review › Approvals or on the run's page
articles.md:
Sometimes a person must agree before a run goes on: a measurement before the wound report is made, a list of drug
interactions before it is sent to the ward, a count before a write-off. An **Approval** step pauses the run at that point.
The steps before it have run; the steps after it wait. Approved, the run continues; rejected, or not decided in time, the
run fails with the reason.

This differs from a run's review ([Review a run's results](#apr-run-review)), which holds a finished run's results.

![An Approval step in a run's steps](apr-step-in-run "A run's Steps: step 10, Wound care approves the measurement, approved by Sam Harper before the report was made")

## Add an Approval step
1. Open the pipeline's **Steps** and add **Approval** from **Add step from the Task Registry…**, after the steps whose
   results need the decision.
2. **Task title**: what the reviewers' task says, filled from the run and the first row, such as
   `Wound {{mrn}}: {{area_cm2}} cm²`.
3. **What to check**: the instructions shown on the task.
4. **Fields**: name and value pairs shown on the task, such as `Abnormal = {{abnormal_count}}`.
5. **Reviewers**: a role or a team. Empty, it goes to the pipeline's review reviewers, or else to the workspace's
   administrators.
6. **Decide within (hours)**: nobody deciding in this time fails the run.
7. Save the pipeline. Who is asked and the reminders follow **Build › Approval workflows › Pipeline step approval**.

> **Tip:** Keep a copy of the rows before the Approval step (a **Save file** or **Upload to bucket** step). The task can then
> list the rows to approve; without one it shows only the step's counts.

## What the reviewer sees
The run's status reads **Running · waiting for approval**, and the task in **Review › Approvals** shows:
- the **Pipeline**, **Run** and **Step**, the **Rows waiting**, when it was **Requested** and by when to decide;
- **What to check**, the **Figures the step reported** and the **Rows to approve** (with **Fewer columns** / **All columns**);
- the **Report PDF** if one was made, and **Open the run**.

![An approval task, decided](apr-step-approval-done "Review › Approvals › Done: the wound measurement approval, with the rows the step held")

## Decide it
1. Open the task from **Review › Approvals**, or open the run: **Next steps** at the top holds the same decision.
2. Choose **Approve**, with an optional note of **What you checked**: the run continues in a moment.
3. Or choose **Reject**, say why, and press **Reject** again: the run fails in a moment, and its message carries your
   reason, such as *Rejected by Claire Martin: Every line unmatched*.

The decision is recorded in **Review › Approvals** as yours. A pipeline set to **Requires individual review** keeps its
Approval steps out of bulk decisions too.

## Example
In *Journey 7 · Wound photo*, step 10 *Wound care approves the measurement* waits for the Wound care team with the task
*Wound SV-000117: area in cm²*. Sam Harper checks the measurement against the photo and approves it: *Measurement checked
against the photo*. The run goes on and makes one wound report per photo.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Decide within | 1 to 720 hours (default 72); not decided in time, the run fails |
| What to check | 2,000 characters |
| Task title | 200 characters |

articles.title: Two-party review: your team, then your customer
articles.summary: A run's results that both your team and your customer (through the API) must approve; how the two decisions combine.
articles.who: Workspace administrators turn it on and decide your team's part; the customer decides theirs through the API
articles.md:
Some results are checked twice: by your own team, and by the organisation you work for, from its own portal. A partner lab's
results, a payer's claim file or a referral answered for another hospital can need both. A pipeline can ask for both
reviews; the run's results count only when both have approved.

![A pipeline's Review settings](apr-review-settings "A pipeline's Settings › Review: Results need review by Our team and The customer (through the API), and individual review")

## Turn it on
1. Open the pipeline under **Build › Pipelines** and go to **Settings**.
2. Under **Review**, in **Results need review by**, tick **Our team** and **The customer (through the API)**.
3. Save. Each run's results now start as waiting for review.

## How the two decisions combine
| Your team | The customer | The run's results |
|---|---|---|
| Not decided | Not decided | Waiting for review |
| Approved | Not decided | Still waiting, for the customer |
| Approved | Approved | **Approved** |
| Rejected | (either) | **Rejected**: the other side need not decide |
| (either) | Rejected | **Rejected** |

- **Your team** decides in the console, like any run review: in **Review**, or on the run's page under **Next steps**
  ([Review a run's results](#apr-run-review)). A workspace administrator records it.
- **The customer** decides through the customer API, from its own systems, with a client allowed to write reviews. The
  console cannot record the customer's decision, and the customer cannot record yours.
- Each side decides once. Either order works; in practice your team checks first.
- A run started through the API can be run again on the customer's rejection, with the same input.

> **Note:** The customer's part is never decided in bulk. Your team's part can be, under the workspace's bulk review rules
> (see [Decide many at once](#apr-bulk)).

## Example
A partner's portal starts *Partner answers the customer review* through the API with a batch of results. Dr. Anika
Patel approves the internal review in Summit Valley's **Review**; the partner's system then sends its own approval, and the
run's results read **approved**, with both decisions in its review.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Who records your team's decision | A workspace administrator (or a reviewer through their task) |
| Who records the customer's decision | The customer, through the API only |
| Decisions | One per side; final once the results are approved or rejected |

articles.title: Design an approval workflow
articles.summary: The designer's steps (approvals, tasks, conditions, notifications, Run pipeline, Call API, Save to dataset, Wait), deadlines, reminders and escalation, publishing and versions.
articles.who: Workspace administrators design, publish and test workflows; anyone whose page access includes Approval workflows reads them
articles.popular: Build an approval workflow
articles.md:
An **approval workflow** lays out who approves, what is checked and what runs, step by step, for a kind of request: a
purchase, a leave request, a bed request, or a whole patient's journey. A request is started by a person, a form, a
pipeline or the API, and walks the workflow's steps; its history records every decision.

![The workflow designer](apr-designer "Build › Approval workflows: the Patient journey, an approval step selected, its settings on the right")

## Make a workflow
1. Open **Build › Approval workflows** and choose **New workflow**.
2. Give it a **Name**, a **Key** (how other screens and the API name it; it cannot change later), **What it approves** (a
   word for the thing requested: request, purchase, form) and a **Description**.
3. Choose **Create and design**. The canvas opens with **Request starts** and **Request ends**.
4. **Add a step**, pick its kind, and fill its settings on the right. **Up**, **Down** and **Add after** place it.
5. Choose **Publish version N** at the foot of the canvas, with an optional note of **What changed**.

## The kinds of step
| Step | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Approval** | Someone approves, rejects or asks for changes |
| **Task** | Someone does a piece of work and marks it done |
| **Condition** | Goes one of two ways on the request's fields |
| **Notify** | Tells someone, and goes on |
| **Run pipeline** | Starts a schedule's run |
| **Call API** | Sends a saved API request and keeps its answer to branch on |
| **Save to dataset** | Keeps the request as a row |
| **Wait** | Pauses for some hours |

## Approvals and tasks: deadlines, reminders, escalation
- **Who approves** (or **Who does it**): see [Who decides](#apr-who-decides).
- **Due in (hours)**: the deadline; blank is no due time. **Remind before (hours)** sends a reminder before it is due.
- **When overdue, it goes to**: whom an overdue task escalates to, by default the requester's manager.
- **A rejection needs a reason**, and **If rejected**: *The request ends, rejected*, or go to another step.
- **Keep the decision as** (optional): a name, such as `nurse`, under which the request keeps the decision. Later steps
  read `nurse.decision` (`approved`, `rejected` or `changes_requested`; `done` for a task), `nurse.byName` (who
  decided), `nurse.at` (when) and `nurse.comment` (their comment, empty when none): in a **Run pipeline** step's **Parameters** as `{{nurse.byName}}`, or in a **Condition** on
  `nurse.decision`. The request's **History** shows what was kept. The name cannot be one another step already keeps
  its outcome under.

## Conditions
Pick a **Field of the request** (such as `amount`, or a value an earlier step kept, such as `careplan.risk`), a **Test**
(*is*, *is not*, *is more than*, *is at least*, *is less than*, *is at most*, *contains*, *is one of*, *is filled in*,
*is empty*) and a **Value**, then **If yes, go to** and **If no, go to**.

## Run a pipeline, call an API
- **Run pipeline**: pick the **Schedule to run** and its **Parameters**, from the request by name (`{{subject.mrn}}`) or an
  earlier step's kept value. Tick **Wait until the run ends, its approvals included** to go on only when it is done; then
  **Keep how it ended as** a name a condition can read, and **Keep values from its answer** (fields of its final output,
  such as `risk`). **Give up after (hours)**, and **If it cannot start or does not complete**: **Stop the request** or
  **Carry on**.
- **Call API**: pick a saved request from **Connections › API collections** (its secrets stay there), the **Environment**,
  the **Variables** and **Keep the answer as**; **If the call is not ok**: stop, or carry on and branch on the answer.
- **Save to dataset**: the **Dataset** the request is kept in, a row per request.
- **Wait**: the **Hours** to pause.
- At **Request ends**, **If the request ends here, it ends as**: *As its latest approval went*, *Approved*, *Rejected*,
  *Completed* or *Failed*.

## Publish, versions and test runs
- A change stays a draft until you publish it: *Version 5 is live. A change here stays a draft until you publish it.*
- Publishing makes a new version. Requests already running keep the version they started on.
- **Versions** lists each published version, the current one marked; **Load into the draft** starts from an older one.
- **Test run** starts a real request on the current version, as you, with a **Title**, a **Reference** and the request's
  fields as JSON. Its tasks go to the people the steps name.
- **Make inactive** stops new requests; **Make active** allows them again.

![A workflow's versions](apr-versions "The Versions tab: each published version, the current one marked")

> **Note:** Five workflows are **Built in**, made by the platform for features that rely on them: *Data access request*,
> *Pipeline run review*, *Pipeline step approval*, *Report approval* and *Signature or stamp approval*. Your workspace may
> still change them.

> **Tip:** Pass the approver to a report: Riverside Health's *Patient intake · intake review* keeps the nurse's approval
> as `nurse`, then runs the summary pipeline with `reviewed_by` = `{{nurse.byName}}`, `reviewed_at` = `{{nurse.at}}` and
> `review_note` = `{{nurse.comment}}`, so the signed PDF names who reviewed it. See
> [Patient intake](#rcp-patient-intake--7-the-approval-workflow).

## Example
Summit Valley's *Patient journey* has 16 steps: run *Registration*, a condition on `registration.eligible`, a nurse
triage task for Ward 4B nursing, run the *Care-plan draft* and keep `careplan`, the attending physician's approval (due in
4 hours, a reminder 2 hours before), a condition *High risk in the care plan* that asks a senior physician too, the medication
safety check, discharge and the signed discharge packet, and a row in the *journey-stages* dataset. Version 5 is live; a
patient admitted on version 1 finished on version 1.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Values kept from a pipeline's answer | Up to 16 KB; masked columns stay masked |
| Who designs and publishes | A workspace administrator |
| A workflow's key | Cannot change after it is made |

articles.title: Who decides: people, roles, teams and managers
articles.summary: A person, a role, a team or the requester's manager; team leads and members; passing a task on; decisions made for someone who is away.
articles.who: Workspace administrators make teams, name their leads and set managers; a team's lead adds and removes its members
articles.md:
Each approval or task names who decides it. Name a team or a role rather than one person where you can: the work still
gets done when someone is busy or away, and the team's lead keeps its members current.

## The choices
In a workflow step's **Who approves** (or **Who does it**), and in **When overdue, it goes to**:

| Choice | Who gets the task |
|---|---|
| **The requester's manager** | The manager set on the requester's user, under **Administration › Users** |
| **The requester** | The person who started the request (for a task such as *add the receipts*) |
| **A person** | One named person |
| **Everyone with a role** | **Administrators** or **Any member** of the workspace |
| **Everyone in a team** | The members of a team |

![An approval step's Who approves](apr-approval-settings "An approval step's settings: Everyone with a role, Administrators, due in 48 hours, overdue to the requester's manager")

A step can also take its reviewers from what starts the request: a pipeline's run review asks the reviewers its settings
name.

> **Note:** No one approves their own request: someone else decides it. When a step's people cannot decide it, the request
> goes to the administrators, and its history says *went to the administrators*.

## Teams
1. Open **Administration & billing › Administration › Teams** and choose **New team**.
2. Give it a **Name** (such as *Wound care nurses*) and an optional **Description**, and choose **Make team**.
3. **Add a person** to add members. An administrator names the team's lead.
4. **Where it is used** shows the workflows, approvals, alerts and Report Studio approvals that name the team.
5. **Archive team** when it is no longer needed: nothing new goes to it, and its history keeps its name.

![Administration › Teams](apr-teams "Administration › Teams: each team with its lead, its members and where it is used")

- A team's **lead** adds and removes its members; an administrator names its leads. A team without a lead is changed only
  by an administrator.
- A person can be in many teams. Teams open no pages: page access does that.
- More on teams: [Teams](#adm-teams).

![Review › Approvals › My teams](apr-approvals "Review › Approvals › My teams: a task for the IT team, with Mark done and Pass on")
- In **Review › Approvals**, **My teams** lists the tasks of the teams you are in; **See who is in your teams** opens the
  team page.

## Managers
On a user's page under **Administration › Users**, **Manager** is whom their workflow approvals go to when a step says
*their manager*, and whom their overdue tasks escalate to.

## Pass a task on
In **Review › Approvals**, open the task, choose **Pass on**, pick the person in **Pass it to**, add a note if you like, and
confirm. The history says *passed by* you *to* them.

## When someone is away
A decision made for someone else shows both names in the request's history: *approved by Dr. Minh Nguyen (for Dr. Anika
Patel)*. How a stand-in is set, and its rules, are in [Out of office](#adm-out-of-office).

## Example
In Summit Valley's *Patient journey*, the attending physician's approval goes to **A person**, Dr. Anika Patel, with a
four-hour deadline; when she is away, Dr. Minh Nguyen decides for her. When the care plan's risk is *High*, a second
approval goes to the **Senior physicians** team, and the nurse triage task to **Ward 4B nursing**. Kevin Lee's
expense claims go to **The requester's manager**, Claire Martin, and escalate to her when overdue.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Who makes teams and names leads | A workspace administrator |
| Who changes a team's members | Its lead, or an administrator |
| Teams per person | Many |

articles.title: Start and follow a request
articles.summary: New request from a published workflow, the request's details and history, asking for changes, and cancelling a request.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes the Task inbox; the workflows you may start are those an administrator published for people to start
articles.md:
A **request** is one walk through an approval workflow: a transfer to another hospital, a leave request, a capital
purchase. **My requests** lists what you asked for, newest first, and where each stands. Requests also start from a form
that names a workflow, from a pipeline, or from the API; they show here for whoever started them.

![My requests, one request open](apr-my-requests "My requests: a Hospice eligibility request, its details and its history")

## Start a request
1. Open **Review › Approvals** and its **My requests** tab, and choose **New request**.
2. Pick the **Workflow**. Only published, active workflows that a person may start are offered.
3. Give it a **Title**: what the request is, in a few words.
4. Under **What it is about**, **Add a field** for each value the workflow needs, as a name and a value
   (`amount` and `12500`, `patient.mrn` and `SV-000204`).
5. Choose **Start the request**. Its first step opens at once, and the people it names see a task in **Review**.

![New request](apr-new-request "New request: pick the workflow, give the request a title, add what it is about")

> **Tip:** A workflow that needs many fields is easier to start from a form: build the form in **Forms**, and say there which
> workflow its submissions start.

## Follow a request
Open the request in **My requests**:
- the header says its state (*Running*, *Approved*, *Rejected*, *Failed*, *Cancelled*), the workflow and its version, and
  when it started and ended;
- **Request details** shows what it is about;
- **History** says every step in words: *Requested by …*, *waiting for the team · due …*, *approved by …*, *yes* or *no*
  for a condition, *started run #2051* for a pipeline, *saved to dataset …*, *overdue, escalated to …*, *Request approved*.
  A decision's comment shows under it.

Search the list, or narrow it with **Any status** and **Any workflow**.

## When changes are asked for
An approver may **Ask for changes**, with a comment saying what should change. The request shows *Changes asked*; the history
carries the comment.

## Cancel a request
Open it and choose **Cancel request**, then confirm. The history says *Cancelled by* you, and its open tasks are no longer
needed.

## Example
Summit Valley's administrator starts *Hospice eligibility* for patient SV-000310, with the patient's record number as its
only field. In **My requests** the history shows *Gather the documents: done by Tamara Brooks*, then *A physician decides:
approved by Dr. Anika Patel*, each with its note, and *Request approved*.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Which workflows you may start | Published, active, this workspace's own, started by a person |
| Who decides your request | Never you: someone else, as the workflow names |

articles.title: Decide many at once
articles.summary: Approve or reject several runs, tasks or documents in one deliberate step; what is checked first, what is skipped and why, and the workspace's rules.
articles.who: Anyone who may decide the items; whether runs and documents may be approved in bulk is a workspace administrator's choice
articles.popular: Approve or reject several items at once
articles.md:
When many items wait for the same decision (a morning's lab results, a batch of invoices that all matched), decide them
together. Each item is still decided on its own, by exactly the rules of a single decision, and recorded on its own with
your name; the console only gathers them, shows you first what will happen, and reports item by item.

![Two documents selected in Review](apr-review-selected "Review › All waiting with two documents ticked: the bar offers Reject and Approve")

## Decide several at once
1. Open **Run & review › Review** (**All waiting**, or one kind's tab).
2. Tick the items, or tick the header to **Select everything shown that you may decide**. With a full page ticked, the bar
   offers to select every match, not just this page.
3. Choose **Approve** or **Reject** in the bar.
4. The panel first checks each item and lists what will be done, **By** source, and what **Will be skipped**, each with
   its reason.
5. Add a **Comment**: one comment is applied to each item. It is required to reject (*Say why these are rejected*) and
   optional to approve.
6. Above 25 items, **Type N to confirm**: say how many, so a decision this wide is never one click.
7. Confirm. The answer lists every item: done, skipped with its reason, or failed with its message.

> **Tip:** If sending fails, **Try again** sends the same decision: an item already recorded is not recorded twice.

## Why an item is skipped
| Reason | What to do |
|---|---|
| *Already decided* | Nothing: someone decided it first |
| *Not yours to decide* | It waits for someone else |
| *The pipeline requires individual review* | Open it and decide it on its own |
| *Bulk approve is off in this workspace* | Approve it one by one, or ask an administrator |
| *The run is not completed (failed, or still running)* | Only a completed run's results can be approved |
| *Cannot be approved as it stands* | A document with a failing rule: open it and correct it |
| *Changed since it was listed* | Refresh and look again |
| *Not an approval* | A task step: open it to do it |

## The workspace's rules
Under **Administration & billing › Administration › Data policies › Bulk review**, a workspace administrator chooses:
- **Allow bulk approve of runs**: off, runs are approved one by one on their page or in Review;
- **Allow bulk approve of documents**, and **Include documents whose rules fail** (off by default: a document with a failing
  rule is skipped and approved on its own screen; on, the failures are accepted and the override is recorded on each).

Documents have their own bulk screen too: [Review many documents at once](#doc-bulk-review). Rejecting in bulk is
always allowed. A pipeline can require individual review in its **Settings**, which keeps its runs and
its Approval steps out of every bulk decision. A customer's decision in a two-party review is never taken in bulk.

## Retry several failed runs
**Runs › Failed** uses the same bar to retry several failed runs from their failed steps: see
[When something fails](#run-failures).

## Example
At 08:00 Claire Martin has 18 supplier invoices that matched their purchase orders waiting in **Review › Documents**. She
ticks them, chooses **Approve**, reads that 17 will be approved and one skipped (*Cannot be approved as it stands*: a total
that does not add up), adds *Matched to PO, checked by CM*, and confirms. She opens the skipped one on its own.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Items in one bulk decision | 100 |
| Typed confirmation | Above 25 items |
| Comment | 500 characters, applied to each item |

articles.title: How usage is counted
articles.summary: Every meter in plain words, what each counts and in what unit, how meters roll up into services, the rate card, and the workspace's billing time zone.
articles.who: Workspace administrators read their workspace's usage and bills
articles.md:
Everything the workspace uses is **metered** as it happens: each run, each model call, each page read, each file kept.
Each meter is priced from the workspace's **rate card**, and **Cost & usage** shows the month as the invoice will read
it. This article lists the meters, so a line on a bill can be traced back to what made it.

## The meters
Each line on **Cost & usage** and on an invoice is one meter: its name, and under it its code in small type.

| Meter | Service | What it counts | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pipeline runs** | Pipelines | Each run of a pipeline | run |
| **Worker minutes** | Pipelines | Time a run's steps spent working | minute |
| **Kafka topics** | Pipelines | Topics the workspace keeps, by the hour | topic-hour |
| **Model tokens in** | Model calls | Text sent to a model: prompts, documents, questions | per 1,000 tokens |
| **Model tokens out** | Model calls | Text a model wrote back | per 1,000 tokens |
| **Images described** | Model calls | Each image a vision model looked at | image |
| **Transcript minutes** | Model calls | Minutes of audio turned into text | minute |
| **Pages read (OCR)** | Analytics & tools | Each page the platform's text reader read | per 1,000 pages |
| **Documents converted** | Analytics & tools | Each document converted, each PDF made from a dataset or a run, each report version generated | document |
| **Analytics queries** | Analytics & tools | Each query of a file, in Analytics Studio or by a dashboard widget | query |
| **Analytics data scanned** | Analytics & tools | The data those queries read | GB |
| **Storage kept** | Storage | The data kept in the workspace's storage, measured nightly | GB-hour |
| **Bytes written**, **Bytes read** | Storage | Data written to and read from storage | GB |
| **Bytes deleted (data churn)** | Storage | Data deleted from storage | GB |
| **Storage reads**, **Storage writes**, **Storage deletes** | Storage | Each operation on a stored file | per 1,000 operations |
| **API calls** | API | Each call your systems make to the API | per 1,000 calls |
| **Webhook deliveries** | API | Each webhook delivery that reaches your receiver | per 1,000 deliveries |
| **Seats** | Seats | Each person in the workspace, by the day | user-day |

The prices are not in this table because they are your account's: they come from your workspace's rate card, and
**Cost & usage** shows the rate beside every line.

## Services
Meters roll up into six services, each with its own colour on every chart: **Storage**, **Model calls**,
**Pipelines**, **Analytics & tools**, **API** and **Seats**. **By service** on **Cost & usage** adds them up.

## The rate card
A rate card is a list of prices, kept in versions by our team. The chip **Priced with** at the top of **Cost & usage**
names the card and version that prices your workspace (for example *Standard 2026 v2*). A card may also have
**allowances and tiers** (an amount included, or a lower price past a threshold) and **pricing rules** (another price
for one pipeline, a pipeline tag or a data class); a line priced by a rule says so.

> **Note:** A price change is a new version of the card with a date it starts from. An invoice already issued keeps the
> version that priced it.

## Your billing time zone
Days and months are counted in your workspace's **billing time zone**: a day runs from midnight to midnight there, and
a month is a calendar month there. **Cost & usage** shows it in the chip **Days in** (for example *America/Chicago*,
the default), and the invoice prints it beside its period. The API's monthly quota counts the same month. Our team
sets the zone; ask your account team to change it.

## Example
At Summit Valley Health System, one run of *Journey 7 · Wound photo: measure, describe* bills a **Pipeline run**, the
**Model tokens in** and **out** of its prompt, an **Image described** for the wound photo, and **Storage writes** for
the files it keeps. The run's own line under **By run** on **Cost & usage** adds them up.

articles.title: Read Cost & usage
articles.summary: The month so far and its forecast, cost by day and by service, every line and what is behind it, cost by pipeline and by run, AI model calls, and the trends over months.
articles.who: Workspace administrators
articles.popular: See what a pipeline costs
articles.md:
**Cost & usage** shows what the workspace used this month and what it costs: the same lines the invoice will carry.
Usage is rolled up every few minutes, so it follows the runs as they finish.

## The top of the page
1. Open **Administration & billing › Billing › Cost & usage**.
2. Pick the month with the arrows beside it (**Previous month**, **Next month**). **Export CSV** saves the lines.
3. The chips say what prices the month: **Priced with** the rate card and version, the currency, **Day** so far of the
   month, **Yesterday**'s cost, and **Days in** your billing time zone.
4. The four figures: **Month to date** (with a forecast at the last week's pace, and last month's total), **Data
   deleted** (with the delete operations and their churn), **Storage kept** (the average of the nights measured) and
   **Seats**.

![Cost & usage](bill-cost "Cost & usage: the rate card and time zone, the month so far, Cost by day and By service")

## By day and by service
- **Cost by day** draws each day's cost by service, before the month's allowances and tiers. Switch between **Daily**
  and **Cumulative**; the dotted **Forecast pace** shows where the month is heading. **Click a day for its lines.**
- **By service** adds the month up by service, then shows **Days added up, before allowances**, **Allowances and
  tiers**, and **Month to date, as the invoice lists it**.

## Line by line
**Line by line** lists each meter with its **Service**, **Quantity**, **Rate** and **Amount**. Lines under a cent are
folded away; **Show N lines under a cent** opens them. Choose a line to see what is behind it: which bucket, which
prompt, which API client, who deleted what, with the number of events and when the last was. A line priced by a
pricing rule shows that rule's part beneath it.

## Cost by pipeline and by run
**Cost by pipeline** splits the month into **From pipeline runs** and **Not tied to a run** (storage kept, analytics,
the console's reads, API calls).

1. **By pipeline** lists each pipeline with its **Runs**, **Cost**, **Per run**, **Share** of the month and what it was
   **Spent on** (for example *mostly model tokens*). **Show all** opens the rest.
2. Choose a pipeline, or its **Runs** button, to fill **By run** below with its runs.
3. **By run** lists each run, grouped by day, with when it **Started**, its **Status**, **What it cost** by meter and
   its **Cost**. Search by pipeline, schedule or run, or pick a status. **Open the run** goes to the run's page.

![Cost by pipeline](bill-pipelines "Cost by pipeline: from runs and not tied to a run, each pipeline's runs, cost and share, and By run")

## AI model calls
**AI model calls** counts the **Calls**, **Tokens in**, **Tokens out** and **Cost at model rates**, with the rates it
used:

- **By source**: what called a model, the dearest first, with its model, calls,
  pipeline runs, tokens, cost, share and last call. **By model** adds them up per model.
- **Every call**: each call with its time, what called it, its pipeline run and who.

![AI model calls](bill-model-calls "AI model calls: calls, tokens and cost at model rates, by source and by model")

## Trends over months
**Administration & billing › Billing › Analytics** shows the last 3, 6 or 12 months: the total, this month so far,
the largest service and the costliest pipeline, **Cost by month** coloured by service, and **By service** and **By
pipeline** for the period.

> **Note:** Figures on **Cost & usage** before a month closes are a running estimate of the invoice, not a bill. The
> invoice for a month is made once it is over in your billing time zone. See [Invoices](#bill-invoices).

## Example
At the start of November, Claire Martin, controller at Summit Valley Health System, opens October on **Cost & usage**:
*Model calls* is 98% of the month. **By pipeline** shows *Patient statements, one per guarantor* as the costliest, and
**AI model calls** shows the prompt behind it. She exports the lines to CSV for the finance pack.

articles.title: Estimate a backfill's cost
articles.summary: Before a backfill starts, see how many runs it makes and what they should cost, worked out from the schedule's recent runs; afterwards, compare with what was billed.
articles.who: Workspace administrators see the estimate; whoever may run the schedule starts the backfill
articles.md:
A **backfill** runs a schedule once for each day (hour or week) of a past range, a few at a time: catching up a quarter
of files, or redoing a month after a fix. Because it can make many runs at once, the console shows a **cost estimate**
before it starts, and what was billed so far while it runs.

## See the estimate before you start
1. Open **Build › Pipelines › Schedules & triggers**, open the schedule's ⋯ menu and choose **Backfill…** (it is also
   on the schedule's runs and in its editor).
2. Under **Range**, pick the **Dates** (counted in your billing time zone) and **One run per**: **Day**, **Hour** or
   **Week**. Under **How it runs**, pick how many run **At once**.
3. Leave **Run again the periods that already have a completed run** off to skip the periods already done.
4. Read the **Preview**: how many runs **will run**, how many are **already done, skipped**, the periods in all, the
   dates, and any warnings.
5. Read the **Cost estimate**: about how much in all, and the cost of a run on average, with what it is worked out
   from.
6. **Start** (it names the number of periods, for example **Start: 14 days**) begins it; **Cancel** closes the panel
   and starts nothing.

> **Note:** A schedule that is switched off cannot be backfilled: the preview says *The schedule is switched off;
> switch it on to backfill it.*

![A backfill's estimate](bill-backfill "Backfill: the periods, how many run at once, the preview and the cost estimate")

## How the estimate is worked out
The estimate is the average cost of the schedule's runs billed in the last 30 days (or, with none, the pipeline's),
times the number of runs the backfill will make. It reads, for example: *The average of 25 billed run(s) of this
schedule in the last 30 days x 90 run(s).* With no billed run to go by, it says there is nothing to estimate from.

> **Note:** An estimate is not a price. The runs are billed like any run, for what they actually use: a run that reads
> a bigger file, or calls a model more, costs more.

## Compare it with what was billed
1. Open **Run & review › Runs › Backfills** and choose the backfill.
2. Its page shows the **Estimate** it started with, and **Billed so far**: what its runs cost to date, and how many of
   its runs are priced yet. Usage is rolled up every few minutes, so the last runs catch up shortly after they end.

## Example
At Summit Valley Health System, Marcus Owens backfills *Denials by month* over the last quarter: daily periods,
**3** at once. The preview says 90 runs will run, and the estimate is the average of the schedule's recent billed runs
times 90. Jordan Reyes reads it before Marcus starts, and checks **Billed so far** on the backfill's page the next day.

articles.title: Invoices, credit notes and paying
articles.summary: The month's running draft, the issued invoice with its lines frozen, credit notes, paying by card or with a payment slip, and receipts.
articles.who: Workspace administrators
articles.popular: Pay an invoice
articles.md:
Each month closes into an **invoice**. Until the month is over in your billing time zone, its invoice is a **draft**,
rebuilt from the meter as the month goes on. Once the month is over it is **issued**: its lines are frozen with the rate
card version that priced them, and its PDF is made.

## Find an invoice
1. Open **Administration & billing › Billing › Invoices**.
2. The figures at the top count what is **Overdue**, **Open**, the **Slips to verify** and what is **Paid**.
3. The list on the left holds every invoice and credit note, newest first, with its number, month, state and amount.
   Search with **Find a number, workspace, month**, or pick a state.
4. Choose one. Its lines, documents and payments open on the right, with a QR code of its number for the printed page.

![An invoice](bill-invoice "This month's running draft: its period and total, and one line per meter with its quantity, rate and amount")

## What an invoice shows
- Its number, its state (**Draft**, **Issued**, **Overdue** with the days, **Paid**), and the rate card version.
- **Billed to**: your billing profile (name, address, tax number). **Period**: the month, in your billing time zone.
  **Total**, and when it was issued and is due.
- **Lines**: one per meter, with **Qty**, **Rate** and **Amount**. A line may say what it includes at no charge, or
