  that a pricing rule priced it. A draft says *A running draft — rebuilt from the meter until it is issued*.
- **Subtotal**, **Paid**, **Credited** and **Balance**.
- **Documents**: the invoice PDF once issued, the payment slips, receipts and credit notes.
- **Payments**: each payment, its method, reference, who sent it and its state.

**PDF** views or downloads the invoice; the ⋯ menu has **View PDF** and **Download PDF**.

## Pay an invoice
- **Pay now** (when card payment is on): pay by card on the payment provider's secure page. The payment counts as soon
  as the provider confirms it.
- **Upload payment slip**: for a bank transfer, upload the slip with the amount, the date and your reference. It shows
  as awaiting verification and counts once our team has seen the money arrive; a receipt is issued then.

If the last card payment failed, the invoice says so and why: try another card with **Pay now**, or upload a slip.

> **Privacy:** Card details are entered on the payment provider's own page, never in the console.

## Credit notes and receipts
- A **credit note** takes an amount off an issued invoice, with a reason. It has its own number (for example
  *CN-2026-09-0002*), is listed beside the invoice it is against, and lowers that invoice's balance.
- A **receipt** is issued for each verified payment. It is a PDF **Signed** with the platform's certificate; choose
  **Signed** to verify it.

Issuing an invoice, adding a manual line, crediting and voiding are our team's; ask your account team if a bill looks
wrong.

## Your billing profile
On **Invoices**, ⋯ › **Billing profile** sets who the invoice is made out to: **Legal name**, **Address**, **Billing email**, **Tax
number (VAT / GST)** (left empty, no tax is applied), the **Tax rate %** and its **Tax label**, the **Currency** and the
**Payment terms (days)**.

## Example
On 1 October, Summit Valley Health System's September invoice is issued: $25.00 on the *Standard 2026* card, due in
30 days. A duplicate conversion run is credited with a $5.00 credit note. Claire Martin uploads the bank transfer's
slip for the $20.00 balance; once it is verified, a signed receipt appears under **Documents** and the invoice is
**Paid**.

articles.title: Billing documents and statements
articles.summary: Every invoice, receipt, payment slip, credit note and statement in one place; a statement for the year; and checking that a receipt is genuine.
articles.who: Workspace administrators
articles.md:
**Billing documents** keeps every billing PDF of the workspace together: invoices, receipts, payment slips, credit
notes and statements. Pick one on the left to read it on the right.

## Find a document
1. Open **Administration & billing › Billing › Billing documents**.
2. The figures at the top count the year's **Documents**, **Invoices** (and how much was invoiced), **Receipts** (and
   how much was received) and **Payment slips**.
3. Narrow the list with **Find a number, file, person**, a kind (**All kinds**, or one) and the **Year**.
4. Choose a document. It opens beside the list, page by page, with **Download**; ⋯ › **Open in a new tab** shows it on
   its own.

![Billing documents](bill-documents "Billing documents: every bill, receipt, slip, credit note and statement, with a statement open")

## Statements
A **statement** lists what was issued in its range, oldest first, in your billing days: each invoice, each payment
against it, each credit note, then what was **Invoiced**, **Credited** and **Paid** (net of refunds), the **Balance
open**, and any credit owed to you.

To make one, pick the **Year** and choose **Statement 2026** (the button names the year) at the top of **Billing
documents**, or, on **Invoices**, ⋯ › **Statement for this year**. It is added to the list.

## Check that a receipt is genuine
Receipts are signed with the platform's certificate.

1. Choose **Verify a receipt** at the top of the page, and give it the receipt's PDF.
2. The console says whether the file is a receipt this platform issued, unchanged since it was signed.

An open receipt has **Verify signature** above it, which checks its digital signature, hash and certificate on the
spot.

## Example
For its year-end audit, Summit Valley Health System's controller Claire Martin makes the statement for 2026: the
September invoice, two bank payments against it and the credit note, with a balance open of zero. She downloads it
with the two signed receipts and checks one with **Verify a receipt** before sending the pack to the auditors.

articles.title: What is not billed
articles.summary: The sandbox, retries that reuse what was done, refused API calls, tokens and signed links, and work that was never done.
articles.who: Workspace administrators
articles.md:
Usage is billed for work the platform actually did for your workspace. Some things look like work but are not billed,
or are not billed twice. This list helps when a bill is lower than expected, or when you plan how to test.

## Never billed
| What | Why |
|---|---|
| Everything in your **sandbox** | Test keys work only in the sandbox, and a sandbox is never billed. Its **Cost & usage** prices the usage to show what it would cost, marked **Sandbox · never billed**, but it is never drafted or invoiced. |
| An API call refused for a limit | Past a rate limit or the monthly quota the API answers *429*: nothing was done, and nothing is billed. |
| Getting a token | The token call is not counted as an API call. |
| Reading through a signed link | Downloading a file, or a run view reading its run, through a signed link is not counted as an API call. |
| A webhook delivery that never arrived | Only deliveries that reach your receiver are billed. |

## Not billed twice
| What | Why |
|---|---|
| Retrying a run from the failed step | The steps before it are not run again: their kept outputs are reused, and not billed again. |
| Retrying failed items | Only the retried items run again; the others are neither called nor billed again. |
| A report a retry did not need to remake | A report already made for the same row, design and settings is reused, not made or billed again. |
| Sending the same API request twice | With the same Idempotency-Key, the second answer is the first result; nothing new is done. |

> **Note:** **Run again from the start** runs every step again, and every step is billed again. Prefer **Retry from the
> failed step** when the earlier steps' outputs are still good.

## Billed, though it may look free
- **The console's own reads** of your files (opening a file, a dashboard's widgets) are billed as storage reads and
  analytics queries, like any other read.
- **Deleting data** is billed as data churn (**Bytes deleted (data churn)**) and storage deletes.
- **Storage kept** is measured every night, whether or not anything ran.

## Example
Before going live, Summit Valley Health System's developers ran the partner portal's calls in the sandbox for a week.
**Cost & usage** for the real workspace did not move. When a run of *Denials by month* failed at its last step and was
retried from that step, only that step's work appeared again on the month's lines.

articles.title: Connect your storage
articles.summary: Add an S3, MinIO, Azure Blob, FTP or FTPS connection, test it, and choose which one the file drop uses.
articles.who: Workspace administrators (the Storage tab is theirs alone)
articles.popular: Connect your storage
articles.md:
A storage connection is a bucket or a server folder that this workspace's pipelines read from and write to: input
files, the results a run keeps, the files that arrive in the file drop, the reports it makes. Everything else in
**Get data in › Connections** builds on it, so a new workspace usually starts here.

**Connections** has six tabs:

| Tab | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **Connectors** | Ready-made connectors that sync a database, an app or a folder into your storage |
| **Storage** | Buckets and FTP servers (this article) |
| **Databases** | Read-only database connections |
| **API collections** | The APIs your pipelines call, with their sign-in and environments |
| **Sources** | What your pipelines read, and sources you test and preview |
| **Data contracts** | The shape the rows you receive must have |

![The Storage tab with four connections, each tested OK](con-storage "Connections › Storage: each connection's alias, provider, target, credentials and last test")

## Add a storage connection
1. Open **Get data in › Connections** and choose the **Storage** tab.
2. Choose **New storage connection**.
3. Pick the **Provider**: **MinIO**, **AWS S3**, **Azure Blob**, **FTP** or **FTPS**. The fields below change with it.
4. Give it a **Name** people will recognise and an **Alias**. The alias is how pipelines refer to the connection:
   letters, numbers, `.`, `_` and `-` only.
5. Fill in where the files are:
   - **AWS S3** and S3-compatible services: the **Bucket** (choose **Discover** to pick from the buckets the key can
     see), the **Region**, and an **Endpoint** only for an S3-compatible service that is not AWS.
   - **MinIO**: the **Endpoint** and the **Bucket**.
   - **Azure Blob**: the **Container**, then either a **Connection string** or an **Account name** with its
     **Account key**.
   - **FTP** and **FTPS**: **Host**, **Port**, **Username**, **Password** and a **Base directory** everything is read
     relative to. Tick **Passive mode** if your server needs it; for FTPS, **Implicit TLS (port 990)**.
6. Give the credentials: **Access key** and **Secret key** for S3 and MinIO.
7. Leave **Status** at **Active** and choose **Create**.

![The New storage connection dialog with AWS S3 picked](con-storage-new "New storage connection: provider, name and alias, the bucket, and the keys")

> **Privacy:** Passwords, secret keys and connection strings are encrypted and never sent back to the browser. When you
> edit a connection, leave a secret field blank to keep the stored one. The **Credentials** column says **Stored** or
> **Not stored**.

> **Warning:** Plain **FTP** sends the user name and password unencrypted. Use **FTPS** or a bucket where you can.

## Test it
Open the connection's menu (⋮) and choose **Test connection**. The **Last test** column shows **OK** or **Failed**
with the time; hover over a failed test to read why. To test several at once, tick them and choose **Test selected**.

The tiles above the list count the connections **In service** (Active), **Tested OK**, **Failing** and **Untested**.
Test a connection after you create it and whenever its keys change.

## Copy, switch off or delete one
- **Clone…** copies everything from a connection except the bucket: give the copy a new name, a unique alias and its
  bucket. The stored keys come along, so the copy works at once.
- **Edit** and set **Status** to **Inactive** to stop pipelines using a connection without deleting it.
- **Delete** removes it. Pipelines that name its alias stop finding it, so check what uses it first.

## The file drop's connection, folder and size limit
Files people drop on **Documents › Intake › File drop** are stored in one of your storage connections, the
workspace's default place for arrivals. An administrator picks it under **Settings › Change** on the file drop:

- **Storage connection**: one of this workspace's own connections.
- **Where files land**: under `intake/` in that bucket, as `intake/<date>/<arrival>-<file name>`.
- **Size limit (MB)**: optional. Empty means the platform's own limit, which the dialog shows; a number lowers it for
  this workspace.

See [The file drop](#doc-file-drop) for the rest.

> **Tip:** Give each workspace its own bucket. A bucket shared between workspaces lets one workspace's runs write where
> another's read.

## Example
Summit Valley Health System keeps four S3 connections: **Summit Valley: files (default, inbox)** (alias
`summit-valley-s3`) takes the file drop's arrivals with a 25 MB limit; the clinical, finance and open-data files each
have a bucket of their own, so a pipeline that reads finance files never sees an X-ray.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Who may add, change, test or delete | Workspace administrators |
| Alias | Letters, numbers, `.` `_` `-`; unique in the workspace |
| Addresses | Endpoints must be public: see [What the console may call](#con-addresses) |
| File drop size | The platform's limit per file, or a lower one you set |

articles.title: Add a read-only database connection
articles.summary: Connect a PostgreSQL database that pipelines and sources may only read, and why the console never writes to it.
articles.who: Workspace administrators add, test and change connections; anyone whose page access includes Connections › Databases sees the list
articles.md:
A database connection lets a pipeline's **Read Database** step, or a database source, run a query against one of your
own databases. The console reads only: it connects read-only, accepts only a query that reads, and keeps what it reads
in your storage. Today a database connection is PostgreSQL.

![The Databases tab with one read-only PostgreSQL connection](con-databases "Connections › Databases: host and database, the user, whether a password is set, TLS and state")

## Add a connection
1. Ask your database team for a user that can only read the tables you need. This is the most important step: the
   console never needs more.
2. Open **Get data in › Connections › Databases** and choose **New connection**.
3. Fill in **Name**, **Host**, **Port** (5432 unless yours differs), **Database** and **User**.
4. Pick **TLS**: **Required**, **Preferred** or **Off**. Choose **Required** for any database outside your own network.
5. Type the **Password**. It is sealed as it arrives and never shown again.
6. Choose **Test connection**. The console connects and reads nothing; the dialog says whether it worked.
7. Choose **Create**.

![Editing a database connection: host, database, user, TLS and a stored password](con-database-dialog "The connection dialog: the password shows only as configured, with Replace")

To change the password later, open the connection (or **Edit or replace password** in its menu), choose **Replace**
and type the new one. Choose **Keep** to change your mind.

## What "read-only" means here
- **The connection reads.** The console opens it read-only and only to run a query.
- **The query reads.** A source's or a step's query is one statement that starts with `SELECT`, `WITH`, `VALUES` or
  `TABLE`. Anything else is refused before it runs.
- **The rows are capped.** A query returns at most the rows it asks for, so a preview never pulls a whole table.
- **Results go to your storage.** What a pipeline makes from the rows (a file, a report, a dataset) is written to the
  workspace's storage connections, never back to the database.

## Why the console never writes to your databases
Your databases are the systems your organisation runs on: the clinical record, the ledger, the shop. A pipeline that
could write to them could change a patient's chart or a balance by mistake, and nobody would see it in a review. So the
console has no step that writes to a customer database, and the user you give it should not be allowed to either. Its
results live in your storage, in datasets and in reports, where people review them first.

> **Tip:** If a system must receive a result, send it through that system's own API with an API collection and a
> **Call API** step, where the system checks what it accepts.

## Use it
- In a pipeline, add a **Read Database** step and pick the connection.
- On **Connections › Sources**, a source of kind **Database** names the connection and the query, so you can test it,
  preview its first rows and infer its schema. See [Sources and connectors](#con-sources).

## Example
Summit Valley's **Store systems (read-only)** connection signs in to the pharmacy shop database as `demo_reader`, a user
allowed `SELECT` and nothing else. The hourly pipeline "Pharmacy store orders from the shop database" reads the new
orders with a **Read Database** step and writes sales by store and category to the retail folder of its bucket.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Databases | PostgreSQL |
| Query | One statement starting with SELECT, WITH, VALUES or TABLE |
| Port | 1 to 65535 |
| Who may add, test, change or delete | Workspace administrators |
| Addresses | See [What the console may call](#con-addresses) |

articles.title: Make an API collection
articles.summary: A collection of APIs with the sign-in they share and the environments they run in; add requests, variables and secrets.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes API collections reads them; workspace administrators make and change them
articles.popular: Make an API collection
articles.md:
An API collection keeps the outside APIs your workspace calls in one place: each **API** (a request: its method,
address, parameters and body), the **default auth** they sign in with, and the **environments** whose variables fill
them in. Pipelines (**Read API**, **Enrich**, **Call API**), sources and the AI Assistant refer to an API here; they
never copy its settings, so a change is made once.

![The API collections list](con-api-collections "Connections › API collections: each collection's source, sensitivity, APIs, version and state")

## Make the collection
1. Open **Get data in › Connections › API collections** and choose **New collection**.
2. Give it a **Name** and a **Description**.
3. Pick a **Sensitivity**: **Public**, **Internal**, **Confidential** or **Restricted**. The workspace's data policy for
   that level applies to what its APIs return.
4. Leave **State** at **Active**. An inactive collection's APIs are not offered to new pipeline steps.
5. Under **Default auth**, choose the **Scheme** most of its APIs use. See
   [Authentication](#con-api-auth).
6. Choose **Create**. The collection opens on its **Overview**.

## Add an environment and its variables
An environment holds the values an API's `{{variables}}` take when it runs: a base address, a page size, a client id,
and the secrets.

1. Under **Environments**, choose **New environment** and name it, for example `Production` or `Sandbox`.
2. Tick **Default** to make a test and a pipeline step use it unless they name another.
3. Add a row per variable: its name (such as `baseUrl`) and its value. Tick **Secret** for a key, a password or a token.
4. Choose **Create**.

A secret is sealed when it arrives and never shown again: the list shows it as **••• configured**. To change it, open
**Edit or replace secrets** and choose **Replace**.

![An environment's variables](con-api-environments "Environments: the default one, with a base address per API family")

## Add an API
1. Choose **Add API**. A panel opens on the right.
2. Pick the **Method** and type the **URL**, using variables: `{{baseUrl}}/v1/orders`.
3. Give it a **Name** (and a **Folder** if the collection has folders) and a short **Description**.
4. Fill in the tabs it needs:
   - **Params**: query parameters. **Headers**: request headers. Write `{{name}}` to take a value from the environment.
   - **Auth**: usually **From the collection**.
   - **Body**: **None**, **JSON**, **Text**, **XML**, **Form (URL-encoded)**, **Multipart**, **Binary** or
     **GraphQL**, with a body template. **Multipart** and **Binary** can send a file from one of the workspace's storage
     connections.
   - **Schemas**: **Params schema** (the values a caller passes in), **Extract rules** (named values to pull from the
     answer) and **Assert rules** (checks a test and a run must pass).
   - **Settings**: **Timeout (seconds)**, **Retry attempts** (tries in all, on a timeout, a 429 or a 5xx answer),
     **Backoff (ms)**, **Paging** (see [Page through results](#con-api-paging)), and whether the AI Assistant may call
     it.
5. Choose **Save & test** to save it and make one real call, or **Save**. See [Test a request](#con-api-test).

![An API open in the side panel, with its parameters and the Test section](con-api-request "An API: method and URL, the tabs, and Test with the environment it uses")

> **Warning:** A credential is always a `{{variable}}`. A header or parameter whose name says it carries one
> (Authorization, token, api-key, password and the like) is refused when it holds a plain value: put the value in an
> environment as a secret and write `{{name}}` instead.

## Look after it
- The tiles count the **APIs**, how many are **Enabled**, the **Folders**, the **Environments** (and which is the
  default) and the **Version**.
- Untick an API's **Enabled** box, or choose **Disable** in its menu, to stop it being offered without deleting it.
- **Used by** lists every pipeline, source and AI tool that uses the collection's APIs. A delete that something still
  depends on is refused, and the console lists what uses it.
- **Edit details** changes the name, sensitivity, state and default auth.

## Example
Summit Valley's **Public health APIs** collection holds 17 keyless public APIs: FHIR patients and observations,
RxNorm, openFDA, ClinicalTrials.gov, the NPI registry and CDC PLACES. Its one environment, **Summit Valley**, sets
`fhirBase`, `fdaBase`, `rxnavBase` and the rest, so a request reads `{{fhirBase}}/Patient` and a new sandbox is one
more environment, not seventeen edited requests.

![A collection's overview](con-api-collection "A collection: its APIs, each with method, endpoint, auth, timeout and state")

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Timeout | 1 to 300 seconds; 30 by default |
| Retry attempts | 1 to 10 tries in all |
| Making, changing and testing | Workspace administrators |
| Where an API may point | Public addresses: see [What the console may call](#con-addresses) |

articles.title: How an API signs in
articles.summary: None, bearer token, basic, API key or OAuth2 client credentials, set once on the collection and kept as secrets.
articles.who: Workspace administrators
articles.md:
Most APIs want to know who is calling. In an API collection the sign-in is set once, as the collection's **Default
auth**, and each API either takes it (**From the collection**) or names its own scheme. The secret parts are never
typed into the scheme itself: they are `{{variables}}` whose values live in an environment, marked **Secret**.

## The schemes
| Scheme | What it sends | Its settings |
|---|---|---|
| **None** | No credentials | — |
| **Bearer token** | `Authorization: Bearer …` | **Token**, a secret such as `{{token}}` |
| **Basic** | A user name and password | **Username** and **Password** (a secret) |
| **API key** | A key in a header or a query parameter | **Header or parameter name** (such as `X-Api-Key`), **Value** (a secret) and **Sent in** (`header` or the query) |
| **OAuth2 client credentials** | A token it first fetches from your identity provider | **Token URL**, **Client id**, **Client secret** (a secret), and **Scope** and **Audience** when the provider wants them |

With OAuth2 client credentials the console asks the **Token URL** for a token with the client id and secret, then sends
that token with each call. You never paste a token that expires.

## Set the collection's default auth
1. Open the collection and choose **Edit details** (or set it while making a **New collection**).
2. Under **Default auth**, pick the **Scheme**.
3. Fill in its settings. Every secret field takes a variable, such as `{{clientSecret}}`.
4. Choose **Save changes**.
5. In each environment the collection uses, add the variables the scheme names, and tick **Secret** on the secret ones.
   See [Make an API collection](#con-api-collections--add-an-environment-and-its-variables).

![Default auth set to OAuth2 client credentials](con-api-auth "Edit collection: the default auth's scheme, with the client secret as a variable")

## Give one API its own scheme
1. Open the API and choose the **Auth** tab.
2. Pick a scheme in **Authentication**. **From the collection** is the usual choice; another scheme still reads its
   settings from the collection's details.
3. The tab shows what the API will sign in with and, per setting, whether its secret is **••• configured**, **not set**
   or **not in this environment**.

The collection's list shows each API's scheme in the **Auth** column, for example **None (from the collection)**.

> **Privacy:** Secret values are sealed as they arrive and never come back to the browser, not even to an
> administrator. A test's answer comes back masked. To change a secret, replace it; you cannot read it.

> **Tip:** Keep one environment per place you call (a sandbox and production), each with its own secrets, and make the
> sandbox the **Default** while you build.

## Example
Summit Valley's **Summit Valley platform API** collection signs in with **OAuth2 client credentials**: the **Token URL**
is `{{apiBase}}/v1/oauth/token` and the client id and secret are `{{clientId}}` and `{{clientSecret}}`, kept as
secrets in its environment. Its one API posts an event that starts the patient's journey. The public health APIs need
no sign-in, so that collection's default auth is **None**.

articles.title: Page through results
articles.summary: Page number, offset, cursor, Link header or a next URL in the answer; where the items are and when to stop.
articles.who: Workspace administrators
articles.md:
Many APIs answer a page at a time: 50 patients, then the next 50. Set an API's **Paging** once and every caller (a test,
a **Read API** step, a source) fetches page after page until there are no more, or until the most pages you allow.

## Set it up
1. Open the API and choose the **Settings** tab.
2. Pick the **Paging** mode the API's documentation describes (the table below).
3. Fill in the mode's fields. The panel says, under the mode, how it moves and when it stops.
4. Set **Items at**: where the list of items is in each answer, as a JSONPath from its root, such as `$.items` or
   `$.entry`.
5. Set **Most pages**, for example `10`, so a large answer cannot run on.
6. Choose **Save & test**, and read the test's line "N items over P pages".

![The Settings tab with Next URL in the answer](con-api-paging "Paging set to Next URL in the answer, with the JSONPath that finds the next page")

## The modes
| Mode | How it moves | What you fill in |
|---|---|---|
| **Page number** | Asks page 1, 2, 3… in a query parameter; stops on an empty or short page | **Page parameter** (`page`), **First page** (1), and if the API takes one a **Size parameter** (`limit`) with its **Page size** |
| **Offset** | Moves a skip parameter by the items received; stops at the total, or on an empty or short page | **Offset parameter** (`offset`), **First offset** (0), **Size parameter** and **Page size**, and optionally **Total at** (`$.meta.results.total`) |
| **Cursor** | Sends the cursor the last answer gave; stops when there is none | **Cursor parameter** (`cursor`) and **Next cursor at** (`$.next_cursor`) |
| **Link header** | Follows the `Link` header's `rel="next"`; stops when there is none | Nothing more |
| **Next URL in the answer** | Follows the next page's full address from the answer; stops when there is none | **Next URL at** (a JSONPath; filters work), or a **Next URL header** |

> **Note:** A next address stays on the first request's host. If the API sends you to another host for later pages,
> name it in **Other hosts** (host names only, comma-separated). Calls to another host are sent without this API's
> credentials.

## When something is wrong
The panel checks the settings before you save:

- A path starts with `$`, such as `$.items`.
- **Most pages**, a page size and a first page or offset are whole numbers.
- A **Size parameter** needs the **Page size** it sends.
- **Other hosts** are bare names, such as `api2.example.org`, without `https://` or a path.

If a test says "stopped at the page cap with more to fetch", there were more pages than **Most pages** allows. Raise it,
or narrow the request with a parameter.

## Examples
Summit Valley's public health APIs use four of the modes:

- **FHIR: patients** follows **Next URL in the answer** at `$.link[?(@.relation=='next')].url`, four pages at most in
  the "Patient 360 from the FHIR sandbox" pipeline.
- **openFDA: drug recalls** pages by **Offset** with `skip` and `limit` for the weekly drug-recall check.
- **ClinicalTrials.gov: studies** uses a **Cursor**, the answer's `nextPageToken`.
- The World Bank's health-spending indicators use **Page number** with `page` and `per_page`.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Most pages | A whole number, 1 or more |
| First page or offset | A whole number, 0 or more |
| Page size | A whole number, 1 or more |
| Other hosts | Public addresses only, sent without credentials |

articles.title: Test a request
articles.summary: Make one real call with an environment's values, and read the answer, its headers, what was extracted and the checks.
articles.who: Workspace administrators (a test calls the API with the workspace's secrets)
articles.md:
Before a pipeline depends on an API, try it. **Test**, at the foot of an API's panel, makes one real call through the
same runner a pipeline uses, with the environment's values and secrets, and shows what came back. Nothing is saved
except the API itself.

## Try a request
1. Open the API collection and choose the API's name. Its panel opens on the right.
2. Under **Test**, pick the **Environment**. The default one is chosen for you; **No environment** sends the request
   with no variables filled in.
3. To try other values once, open **Values for this test only** and add them: `fhir_id` = `example`. They are used for
   this call and not kept.
4. Choose **Test**. If you changed the API, the button says **Save & test** and saves it first.

![An API's panel with the Test section](con-api-request "Test: the environment, values for this test only, and the call's answer below")

## Read the answer
The first line sums the call up:

- **OK**, **Failed** or **Blocked**, then the HTTP status (`HTTP 200`), how long it took and the answer's size.
- How many attempts it took, when retries were needed.
- How many assertions passed, when the API has **Assert rules**.
- For a paged API, "N items over P pages", and whether it stopped at the page cap with more to fetch.

Below it, four tabs:

| Tab | Shows |
|---|---|
| **Body** | The first page's answer, formatted when it is JSON |
| **Headers** | The answer's headers |
| **Extracted** | The values the **Extract rules** pulled out |
| **Assertions** | Each **Assert rule**, passed or not, with the value found |

**Blocked** means the call was never sent: the address it would have reached is not one the console may call. See
[What the console may call](#con-addresses).

> **Privacy:** The answer is masked before it reaches the browser: nothing in it holds a secret the call used.

> **Warning:** A test is a real call. Testing a **POST**, **PUT**, **PATCH** or **DELETE** API changes the system it
> calls, as a run would. Test those against a sandbox environment.

## When a test fails
- **401 or 403**: the sign-in is wrong or missing. Check the **Auth** tab and the environment's secrets.
- **404**: the address is wrong; check the URL and the environment's base address.
- **Failed** with no status: the host did not answer in the **Timeout**, or could not be reached.
- An assertion failed: the API answered, but not as your rules expect; read the **Assertions** tab.

The collection's **Last test** column shows the status and time of each API you tested in this browser session; the
others say **not tested**.

## Example
Before switching the "Patient 360" pipeline to a new FHIR sandbox, Summit Valley's administrator opens **FHIR:
patients**, picks the sandbox environment and chooses **Test**: **OK**, `HTTP 200`, 100 items over four pages. The
**Body** tab shows the first page's patients, so the pipeline's **Items at** path is right before anything runs.

articles.title: Versions and pinning
articles.summary: Every save of a collection is a version; see who uses which, and pin a source to one so a later change cannot break it.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes API collections reads versions and Used by; workspace administrators change collections and sources
articles.md:
Every time a collection or one of its APIs is saved, the collection gets a new version: v1, v2, v3… The earlier ones are
kept. A caller either follows the **Latest** version or is **pinned** to one, so you can change an API without
surprising the pipelines that rely on it.

## See the versions
1. Open the collection. The **Version** tile and the line under its name show the current version.
2. Choose the **History** tab. Each version is listed with when it was saved; the newest is marked **current**.

![A collection's History tab](con-api-history "History: every save kept as a version, the newest marked current")

## See who uses which version
On the collection's **Overview**, **Used by** lists each pipeline, source and AI tool that calls one of its APIs:

| Column | Says |
|---|---|
| **Used by** | Pipeline, Source or AI tool |
| **Name** | Which one |
| **API** | The API it calls |
| **Pinned** | **Latest**, or the version it is pinned to, with **behind** when a newer one exists |

![Used by, with each pipeline and the API it calls](con-api-used-by "Used by: what calls each API, and whether it follows the latest version")

## Pin a source to a version
A source always names the version it runs:

1. Open **Connections › Sources**, open the source (or choose **New source**) and pick **Reads from: API**.
2. Pick the **Collection** and the **API**.
3. Pick the **Version**. The newest says **(current)**. A later save of the collection does not change the version the
   source runs.
4. Choose **Save**.

When you have changed the API and tested the new version, open the source again, pick the newer version and save.

## When a change would break something
Deleting an API, an environment or a whole collection that something still uses is refused. The console names what
uses it, in the same columns as **Used by**, with the version each one pinned and the version the collection is at now.
Move or remove those uses first.

> **Tip:** Change an API in steps: save the change (a new version), test it, then move the pinned sources one by one.
> Anything still on the older version keeps working meanwhile.

## Example
Summit Valley's lab partner changes how its order status answers. The administrator edits **Order status** in the
partner's collection and saves it: the collection moves from v4 to v5. The source "Open lab orders", pinned to v4, keeps
reading the old way. Once a test of v5 looks right, the administrator opens the source, picks **v5** and saves; **Used
by** then shows it on v5, and no run ever saw a half-made change.

articles.title: Import a Postman or Bruno collection
articles.summary: Bring a Postman v2.1 collection (with its environments) or a Bruno folder in as a new API collection, and read the import report.
articles.who: Workspace administrators
articles.popular: Import a Postman collection
articles.md:
If a partner or your developers already keep their APIs in Postman or Bruno, import them instead of typing each request
again. The import makes a new API collection with the requests, folders, variables and sign-in it could carry over,
and a report of what needs a look.

The files are read in your browser and nothing in them is run: a Postman script or test never runs here.

## Import from Postman
1. In Postman, export the collection as **Collection v2.1** (a `.json` file). Export its environments too if you want
   them.
2. Open **Get data in › Connections › API collections** and choose **Import**.
3. Keep **Postman** selected and, under **Collection file**, choose **Choose file** and pick the collection.
4. Optionally, under **Environment files**, choose **Choose files** and pick the environments. Each becomes an
   environment of the collection; its secret values are sealed on arrival.
5. Optionally give the collection a **Name**; empty keeps the name the file gives it.
6. Choose **Import**.

![The Import a collection dialog](con-api-import "Import a collection: Postman or Bruno, the files, and an optional name")

## Import from Bruno
1. Choose **Import**, then **Bruno**.
2. Under **Bruno collection**, choose **Choose folder** and pick the collection's folder, or **Choose .bru files** to
   pick files. Files other than `.bru` and `.json` are left out.
3. Optionally give it a **Name**, and choose **Import**.

## Read the import report
When it is done, the dialog becomes the **Import report**:

| Count | Means |
|---|---|
| **Imported** | Came across as it was |
| **Converted** | Came across, changed to fit how the console works; the note says how |
| **Needs a look** | Came across, but check it before you use it |
| **Skipped** | Left out, with the reason |

The table below lists each item with a note, those that need you first. "Imported as a new collection. Nothing needs a
look." means you can go straight on. Choose **Open collection**.

## After the import
1. Open each environment and check its variables. Replace any secret that came across empty.
2. Check the collection's **Default auth** (**Edit details**) and each API's **Auth** tab. See
   [How an API signs in](#con-api-auth).
3. Test each API against a sandbox. See [Test a request](#con-api-test).

The collections list counts imports in its **Imported** tile, and the **Source** column says **Postman** or **Bruno**.

> **Note:** Each import makes a new collection; it never changes one you already have. To bring in a partner's newer
> export, import it again (it arrives as a separate collection), compare, and move your pipelines across when it is
> tested.

## Example
Summit Valley's lab partner sent its order API as a Postman collection. The administrator imported it as **Northgate
Labs partner (imported)**: three APIs (**Place a lab order**, **Order status**, **Cancel an order**) and one environment
whose `baseUrl` points at the partner's sandbox. When the partner sent a newer export, it came in alongside as
**Northgate Labs partner (imported v2)**.

articles.title: Data contracts
articles.summary: Describe the records you expect, keep versions of the description, check a payload against it, and see where contracts are used.
articles.who: Workspace administrators make contracts and activate versions; anyone whose page access includes Data contracts reads them and validates a payload
articles.md:
A data contract says what a record must look like: which fields it has, their types, and which ones every record must
carry. Pipelines check incoming rows against a contract, and the API refuses a record that does not meet it, so a
malformed file or message is caught where it enters instead of three steps later.

![The Data contracts tab](con-contracts "Data contracts: each one's direction, active and latest version, and sensitivity")

## The list
| Column | Says |
|---|---|
| **Contract** | Its name; a shared system contract is marked **System · read-only** |
| **Direction** | **In: a customer's payload** (what you receive) or **Out: our result** (what you send) |
| **Active** | The version checks use, unless they name another |
| **Latest** | The newest version saved |
| **Sensitivity** | The data level of what it describes |
| **Created** | When it was made |

## Start from a template
Choose **Install template** to pick one of the platform's generic contracts. A template becomes this workspace's own
contract with v1 active; change it from there.

## Make one from a sample
1. Choose **New from sample**.
2. Give it a **Name** (letters, digits, spaces, `_`, `.` and `-`), a **Direction** and a **Sensitivity**.
3. Paste a **Sample**: one record as JSON, or a list of them. Values a data policy hides are masked before the sample is
   kept.
4. Choose **Propose schema**. The console reads the sample and lists its fields with their types. Nothing is saved yet.
5. Under **Fields**, tick **Required** on each field every record must carry.
6. Choose **Save v1**.

## Versions
Open a contract to see its **Versions**, its **Schema** and **Validate a payload**.

- **New version from sample** proposes a new schema from a new sample and saves it as the next version
  (**Save version**). It does not change what checks use yet.
- **Activate** on a version makes it the one checks use. The one that was active becomes **Retired**.
- **Schema** lists the picked version's fields, types and which are **Required**; **Raw JSON** shows it as JSON
  Schema.

![A contract's panel](con-contract-panel "A contract: its versions, the active one's schema, and Validate a payload")

## Check a payload by hand
1. Under **Validate a payload**, leave **Against** at **The active version**, or pick another.
2. Paste the JSON a customer would send (or you would answer) into **Payload**.
3. Choose **Validate**. Each problem is listed by **Path**, **Rule** and **Message**. Nothing is recorded.

## Where contracts are used
- **In a pipeline**: a **Validate** step checks each row against a contract, and either fails the run or marks the
  rows that do not pass.
- **On the customer API**: a pipeline may name an input contract; a record sent to start it is checked first and
  refused, with each field's path, when it does not meet the contract. An event route may name one too. See the
  Developers chapter.
- **For forms**: a form's submission becomes a row, so the pipeline it starts can check it with a **Validate** step.

> **Tip:** A check uses the **Active** version unless it pinned another. Save a new version, try it with **Validate a
> payload**, then **Activate** it when the senders are ready.

## Example
Summit Valley's `lab_result` contract describes a lab result as nine fields, four of them required: `loinc`, `value`,
`result_id` and `patient_ref`. v2 is active and v1 is retired. The same contract is the input contract of the API the
lab partner posts results to, so a result without a LOINC code is refused before any pipeline runs.

articles.title: Sources and connectors
articles.summary: What your pipelines read, sources you test and preview, and the ready-made connectors that sync data into your storage.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Sources or Connectors reads them; workspace administrators add sources and connections, and test and preview them
articles.md:
Pipelines read data straight from their steps: a bucket and folder, an API, a database query, a document type. Two tabs
of **Connections** help around that: **Sources** shows what is read and lets you try a source before a pipeline
depends on it, and **Connectors** syncs data from other systems into your own storage, where pipelines pick it up.

## What your pipelines read
The top of **Sources**, **What your pipelines read**, lists every place the workspace's pipelines read, grouped by
place: **What** (a connection and path, an API, a database), its **Kind**, and **Read by** (the pipelines that read it,
each a link). There is nothing to set up: open a pipeline to change what it reads.

![What your pipelines read, on the Sources tab](con-sources "Places read: each storage folder, API and database, with the pipelines that read it")

## Make a source to test and preview
A source is a named place to read that you can test, preview and keep a schema for.

1. On **Sources**, choose **New source**.
2. Give it a **Name** and a **Description**.
3. Under **Reads from**, pick one:
   - **API**: a **Collection**, one of its **API**s, the **Version** it runs (see
     [Versions and pinning](#con-api-versions)), the **Environment** (empty: the collection's default) and **Rows at**,
     the JSONPath to the rows in the answer.
   - **File** or **Bucket folder**: a **Storage connection**, the **Format** (**CSV**, **JSON**, **JSON Lines** or
     **Parquet**), the **Path** inside the connection (a file for **File**, a folder for **Bucket folder**), and for CSV
     the **Delimiter** and whether **The first line is a header**.
   - **Database**: a **Database connection** and a **Query** that only reads.
4. Under **Try it**, choose **Test connection**, then **Preview** for the first rows and **Infer schema** to keep the
   schema they suggest.
5. Choose **Save**.

The list shows each source's **Kind**, **Format** and **Last test**: **Answered**, **Did not answer** or **not tested**.

> **Note:** Parquet is kept as a source's format but cannot be previewed yet; CSV, JSON and JSON Lines can.

## Connectors
**Connectors** is a gallery of ready-made connectors for databases, SaaS apps and files. Connect once, and the
connection syncs on a schedule into this workspace's own storage, under `connectors/`, where the Data Catalog, Sources
and pipelines find the data.

Each card says where it stands on your platform:

| On the card | Means |
|---|---|
| **Connect** | Ready: choose it to set one up |
| **Connected** | This workspace already has a connection |
| **On request** | Available once the platform's operator has registered the app's sign-in; ask your account team |
| **Not yet** | Not available yet; hover over it for why |

![The connector gallery](con-connectors "Connectors: databases, SaaS apps, files and APIs, with what each can do today")

To connect:

1. Choose **Connect** on a card, or **New connection** and pick the connector.
2. Give the connection a **Name** and pick **Write to**, the storage connection the synced data lands in.
3. Fill in what the connector asks for. For a SaaS app, saving sends you to that app to grant read-only access; come
   back when it asks you to.
4. Pick what to sync and how often under **Sync**, and save.

**Build custom (REST)** makes a connector over one of your API collections. The **Connections** table under the
gallery shows each connection's **Mode** (change capture, incremental or full refresh), **Last sync**, **Rows**, **Lag**
and **Status**, and **Schema change** when a change in the source waits for you.

## Example
Summit Valley's **What your pipelines read** shows the clinical bucket's `imaging/xray/images/` folder read by "X-ray
triage: model against the label" and `journey/wound/history.csv` read by the wound-photo pipelines. Before pointing a
new pipeline at the World Bank API, the administrator makes a source over it, previews the first rows and infers the schema.

articles.title: What the console may call
articles.summary: APIs, storage endpoints, paging links and webhooks must be public addresses; private and internal ones are refused, and why.
articles.who: Everyone who sets up connections
articles.md:
The console calls out to other systems for you: an API in a collection, a storage endpoint, the next page of a paged
answer, a webhook. Each of those calls goes to a **public** address on the internet. An address inside a private
network is refused, whoever asks for it.

## What is refused
- **Private network addresses**, such as `10.x.x.x`, `172.16.x.x` to `172.31.x.x` and `192.168.x.x`.
- **Loopback**, such as `localhost` and `127.0.0.1`.
- **Link-local** addresses.
- **Cloud metadata** addresses, the ones a cloud server asks about itself. These are never allowed.

The check is made on the address a name leads to, not only on the name you typed: a public-looking host name that
resolves to a private address is refused too. It is made again on every call, not only when you save.

## Where you see it
- **Test** on an API says **Blocked**, and nothing is sent. See [Test a request](#con-api-test).
- A pipeline step that would call such an address fails instead of calling it.
- A storage connection whose **Endpoint** is private does not pass **Test connection**.
- A webhook's address must be `https` and public; a private one is refused when you save it and again at every
  delivery.

## Paging and other hosts
A paged API's next-page address stays on the first request's host. If the API hands out later pages from another
host, name that host in **Other hosts** on the API's **Settings**. Calls there are sent without this API's
credentials, so a link in an answer can never carry your secrets somewhere else. See
[Page through results](#con-api-paging).

## Why
Your workspace shares the platform with others. If the console would call any address it was given, someone could
point an API or a storage endpoint at the platform's own internal services, or at another organisation's systems
behind the same network, and read what they answer. Refusing private and metadata addresses closes that door for
everyone, your workspace included.

> **Note:** Your own systems on a private network are not reachable this way. Expose what a pipeline needs through a
> public, secured address (with TLS and its own sign-in), or ask your account team about connecting a private system.

## Example
Summit Valley's public health APIs (FHIR, openFDA, RxNorm, ClinicalTrials.gov) are all public and keyless, so they pass.
A test against `http://192.168.1.40/fhir`, the hospital's own server, says **Blocked**; the integration team publishes
the endpoint through the hospital's API gateway instead and the collection points there.

articles.title: Read a dashboard
articles.summary: Open a board, run its widgets, narrow it with the date range and filters, and share it with people in your workspace.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Dashboards; changing a board needs Edit dashboards (or Analytics Studio)
articles.popular: Filter a dashboard by date
articles.md:
A dashboard is a page of widgets (tiles) over your pipelines' results: figures, charts and tables. Nothing on a board is
a stored picture. Each widget points at a saved analysis or a saved query, and runs it again every time the board is
opened, so the board always shows what the files hold now, read as the person looking at it.

## Find a board
1. Open **See results › Dashboards**.
2. The cards are grouped: your **Favourites** first, then one group for each pipeline that feeds boards (the group is
   the pipeline's name), then **Not fed by a pipeline**. Each card shows the board's name, how many widgets and files it
   has, its description, who made it and when it was last updated.
3. With more than six boards, type in **Find a dashboard** to narrow the cards by name or description.
4. Choose a card to open the board.

To keep a board at the top, choose the star on its card (**Add to favourites**). Favourites are yours and are kept in
this browser.

![The dashboards list](dash-list "Dashboards: favourites first, then the boards grouped by the pipeline that feeds them")

## Read a board
The line under the board's name says what you are looking at: the number of widgets and files, who made it,
**Made by** (the pipeline and run that wrote its files, linked to the run), **Last run** (how many widgets drew, and
how many failed) and how long the board took to load.

- **Run every widget** runs the whole board again; **Stop** stops it. Each widget also has its own refresh button.
- A widget's foot says how many rows it drew and when it ran. **Show all** opens rows a chart had to leave out, and
  **Open every row in a window** (in the widget's ⋯ menu) shows a long result in full.
- A table widget pages, sorts and filters on the server: use **Search the rows**, **Columns** and **Export CSV** on
  the widget itself.
- **Files this board reads** (folded under the facts line) lists every file the widgets read.
- A widget that cannot draw says why in its own tile, with **Try again**. The rest of the board still draws.

![A board](dash-board "A board: the facts line, Run every widget, and figures, a gauge and tables read from the pipeline's files")

![The same board in Dark](dash-board-dark "The same board in the Dark theme: every widget follows the theme each person picks")

> **Note:** A widget that shows **Partial result — stopped at the server's row ceiling** read only part of its data.
> Ask the board's editor to narrow its query, or open the file in [Analytics Studio](#dash-studio).

## Narrow it with the date range and filters
A board whose editor added a **filter bar** shows it above the widgets: a date range first, then one chip for each
filter (for example **Department** or **Ward**), then **Clear all**.

1. Pick a range: **30 days**, **90 days**, **12 months**, **This year**, **All time**, or **Custom** for your own
   **From** and **To** dates.
2. Open a filter chip and tick the values you want. Only the values you set narrow the board.
3. Every widget whose data has that column runs again, narrowed. It shows **Filtered** in its foot. A widget whose data
   has no such column says **Not by** and the filter's name, and keeps showing everything.
4. **Clear all** puts the board back.

Your choice is kept in the board's address and in this browser, so the board opens the way you left it.

You can also narrow a board without a filter bar:

- **Click a bar or a slice** on a chart: the board is filtered to that value at once.
- Or choose ⋯ › **Filter this board**, pick the dataset under **Filter the widgets that read**, build the conditions,
  and press **Apply to the board**. Nothing runs again until you press it.

The facts line then shows **N filters on**. Choose it to see the filter, or the × beside it to clear it.

## Share a board
A board belongs to the workspace, so everyone in it whose page access includes **Dashboards** can open it.

1. Open the board, filtered the way you want it.
2. Copy the address from your browser and send it to a colleague.
3. They sign in and see the same board with the same filters. Their widgets run as them: a column the Data Catalog
   holds sensitive stays masked for anyone without access to it.

> **Privacy:** A board link never works without signing in, and a link to another workspace's board says
> **This dashboard isn't here**.

## Who may do what
| Who | May |
|---|---|
| Page access **Dashboards** | Open, run and filter every board, and export a table widget |
| **Edit dashboards**, or **Analytics Studio** | Also make, change and delete boards, and pin answers to them |
| **Analytics Studio** | Also read a file's rows outside a board, and write queries of their own |

Someone with **Dashboards** alone sees: *You can open, run and filter these dashboards. Changing them needs the Edit
dashboards page, and reading data outside their tiles needs Analytics Studio.*

## Example
At the morning huddle Jordan Reyes, operations director at Summit Valley Health System, opens **Bed board**, sets the
range to **30 days** and clicks the bar for ward 4B on **Occupancy by ward (%)**. Every widget narrows to 4B. He copies
the address into the huddle notes, and Rosa Alvarez, the charge nurse, opens the same view.

articles.title: Build and edit a dashboard
articles.summary: Make a board, add widgets from saved analyses and queries, choose each chart, set widths and sections, and add a filter bar.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Edit dashboards or Analytics Studio
articles.popular: Add a chart to a dashboard
articles.md:
A board is built from work already saved: an **analysis** or a **query** saved in [Analytics Studio](#dash-studio), or
an answer pinned from [Ask your data](#dash-ask-pin). A widget points at that saved work and never keeps a copy of its
result, so changing the saved query changes every widget that uses it.

## Make a board
1. Open **See results › Dashboards** and choose **New dashboard**.
2. Give it a **Name** (for example *Bed board*) and, if you like, **What it is for (optional)**: the line every card and
   the board show under the name.
3. Choose **Create**. The board opens empty, with **Add a widget**.

## Add a widget
1. On the board, choose ⋯ › **Add a widget**.
2. Fill in **Title**.
3. Under **Shows**, pick **A saved analysis** or **A saved query**, then pick **Which one**. It runs once, so you can
   see it.
4. Under **Drawn as**, point at a chart kind: the widget's own result is drawn in that kind as you move over it. Kinds
   that cannot draw this result say why; **Only what fits** hides them, and **Search chart types** finds one by name.
5. Optionally set **Height** (in pixels) and a **Caption**: what the reader should take from it.
6. Choose **Add**. Only the new widget runs, not the whole board.

![Adding a widget](dash-add-widget "Add a widget: what it shows, its title and height, and the chart kinds drawn with its own result")

> **Tip:** If the list under **Which one** is empty, save an analysis or a query in Analytics Studio first: a widget has
> nothing else it can point at.

## Change a widget
Open the widget's ⋯ menu:

- **Choose a chart, with a preview…** opens every kind with the widget's result drawn in it.
- **Suggested for this data** lists the kinds that suit the result; **All charts** lists every kind by category, with
  **Search charts** to find one by name.
- **Chart settings…** sets the widget's **Title** and **Subtitle**, its **Legend**, **Colours**, **Data labels**,
  **Tooltip**, **Number format**, and **Sort and top N** (with **Add the rest as "Other"**), with a preview.
- **Width**: **Auto**, or 3/12 (a quarter), 4/12 (a third), 6/12 (half), 8/12 (two thirds), 9/12 (three quarters) or
  12/12 (the whole row). On Auto a single figure takes a quarter, a chart half and a table the whole row.
- **Start a section here** puts a heading (and an optional description) above the widget; the section starts a new
  row. **Edit the section heading above** changes it; an empty heading removes it.
- **Remove from board** takes the widget off. The saved analysis or query it pointed at is kept.

![Choose a chart](dash-kind-picker "Choose a chart: every kind by group, with the widget's own result drawn in the one under the pointer")

### The chart kinds
There are 52 kinds in eleven groups: **Figures and tables** (a single figure, a figure with its trend, a table, a
cross-tab, two figures compared), **Bar**, **Line and area**, **Pie**, **Scatter**, **Distribution**, **Hierarchy**
(treemap, sunburst, tree), **Flow** (Sankey, chord), **Grid** (heatmap, calendar), **Other** (funnel, gauge, radar and
more) and **Summaries**. Each says what it needs, for example *Two text columns and a number* for a heatmap.

## Add a filter bar
A filter bar lets every reader narrow the board without editing it.

1. Choose ⋯ › **Add a filter bar** (or **Edit filters** on the bar).
2. Choose **Add a date range** for the one date filter, or **Add a filter** for a list of values.
3. For each, give a **Label** (for example *Ward*), pick the **Dataset** and **Column** its values come from, and, if
   other files call the column something else, list those names under **Also lands on columns named…**.
4. A date range can open on a default (**Opens on**).
5. Choose **Save filters**.

A filter narrows every widget whose data has its column; the others say so. See
[Narrow it with the date range and filters](#dash-boards--narrow-it-with-the-date-range-and-filters).

## The board's chart theme
The theme button beside ⋯ (it reads **Console** until you pick another) sets the theme every widget draws in. A widget can still choose its own in its
**Chart settings**. Choosing a theme runs nothing.

## Delete a board
Choose ⋯ › **Delete this dashboard** and confirm. The saved analyses and queries its widgets used are kept.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Widget height | 120 to 600 pixels, or empty for automatic |
| Filters on one board | 12, of which one date range |
| Chart kinds | 52 |

## Example
Ana García, the retail analyst at Summit Valley Health System, saves *Sales by store* in Analytics Studio, adds it to
**Retail stores** as a **Ranked bars** widget at 6/12, and starts a section *This month* above it. She adds a filter
bar with a **Store** filter, so the pharmacy managers can each look at their own store.

articles.title: Where a board's data comes from
articles.summary: Pipelines keep files for a board; the board reads them where they are, names the pipeline that made them and follows each new run.
articles.who: Workspace administrators build the pipelines that feed boards; anyone who opens a board sees where its data comes from
articles.md:
A board holds no data of its own. Its widgets read files in your workspace's storage, where they are, each time the
board is opened. Those files are usually written by a pipeline, so a board is as fresh as the last run of the pipeline
that feeds it.

## How a pipeline feeds a board
1. A pipeline reads its sources, works out the figures (for example one row per ward with its occupancy), and ends with
   an **Upload to bucket** step that writes the rows as a CSV, JSON or JSON Lines file into one of your workspace's
   buckets.
2. Give the file a fixed name, such as `ops/beds/occupancy.csv`, so each run replaces it. A name with the run's date in
   it (`census-{{date}}.csv`) keeps one file a day instead; a widget can read all of them together as one dataset.
3. In Analytics Studio, open that file and save an analysis or a query over it.
4. On the board, add a widget that shows the saved analysis or query.
5. Schedule the pipeline. Each run replaces the file, and the board shows the new figures the next time it is opened or
   run.

```A file a board reads
summit-valley/ops/beds/occupancy.csv
```

> **Tip:** Use **Upload to bucket** for a board's files rather than **Save File**. **Save File** keeps a file with the
> run only for as long as the pipeline keeps its runs' data, so a board that reads it goes empty when it expires.

## See which pipeline made a board's data
- On the cards of **See results › Dashboards**, boards are grouped under the pipeline that writes their files. A board
  no pipeline writes for is under **Not fed by a pipeline**.
- On a board, **Made by** names the pipeline and its newest run (**run #1976**), linked to that run's page; **and N
  more** says other pipelines feed it too. Point at it to list them all.
- **Files this board reads** lists every file its widgets read.

![Where the data comes from](dash-made-by "A board's facts line: Made by the pipeline and its run, and Files this board reads opened")

## When a board shows old or no figures
| What you see | What to do |
|---|---|
| **Nothing to read at** a file, *The connection worked, so check the path* | The pipeline has not written the file yet, or wrote it under another name. Open the pipeline's last run and check its **Upload to bucket** step. |
| The figures are from yesterday | The feeding pipeline has not run since. Open **Made by** and check its schedule, or run it. |
| One widget fails, the others draw | That widget's saved query no longer fits the file (a column was renamed). Its editor changes the query in Analytics Studio. |
| **This dashboard isn't open to you** | Your page access does not include Dashboards; ask your workspace administrator. |

## Example
At Summit Valley Health System, the pipeline *Bed occupancy by ward* runs every morning at 06:00. It reads the night's
census, counts beds and occupied beds per ward, works out the occupancy percentage and writes
`ops/beds/occupancy.csv`. **Bed board** reads that file in two widgets, *Occupancy by ward (%)* and *Beds occupied*, so
at 06:05 the board shows the new day. Its facts line reads **Made by Bed occupancy by ward · run #1976**.

articles.title: Put an Ask your data answer on a board
articles.summary: Ask a question in plain words, read the chart answer and its query, change the chart, and pin it to a dashboard as a widget.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Ask your data; pinning needs Edit dashboards or Analytics Studio

where.label: See results › Analysis › Ask your data

articles.md:
**Ask your data** answers questions about what you can open in the workspace: documents, forms, pipeline results and
datasets. When a question is about figures in a dataset, the answer is a query the console wrote and ran as you, drawn
as a chart with its rows beneath. That chart can become a widget on a board, which runs the same query every time the
board is opened.

The AI side of Ask your data (what it searches, which model answers, the search index) is in the AI topic. This
article is about using its chart answers.

## Ask and read a chart answer
1. Open **See results › Analysis › Ask your data**.
2. Type your question (up to 500 characters), or start from one of the suggestions under **Try:** or
   **Start with an example**, and choose **Ask**.
3. A question about figures comes back as:
   - a sentence answering it,
   - a chart of the rows (with **Change chart**, **Chart settings** and **Pin to dashboard** above it),
   - the rows as a table (the first 20 shown; the line under it says how many there were),
   - **The query, run as you over** the dataset's name: the exact statement that produced the rows.
4. **Open in Analytics Studio** opens the dataset on its SQL tab with that query, to change and save it.
   **Download CSV** saves the rows.

> **Warning:** The answer is written by a model. Read the query and the rows before you rely on the sentence above
> them: the rows are what the data holds, the sentence is a DRAFT.

## Change the chart
- **Change chart** lists the kinds **Suggested for this data**; **All charts, with a preview…** opens every kind.
- **Chart settings** sets the title, legend, colours, labels and number format.

## Pin it to a board
1. Under the chart, choose **Pin to dashboard**.
2. Check the **Title**: it becomes the widget's title.
3. Under **Dashboard**, pick **An existing dashboard** from the list, or **A new dashboard** and type its name.
4. Choose **Pin**. The panel says **Pinned to** the board; **Open the dashboard** takes you there.

![Pin to dashboard](dash-pin "Pin to dashboard: the widget's title, and an existing or a new dashboard")

The query is saved with the widget. It runs when the board is opened, as whoever opens it, so their masked fields stay
masked. **Pinned answers** on the Ask your data page lists what you pinned from here, each linked to its board.

> **Note:** If **Pin to dashboard** is greyed out, your access does not let you change dashboards. Ask your workspace
> administrator for **Edit dashboards**, or send the question to someone who has it.

## Example
At Summit Valley Health System, Jordan Reyes asks *Which ward was fullest last week?* The answer is a bar chart of
occupancy by ward from the operations figures, with the query beneath it. He changes it to **Horizontal bars**, pins it
to **Bed board** with the title *Fullest wards last week*, and the huddle sees it there every morning.

articles.title: Explore a file in Analytics Studio
articles.summary: Open a file or a folder as a dataset, preview and profile it, group and measure it, write a query, save it for a board, and export the result.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Analytics Studio
articles.popular: Group and count a file's rows
articles.md:
Analytics Studio reads a file where it lives, in your workspace's storage: nothing is copied. The query engine reads
the file and your browser only ever receives a page of rows, so a file of millions of rows opens as quickly as a small
one. What you save here (an analysis or a query) is what a dashboard widget points at.

## Open a file
1. Open **See results › Analysis › Analytics Studio** and choose **Choose a file**.
2. In the **Files** panel, pick the **Connection**, walk to the folder and pick a file. CSV, TSV, JSON and Parquet can
   be read. A whole folder can be read as one dataset: it is marked **Folder dataset**, and every figure covers all the
   files in it.
3. The header shows the file's name, its format, its rows, columns, size and when it last changed, and where it lives.

You can also arrive here from **Open in Analytics Studio** on an Ask your data answer. Not sure where a file is? Choose
**Find it in the Data Catalog** and search there.

> **Tip:** ⋯ › **Name this dataset** registers the location under a name of its own, so it can be opened by name. It
> reads no rows.

## Look at it
The tabs are in three groups, by what each costs:

| Tabs | What they show |
|---|---|
| **Overview**, **Data** | The file's columns and a page of its rows. **Data** sorts, filters and pages through the rows. |
| **Compact**, **Profile**, **Quality** | One scan of the whole file, read three ways: each column's type, how many are empty and distinct, the most common values, and what looks wrong. The scan runs once, on the first of these you open. |
| **Canvas**, **SQL**, **Charts**, **Activity** | Questions you ask the file. Each run is a real query. |

**Visualise** (beside **Files**) suggests charts of the file from its columns; a chart there can be pinned to a
dashboard.

![Analytics Studio](dash-studio "Analytics Studio: a file's facts, the tabs in three groups, and the Profile of its columns")

## Group and measure (Canvas)
1. Open **Canvas**. Under **Build an analysis**, pick a **Dimension** (a column to group by). Up to three: each next
   one appears as **then by**.
2. For a date column, pick a **Bucket**: **every value**, **by day**, **by week**, **by month**, **by quarter** or
   **by year**.
3. Pick a **Measure**: **Count rows**, **Count non-null**, **Distinct count**, **Sum**, **Average**, **Minimum**,
   **Maximum** or **Median**, and the column it measures.
4. Choose **Run analysis**. The result shows as a table or a chart.
5. **Save analysis** keeps it under a name, for a dashboard widget. Saving a changed one again updates it; **Save as
   new** keeps both.

## Write a query (SQL)
1. Open **SQL**. **What your SQL can name** lists the dataset as `dataset` (and a second one, if you add it, as
   `dataset2`). You never type a bucket or a path.
2. Write the statement and choose **Run** (or press ⌘ / Ctrl + Enter).
3. Type a name under **Name this query** and save it, for a dashboard widget.

```A first query
select * from dataset
```

## Take the result away
Under a result, **Take it away** offers:

- **Download** as **CSV**, **TSV** or **JSON**. The query runs again to build the file.
- **Write back**: the result as a new file in the same connection's bucket, in the folder you type. There is no undo.

> **Warning:** A result that stopped at the server's row ceiling says so above the buttons. A file made from it holds
> only that part, not all of it.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| File formats | CSV, TSV, JSON, Parquet |
| Grouping | Up to three dimensions and one measure |
| Rows a result returns | The server's row ceiling; the screen says when a result stopped at it |

Every query here is metered as an analytics query (see [How usage is counted](#bill-usage)).

## Example
Claire Martin, controller at Summit Valley Health System, opens `rcm/kpis.csv`, groups by **month** of `posted_at` and
measures **Average** of `days_in_ar`. She saves it as *Days in A/R by month*, and Marcus Owens adds it to **Revenue
cycle** as a line.

articles.title: The Data Catalog
articles.summary: Every dataset, file and document type in the workspace, who owns it, how fresh it is, which fields are sensitive, and asking for access to masked values.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Data Catalog; marking fields and deciding access requests is a workspace administrator's
articles.popular: Ask for access to masked data
articles.md:
The Data Catalog lists every **asset** in the workspace: datasets, files and document types. For each it says what it
holds, who owns it, how fresh it is, and which of its fields are sensitive. A field marked sensitive is masked for
anyone without access to it, here, in Analytics Studio, on dashboards and in Ask your data alike.

## Find an asset
1. Open **See results › Analysis › Data Catalog**. The figures at the top count the **Assets**, those **With
   sensitive fields**, those **Stale over 30 days** and those **Without an owner**.
2. Narrow the list: **All**, **Datasets**, **Files** or **Document types**; **Any**, **Sensitive**, **Stale** or
   **Without an owner**; or type in **Search name, column or tag…**. **Deleted too** adds assets whose source has gone.
3. Each row shows the **Asset** and where it is, its **Type**, **Owner**, **Freshness**, **Sensitive fields**,
   **Sensitivity** and **Quality**.
4. Choose a row to open its panel.

The notice above the list says how many assets hold fields marked sensitive, with **Show them**.

![The Data Catalog](dash-catalog "The Data Catalog: the figures, the sensitive-data notice, and the assets with their sensitivity")

## What an asset's panel shows
- Its **sensitivity** (**Unclassified**, **Public**, **Internal**, **Confidential** or **Restricted**), where it is,
  its quality and when it last changed.
- **About**: its description and owner.
- **Columns**: each column's type, how much of it is empty, and what it **Holds**. A column marked sensitive shows
  **Sensitive**; one whose name looks like patient data but carries no mark says *looks like* and what.
- **Lineage**: what feeds the asset and what reads it, and **Used by**.

## Sensitive fields and masking
A column can be marked as holding: email, phone, national id, card number, bank account, person name, address, date of
birth, medical record number, health plan number or ZIP code. An asset's sensitivity follows its marks: a national
id, card number, bank account, date of birth, medical record number or health plan number makes it **Restricted**, any
other mark **Confidential**.

A new file (an upload, or a file a pipeline writes) is checked from a sample of its first rows before Analytics first
reads it, so its sensitive columns are masked from the first read.

A workspace administrator can, in an asset's panel:
1. Choose **Scan for sensitive data** to check the columns again, or **Profile** to read them.
2. Set what each column **Holds**, or **nothing sensitive**.
3. Set the asset's **Sensitivity** by hand, or leave it on **Follow its tags**.
4. Write the description, choose **Make me the owner**, and **Save details**.

## Ask for access to masked values
When an asset's values are masked for you, its panel says *Its sensitive values are masked for you*.

1. Under **Why you need it**, say what you will use the values for.
2. Under **For**, pick **1 day**, **7 days**, **30 days** or **90 days**.
3. Choose **Request access**.

The panel then says when you asked. A workspace administrator decides in their task inbox; once granted, the panel says
*You can see its values until* the date and time it ends, and the masking lifts for you until then.

![Masked for a researcher](dash-catalog-access "An asset masked for a researcher, with Why you need it, For and Request access")

> **Privacy:** Access is granted for a time, never for good. When it ends, the values are masked for you again.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Reason for an access request | 1,000 characters |
| Access lasts | 1, 7, 30 or 90 days |
| An asset's description | 4,000 characters |

## Example
Dr. Hana Ito, a researcher at Summit Valley Health System, opens the Patient 360 file *latest.csv*. Its `name`, `dob`
and `mrn` columns are masked for her. She asks for access for **7 days**, *to check the ages in the diabetes cohort*.
The workspace administrator approves it, and for a week she sees the values; then they are masked again. Her usual
work uses *research.csv*, a de-identified extract that needs no access at all.

articles.title: Files: browse, preview and chat with a file
articles.summary: Walk the storage behind each connection, preview any file, upload, email or download it, and ask a model about it with File Chat.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Browse files; adding a storage connection is a workspace administrator's
articles.md:
**Files** (the page is titled **Browse files**) shows the storage behind each of your workspace's connections: the
files your runs wrote, the uploads, the documents that came in. Every file opens in a preview, and any document can be
asked about with **File Chat**.

## Browse
1. Open **See results › Analysis › Files**. Each storage connection is a card; type in **Search connections** to find
   one.
2. Choose a card. The folders and files are listed with their **Name**, **Modified**, **Size** and **Type**; the path
   above the list takes you back up.
3. Narrow the list with **Find a file…** and **Modified from** / **Modified to**. The line beside them counts the
   folders, files and bytes shown.
4. **Insights** charts what is here, the file types, when they last changed and the largest files.

![Files](dash-files "Browse files: a connection's folders and files, with the filters and Insights")

> **Note:** *No storage is connected yet* means the workspace has no storage connection. A workspace administrator adds
> one under **Get data in › Connections › Storage**.

## Open, preview and share a file
Open a file's ⋯ menu:

- **View** previews it: a PDF page by page, an image with zoom, a table 100 rows at a time with a search, an archive's
  entries, audio and video to play. A file nobody can preview shows its first bytes, so you can tell what it is.
- **Details** shows its size, type, path and checksum, who uploaded it or which pipeline run wrote it (**Made by**), and
  its **Retention**: the policy that keeps it and when it expires.
- **Download** saves it; **Email this file** sends it to a **Recipient** with an optional **Message**.
- **Copy path** and **Copy checksum (ETag)** copy those for a pipeline's settings or a support request.
- **Delete** removes it, after you confirm.

Tick several files to **Download**, **Email** or **Delete** them together. **New folder**, **Upload** and **Upload
folder** (every file inside it, keeping its sub-folders) add to the folder you are in. A folder's ⋯ menu also has
**Rename**.

> **Warning:** **Delete** removes the file from your storage itself, not only from this list. A pipeline or a dashboard
> that reads it will find nothing.

## Ask about a file with File Chat
1. In the file's ⋯ menu choose **Chat with this file**. The chat opens in the corner of the page.
2. Pick the **Agent** to ask, if there is more than one.
3. Type in **Message** and send. **View** opens the file beside the chat.

A long file may be longer than the model can read at once: the chat then says *Answers cover the first* so many
characters, or that answers are drawn from the excerpts most relevant to each question. Each answer can be copied.

> **Warning:** A File Chat answer is a model's DRAFT. Check it against the file before you use it.

## Example
At Summit Valley Health System, Jordan Reyes opens the week's operations board pack PDF under `ops/board/`, chooses
**Chat with this file** and asks *Which ward had the most delayed discharges?* The answer quotes the page it came from,
and he checks it in **View** before passing it on.

articles.title: Tools: Document Converter and Audio Transcript
articles.summary: Convert a document between formats or make a PDF from a dataset or a run, and turn a recording into text, by hand.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Document Converter or Audio Transcript
articles.md:
The two tools do by hand, for one file, what a pipeline's steps do for many: the **Document Converter** converts a
document, and **Audio Transcript** turns a recording into text, the same way a scheduled run does it. Both are billed
like the steps they stand in for.

## Convert a document
1. Open **See results › Tools › Document Converter**.
2. Choose the source:
   - **Upload a file**: drop a document on the page, or **Choose a file**.
   - **From a bucket**: **Choose a file…** and search, filter and page through any bucket you can see.
   - **PDF from a dataset** or **PDF from a run**: rows printed into a PDF through a template, rather than a file
     converted.
