3. The page says what the file was **Detected as**. Pick the format under **Convert to**.
4. Optionally, under **Save to bucket**, pick a bucket, a **Folder** (for example `converted/`) and a **Name**.
   Left empty, the file goes to the bucket's root under its own name.
5. Choose **Convert**, then **Download** the result.

**Supported formats** lists, for each family (Office, OpenDocument, PDF, Markdown and images), what it converts
**From** and **To**. The chip in the panel's corner shows the converter's queue right now. **Recent conversions** lists
what was saved to a bucket, with links to the original and the converted file.

![Document Converter](dash-converter "Document Converter: the limits, the four sources, and Recent conversions")

## Turn a recording into text
1. Open **See results › Tools › Audio Transcript**.
2. Under **Choose the recording**, **Upload a file** (drop an .mp3 or .m4a) or pick one **From a bucket**.
3. Tick **Include timestamps before each segment** if you want them.
4. Choose **Extract transcript**. A long recording can take a few minutes; the page says so while it works.
5. Read the **Transcript** as a **Timeline** (each segment with its time, which you can copy, and a play button to have
   it read aloud from there), **Table** or **Console**. **Read aloud** and **Copy** are above it.

![Audio Transcript](dash-transcript "Audio Transcript: what it takes, upload or a bucket, and timestamps")

> **Note:** If the converter or the transcriber is busy, the page tells you so. Nothing is lost: try again in about 30
> seconds.

## Limits
The limits strip at the top of each tool shows this platform's limits; when this was written they were:

| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| A document to convert | 50 MB |
| A CSV or TSV to PDF | 500 MB; the PDF prints the first 5,000 rows |
| An XLSX to PDF | 100 MB |
| A converted file | 50 MB, 2,000 pages |
| Time to convert | 140 seconds a file |
| Converter queue | 2 at once, 4 more waiting |
| A recording | .mp3 or .m4a; upload up to 250 MB, from a bucket up to 500 MB |
| Time to transcribe | Up to 30 minutes a recording |

A recording over the upload limit can go to a bucket first. Conversions are billed per document and transcripts by
the minute of audio (see [How usage is counted](#bill-usage)).

## Example
Greta Fischer in health information at Summit Valley Health System receives a discharge letter as a DOCX. She converts
it to PDF, saves it to `docs/letters/` and attaches it to the record. Later she transcribes a 6-minute care call with
timestamps, copies it, and checks what was agreed.

articles.title: What the API is for
articles.summary: How your own systems start runs, send events, files and form answers, read results, decide reviews and hear back, and what an administrator sets up for them.
articles.who: Workspace administrators set up access; your developers use the API
articles.md:
The console is where your people build and run pipelines. The **API** is how your organisation's own systems (a
patient portal, a partner's lab system, a device hub, a finance tool) reach the same workspace without anyone clicking:
they start work, follow it, decide on it, and are told when something happens. It works with any pipeline, any form
and any event type of yours; nothing in it is specific to one kind of data.

## What your systems can do
| They can | How, in a few words |
|---|---|
| Start a run of a pipeline and read it back | Its steps, its outputs, its items and its review: [Start a run and read it back](#dev-runs) |
| Send events | An event of your own type starts the pipeline or workflow you route it to: [Events and event routes](#dev-events) |
| Send files and form answers | Upload a file for a run; submit a form as a person would: [Files and forms](#dev-files-forms) |
| Decide a review | Approve or reject a run's results when the pipeline asks for your decision |
| Hear back | Webhooks POST each event to a URL of yours, signed: [Webhooks](#dev-webhooks) |
| Show a run in their own page | A short-lived view link in a frame: [Embed a run view](#dev-embed) |

## What an administrator sets up
1. One **API client** for each system that calls the API, with only the scopes it needs, under **Administration &
   billing › Developers › API Clients**. See [API clients](#dev-clients).
2. **Test keys** in the **Sandbox** first, so the developers build against sample pipelines that are never billed. See
   [The sandbox](#dev-sandbox).
3. **Event routes** for the event types your systems will send.
4. **Webhooks** for the events your systems want to hear about.
5. The **Developer portal** for your developers: the guides, the reference and samples to copy. See
   [The Developer portal](#dev-portal).

![API Clients](dev-clients "API Clients: the limits, each client with its scopes, where it may call from, its calls this month and its state")

## How a call works
A system exchanges its API client's id and secret for a **token** that lasts 15 minutes, then sends that token with
every call. Every call is checked against the client's **scopes** (what it may do) and its limits. A call that creates
something carries an **Idempotency-Key**, so sending it twice never does the work twice. Errors come back as problem
details that name the field at fault.

> **Note:** The API's address (the **Base URL**) is on the Developer portal's front page, with a button to copy it.

## Who may do what
| Who | May |
|---|---|
| Workspace administrator | Everything on **API Clients**: clients, test keys, event routes and webhooks. In a managed workspace, event routes and webhooks are read-only, and deliveries can still be sent again |
| Administrators, and members whose page access names **Developer portal** | Open the Developer portal |

## Example
Summit Valley Health System's partner lab, *Northgate Labs*, sends each lab result as an event; the event route
*lab.result.created* starts the pipeline that checks it and tells the physicians when a value is critical. The
patient portal, *Partner portal*, starts runs, uploads files, decides reviews and hears back by webhook. Each has its
own API client with only the scopes it needs.

articles.title: API clients
articles.summary: Make one client for each of your systems with only the scopes it needs, its limits, IP allowlist and embed sites; copy the secret once; rotate or revoke it.
articles.who: Workspace administrators
articles.popular: Make an API client
articles.md:
An **API client** is one of your systems as the API knows it: a name, an id, a secret, the **scopes** it may use and
where it may call from. Make one client for each system, so each can be limited, watched and switched off on its own.

## Make a client
1. Open **Administration & billing › Developers › API Clients** and choose **New API client**.
2. **Name**: what the client is for, for example *Partner portal*.
3. **Expires (optional)**: the client stops working at the end of that day.
4. Tick the **Scopes** it needs, and no more (see the table below).
5. **Calls a minute (optional)** and **Burst (optional)**: a lower limit than the workspace's most, if you want one.
6. **IP allowlist (optional)**: one address or range per line, such as `203.0.113.0/24`. Empty means any address.
7. **Sites that may embed its run views (optional)**: one origin per line, such as `https://portal.example.com`. See
   [Embed a run view](#dev-embed).
8. Choose **Make client**. The console shows **API client made** with the **Client id** and the **Client secret**.
9. **Copy** both into your system's secret store now.

> **Warning:** The secret is shown once. Copy it now: it is not shown again. If it is lost, make a new secret.

> **Privacy:** Never put a secret in code, a ticket, an email or a screenshot. Keep it in your system's secret store.

## The scopes
| Scope | Lets the client |
|---|---|
| `pipelines:read` | Read pipelines |
| `runs:read` | Read runs, steps, outputs and reviews; make view links |
| `runs:write` | Start and retry runs |
| `files:read` | Download files |
| `files:write` | Upload files |
| `reviews:write` | Record your organisation's review decision on a run |
| `forms:read` | Read forms and their submissions |
| `forms:write` | Submit forms |
| `events:write` | Send events |
| `webhooks:manage` | Manage webhook subscriptions and read the list of event types |

## The client list
Each row shows the **Client** (its name and id), its **Scopes**, **Allowed from** (its allowlist, or **Any address**,
and the sites that may embed its run views), its **Limit**, **Calls this month**, **Last used**, **Expires** and
**State**. **Show revoked** adds the clients that were switched off.

![A client's settings](dev-client-change "Changing a client: its scopes, its limits, the IP allowlist and the sites that may embed its run views")

## Change, rotate or revoke
Open a client's ⋯ menu:

- **Change**: its name, expiry, scopes, limits, allowlist and embed sites. Changing the scopes ends its current
  tokens, so the system asks for a new one.
- **New secret**: the current secret stops working at once, and so does every token the client holds. Your system
  needs the new secret before it can ask for another token. Plan it with the system's owner.
- **History**: the changes made to the client, by whom and when.
- **Revoke**: the client and every token it holds stop working now, for good. To connect that system again, make a new
  client.

## Limits
The box above the list shows the limits that apply:

| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Each client | At most 600 calls a minute, bursts of 100, unless your account says otherwise |
| All the workspace's clients together | 1,200 calls a minute, bursts of 200 |
| This month | The calls so far and the monthly quota, if your account has one |

Past a limit the API answers *429* with how long to wait, and nothing is done or billed. API calls are billed per
1,000 (see [How usage is counted](#bill-usage)). Our team sets the workspace's limits; ask your account team to change
them.

> **Note:** In a managed workspace, our team sets each client's limits and embed sites too.

## Example
Summit Valley Health System has five clients: *Journey orchestrator* (pipelines, runs, events), *Northgate Labs* and
*HomeLink devices* (events only), *Partner portal* (runs, files, forms, reviews and webhooks, with its run views
embedded on the portal's site), and *Locked-down client*, allowed only from `10.0.0.0/8`, which is refused from
anywhere else.

articles.title: The sandbox and test keys
articles.summary: A workspace of your own to build an integration in, with sample pipelines and test keys that work only there and are never billed.
articles.who: Workspace administrators make test keys; your account team creates the sandbox

where.label: Administration & billing › Developers › API Clients › Sandbox

articles.md:
The **sandbox** is a separate workspace, made for yours, where your developers build and test an integration before it
touches your real pipelines. It has sample pipelines and data, behaves exactly like a real workspace (runs, files,
webhooks, events, retries, limits and errors), and nothing done there is billed.

## Get a sandbox
Your account team creates it once, on request. Until then **API Clients** says *No sandbox yet*. Once it exists, the
**Sandbox** part of **API Clients** names it (for example *Summit Valley Health System (sandbox)*), with a **Test**
badge.

## Make a test key
1. Open **Administration & billing › Developers › API Clients** and scroll to **Sandbox**.
2. Choose **New test key**.
3. Give it a **Name** and tick its **Scopes**, as for any client (see [API clients](#dev-clients)).
4. Choose **Make test key**, and copy the **Client id** and the **Client secret**. The secret is shown once.

A test key's client id starts with `cl_test_`. Its list shows each key's **Name**, **Client id**, **Scopes**, **Last
used** and **State**, with **New secret** and revoke in its menu.

![The sandbox](dev-sandbox "Sandbox: the sandbox workspace, its test key, and the way to the quickstart")

## What a test key can reach
- Only the sandbox. Your real workspace's pipelines, runs and files are *not found* to it, as another
  organisation's are. An ordinary key gets no token for the sandbox either.
- The sample pipelines, a sample data contract and a sample event route, listed in the Developer portal's
  **The sandbox** guide.
- Its own rate limits, so testing never uses up your real clients' calls.

Use only made-up records in the sandbox: it is for testing an integration, not for keeping data.

## What it costs
Nothing. **Billing › Cost & usage** in the sandbox prices its usage to show what it would cost, marked **Sandbox ·
never billed**, but it is never drafted or invoiced.

## Going live
When the integration works in the sandbox:
1. Make an ordinary client under **API Clients** with the same scopes.
2. Your developers swap the test key's id and secret for the new ones, and use your real pipelines' ids.
3. Keep the test key for future tests; it never reaches your real data.

## Example
Priya Singh, a developer working with Summit Valley Health System, gets a test key *Summit Valley sandbox key* with
`pipelines:read`, `runs:read` and `runs:write`, follows the portal's **Quickstart** against the sandbox's sample
pipeline, and checks that **Cost & usage** for the real workspace has not moved. Only then does the administrator make
the real *Partner portal* client.

articles.title: Start a run and read it back
articles.summary: Tokens, starting a run with a record and files, idempotency, following it, its steps, outputs, items and review, retrying, run-and-wait, and the result as JSON, PDF, HTML or Markdown.
articles.who: Your systems, with an API client that has runs:write (start) and runs:read (read)
articles.popular: Start a run from another system
articles.md:
Most integrations do one thing over and over: start a run of a pipeline with some data, then read what it made. This
article says what happens at each step, for an administrator or a project lead. The exact calls, with samples in curl,
Python and Node.js, are in the Developer portal's **Quickstart** and the **API reference**.

## The path of a run
1. **Get a token.** The system exchanges its client id and secret for a token that lasts 15 minutes, and asks again
   when it ends.
2. **Find the pipeline.** The list of pipelines gives each one's id, its **input contract** (what a record must look
   like) and its parameters.
3. **Upload files first**, if the run needs any (see [Files and forms](#dev-files-forms)).
4. **Start the run** with the record, the file ids and, if you like, a **reference** of your own (an order number).
   The record is checked against the input contract before anything is stored: a record that does not fit is refused
   with each wrong field named, and no run starts.
5. **Follow it**, by reading the run until it is completed, or better, by a [webhook](#dev-webhooks) that says when it
   is.
6. **Read what it made**: its outputs.

## Send it twice, get one run
Every call that creates something carries an **Idempotency-Key** of your system's choosing. The same key with the
same request within 24 hours answers the first result again and starts nothing new; the same key with a different
request is refused. Your developers make one key per piece of work (an order, a form) and reuse it on every retry.

## What a system can read back
| It reads | What it holds |
|---|---|
| The run | Its status, its times, its attempt and your reference |
| Its steps | Each step of the latest attempt, in order, with its status, rows in and out, and times |
| Its outputs | The files it was given and made, each by its own file id, and its review; a report's PDF beside its data |
| Its items | For a pipeline that works item by item (each file, recording, document or row): each item's status, the step it failed at and why, its files |
| Its review | Who must decide and what they decided |
| Its result | The rows of its final output, for a quick answer |

A system never sees a bucket, a storage key or a connection: a file is only ever its id.

## Decide a review
When a pipeline asks for your organisation's decision on its results, your system records it with `reviews:write`:
approve, or reject with a reason (and, for a run it started, ask for it to run again). The console's reviewers and
your system see the same review.

## Retry a failed run
A failed run can be retried from the step that failed (the steps before it are not run again or billed again) or
from the start. The run keeps its id; its attempt number goes up.

## Run and wait
A pipeline that answers in seconds (an eligibility check, a lookup) can be started and waited for in the same call,
for 1 to 60 seconds. If it finishes in time, the answer carries its result; if not, it is followed as usual.
Columns your data policy marks sensitive are masked in the result.

## The result as JSON, PDF, HTML or Markdown
The system that starts a run chooses the format it gets the result in -- on the run's result, on run and wait, and for
a webhook's `run.completed`:

| Format | What it is |
|---|---|
| JSON (the default) | The rows of the run's final output, masked by your data policy |
| PDF | The run's report (its Generate report step): the signed PDF once it is approved and signed |
| HTML | The report's page; with no report, the rows as a table |
| Markdown | Made from the report's page: headings, tables, lists; pictures and signatures as links to the PDF. Its first line says which report it is from and whether it is signed. Markdown is never signed itself: the PDF is the record. With no report, the rows as a table |

A run with no report has no PDF. A run that made one report per row names the one it wants. Anything else -- Word,
Excel -- is refused, naming the four formats. A pipeline marked sensitive keeps its report from the API in every
format, as it keeps its files; the JSON stays masked. Choosing a format costs nothing more than the call.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| A token | 15 minutes |
| An Idempotency-Key | Kept 24 hours; 8 to 128 characters |
| Waiting for a run | 1 to 60 seconds |
| A run's result through the API | The first 100 rows, up to 16 KB (a report as PDF, HTML or Markdown: the whole report) |
| A webhook's result formats | Up to 5 MB of documents a delivery; past it, the system reads that format through the API |
| Runs of one pipeline at a time | One in flight; a second start while one runs is refused |

## Example
Summit Valley Health System's *Partner portal* starts the pipeline *Partner starts a run through the API* for each lab
record, with the record's id as its reference and as its Idempotency-Key. A record missing its test code is refused at
once with the field named. When the same request is sent twice after a network error, the second answer is the first
run. The portal then reads the run's outputs and downloads the report made for each result.

articles.title: Events and event routes
articles.summary: Your systems send events of your own types; an event route says which pipeline or workflow each type starts, and the data contract it must meet.
articles.who: Workspace administrators make event routes; your systems send events with events:write

where.label: Administration & billing › Developers › API Clients › Event routes

articles.md:
An **event** is a message from one of your systems saying that something happened: *a referral was accepted*, *a lab
result is ready*, *a device took a reading*. Its **type** is yours to name. An **event route** says what that type
starts in the workspace: a run of a pipeline (with the event's data as the run's record) or a workflow request.

## Add an event route
1. Open **Administration & billing › Developers › API Clients** and scroll to **Event routes**.
2. Choose **New event route**.
3. **Event type**: letters, digits and `. _ : -`, such as `lab.result.created`.
4. **Starts**: **A pipeline's run** (then choose the **Pipeline**) or **A workflow request** (then type the
   **Workflow key** of one of your approval workflows).
5. **Data contract (optional)**: the name of a data contract the event's data must meet.
6. Choose **Add route**.

![Event routes](dev-routes "Event routes: each event type, what it starts, its data contract and its state")

Each route's row shows its **Event type**, what it **Starts**, its **Contract** and its **State**, with **Change** and
**Remove**.

## What happens when an event arrives
- A type with a route starts what the route names, at once. The answer lists what it started, and what could not start
  and why (for example a run of that pipeline still in flight).
- With a data contract, data that does not meet it is refused with each wrong field named, and nothing starts.
- A type that no route takes is refused.

> **Tip:** Name event types for what happened, from your system's side (`admission.accepted`), not for what you want
> the console to do. Then one event can later start a second pipeline without your system changing.

## Events the platform sends back
The other direction is **webhooks**: the platform's own events (a run started, completed or failed, a review requested
or decided, an item finished, a file ready, an alert opened or resolved) sent to a URL of yours. See
[Webhooks](#dev-webhooks).

## Example
Summit Valley Health System routes three event types:

| Event type | Starts | Contract |
|---|---|---|
| `admission.accepted` | The workflow *Patient journey* | — |
| `lab.result.created` | The pipeline *Journey 6 · Lab results from the partner lab* | `lab_result` |
| `device.reading` | The pipeline *Remote monitoring: readings over threshold* | `device_reading` |

When *Northgate Labs* sends a lab result without its test code, the contract refuses it and no run starts. When
*HomeLink devices* sends an SpO2 reading of 88, the remote monitoring pipeline runs and pages the care team.

articles.title: Files and forms through the API
articles.summary: Upload files for a run, download what a run made through short-lived links, and submit your workspace's forms from another system.
articles.who: Your systems, with files:write, files:read, forms:read or forms:write
articles.md:
Files and form answers travel through the API without your systems ever seeing a bucket, a storage key or a connection.
A file is an id; a form is an id and its fields.

## Send a file in
1. The system uploads the file (scope `files:write`), with an **Idempotency-Key**, and gets back the file's id.
2. It names that id when it starts a run, or in a file field of a form submission. An upload by itself starts nothing.
3. Uploading the same file again with the same key gives the same file, never a second one.

## Get a file out
1. A run's outputs list every file it made, each by its id, with its checksum (see
   [Start a run and read it back](#dev-runs)). A webhook can say when one is ready (`file.available`).
2. The system asks for the file (scope `files:read`) and is sent to a **signed link** that works without a token for
   5 minutes. It can download it there, or hand the link to the person's browser so the file never passes through
   its own server.
3. When a link has expired, it asks for a fresh one.

> **Note:** A file a run made is kept for as long as the pipeline keeps its runs' files. After that it is still
> listed, marked expired, and can no longer be downloaded: run the pipeline again for a new one.

## Submit a form
1. The system lists the **active forms** it may fill in (scope `forms:read`), each with its fields.
2. It submits the answers (scope `forms:write`). A file field names the id of a file it uploaded first.
3. The submission starts the form's pipeline or workflow, if the form has one.

A webhook subscribed to `form.submission.received` hears of every submission, from the console, a share link or the
API.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| One upload | 100 MB |
| A download link | 5 minutes |
| A file made by a run | Kept as long as the pipeline keeps its runs' files |

## Example
Summit Valley Health System's *Partner portal* uploads a 2 MB CSV of partner lab results, then starts the pipeline
*Partner files: upload and process* with the file's id. When the run completes, the portal reads its outputs and
gives the clinic's browser a 5-minute link to the processed file.

articles.title: Webhooks
articles.summary: Be told when runs start, finish, fail or wait for review: subscribe a URL, check the signature, read the delivery log, send a delivery again and rotate the secret.
articles.who: Workspace administrators add and change webhooks (read-only in a managed workspace); your receiver checks each delivery

where.label: Administration & billing › Developers › API Clients › Webhooks

articles.popular: Set up a webhook
articles.md:
A **webhook** is a URL of yours that the platform calls when something happens in the workspace, instead of your
system asking again and again. Each event is sent as a signed POST of JSON, retried until your receiver takes it, and
logged.

## Add a webhook
1. Open **Administration & billing › Developers › API Clients** and scroll to **Webhooks**.
2. Choose **New webhook**.
3. **URL**: an `https` address on the public internet, such as `https://portal.example.com/hooks/etl`. A private or
   local address is refused.
4. Tick the **Events** to send (see the table below).
5. With `run.completed` ticked, you may also tick **The run's result** formats it carries: **JSON** (the result rows,
   masked), **PDF** (the run's report, signed once approved), **HTML** and **Markdown** (made from the report's page;
   with no report, the rows as a table). None ticked sends the run alone.
6. Choose **Add webhook**. The console shows **Webhook added** with its **Signing secret**.
7. **Copy** the signing secret into your receiver's settings now: it is not shown again.

Only events after the webhook is added are sent.

| Event | Sent when |
|---|---|
| `run.started` | A run began its steps, or a retry began its next attempt |
| `run.completed` | A run finished; its outputs can be read |
| `run.failed` | A run ended in failure; the event says why |
| `run.item.completed` | One item of a run (a file, recording, document or row) finished, done or failed |
| `run.review.requested` | A completed run waits for a review your organisation takes part in |
| `run.review.decided` | Someone decided on a run's results |
| `file.available` | A file a run made can be downloaded |
| `form.submission.received` | A form received a submission, from the console, a share link or the API |
| `alert.opened`, `alert.resolved` | An alert rule of the workspace fired, or its alert cleared (see [Alerts](#set-alerts)) |
| `run.step.sent` | A pipeline's **Send webhook** step sent its rows to this webhook (only the webhook the step names) |

![Webhooks](dev-webhooks "Webhooks: each URL, its events, when it last delivered, and its state")

## The run's result with run.completed
A webhook with result formats gets `run.completed` with the run's result inside it (`data.results`), in each format
ticked: JSON as data, HTML and Markdown as text, the PDF as base64. The list of webhooks shows the formats under the
events. The result is read when each delivery is sent, so a retry or a **Send again** carries it as it is then, and the
signature covers it. A format the run cannot be given in is named with the reason instead -- a sensitive pipeline's
report, a PDF of a run with no report, more than 5 MB of documents -- and your system reads that one through the API.

## How your receiver checks a delivery
Every delivery carries a `Webhook-Signature` header with a time (`t`) and a signature (`v1`): an HMAC-SHA256 of the
time, a dot and the raw body, made with the signing secret. Your receiver should:

1. Work out the same signature over the body exactly as received, and compare it with `v1`.
2. Refuse a delivery whose time is more than five minutes from its own clock.
3. Answer with a success code within 10 seconds, then do the work.
4. Keep the `Webhook-Id` of each event it has handled, and ignore one it has seen: a delivery can arrive twice.

The portal's **Webhooks** guide has a receiver to copy in Python and Node.js.

## Retries and pausing
- Anything but a success answer within 10 seconds is a failed attempt. It is tried again after 10 s, 30 s, 90 s and
  so on, at most an hour apart, for a day; then the delivery is **failed**.
- A webhook with no successful delivery for 3 days is **paused**, and the person who added it is told. Fix the
  receiver, then **Resume** it.
- Order events by the time in the event, not by when they arrive: a retry does not hold later events back.

## The delivery log, and sending one again
1. In the webhook's ⋯ menu choose **Deliveries**.
2. Each delivery shows **When**, the **Event**, its **State** (pending, retrying with the next try's time,
   delivered or failed), its **Attempts** and the receiver's **Last answer**. Open the attempts to see each one.
3. **Send again** sends a delivery once more, with the same `Webhook-Id`, so your receiver's check for repeats still
   holds. **Older deliveries** reads further back.

![Deliveries](dev-deliveries "Deliveries: each event sent, its state, its attempts and the receiver's last answer")

## Rotate the signing secret
1. In the webhook's ⋯ menu choose **New secret** and confirm with **Make a new secret**.
2. Copy the new signing secret into your receiver.
3. For 24 hours deliveries are signed with both the new and the old secret, so your receiver can switch over without
   missing one.

The same menu has **Change** (its URL and events), **Pause** and **Remove**.

## What it costs
Each delivery that reaches your receiver is billed as a webhook delivery, per 1,000 (see
[How usage is counted](#bill-usage)).

## Example
Summit Valley Health System's webhook *Partner portal* hears `run.completed`, `run.failed`, `run.review.decided` and
`run.item.completed`. When the portal's receiver was down for two minutes, the log showed three retrying attempts and
then **delivered**; the team sent one delivery again from the log to test their repeat check, and rotated the secret
the next morning.

articles.title: Embed a run view in your portal
articles.summary: Show one run's progress, steps, files and review inside your own portal with a signed 15-minute link, framed only by the sites you allow.
articles.who: Workspace administrators allow the sites; your portal asks for the links with runs:read
articles.md:
A **run view** is a page of one run that your own portal can show in a frame, so your users follow their work without
signing in to the console. It shows the run's status and times, its steps, the files it made (each with a download)
and its review, and refreshes itself while the run moves. It has no console menu, needs no sign-in, sends no cookies,
and shows that one run only.

## Allow your portal's site
1. Open **Administration & billing › Developers › API Clients**, open the portal's client's ⋯ menu and choose
   **Change**.
2. Under **Sites that may embed its run views (optional)**, list your portal's origins, one per line, such as
   `https://portal.example.com` or `https://*.example.com`.
3. Choose **Save**. The client's row then says **Run views embed on** those sites.

With no sites listed, a view link still opens on its own in a browser tab, but no page can show it in a frame.

## How the portal shows a run
1. When a user opens a run in your portal, the portal's server asks the API for a **view link** for that run
   (scope `runs:read`).
2. The link lasts 15 minutes, or less if the portal asks for less. The portal puts it in a frame.
3. The page can follow the portal's light or dark look and its accent colour.
4. When the link expires, the page says so and reads nothing more; the portal asks for a new link.

> **Privacy:** The portal's own token never goes to the browser, only the view link. Revoking the API client, or its
> expiry, ends all its links at once.

![A run view's sites](dev-client-change "A client's settings: Sites that may embed its run views")

## What it costs
Asking for a link is one API call. What the page then reads, and the files downloaded from it, are not counted as
calls.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| A view link | Up to 15 minutes, one run |
| Who may frame it | Only the sites listed on the client |

## Example
Summit Valley Health System's *Partner portal* client lists the portal's development site as a site that may embed its
run views. When a clinic opens a lab result in the portal, the portal asks for a 10-minute view link and shows the run
in a frame beside the patient's record.

articles.title: The Developer portal
articles.summary: The API's guides with samples in curl, Python and Node.js, the reference, your clients' scopes, the APIs your pipelines call, the changelog and the downloads.
articles.who: Workspace administrators, and members whose page access names Developer portal
articles.md:
The **Developer portal** is the API's documentation inside the console, for the developers who connect your systems.
Every sample in it comes in curl, Python and Node.js. Give your developers access to it rather than copying its
contents elsewhere: it is kept up to date with the API.

## What is in it
| Part | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **Overview** | What the API is for, the **Base URL** to copy, your sandbox, and the **Downloads** |
| **Guides** | Quickstart, The sandbox, Webhooks, Files and file links, Run items, Run and wait, Reports from a pipeline, Idempotency, Paging and filters, Errors, Rate limits and quotas, Embedding a run view |
| **Your API clients** | What each of this workspace's clients may call with its scopes, and a quick start for each |
| **APIs this workspace calls** | The other direction: the saved requests your pipelines and workflows send out, and what each last answered |
| **API reference** | Every call, its scope, parameters, answers and errors, with a curl call to copy; the schemas |
| **Event types**, **Problem types**, **Rate limits** | The events a webhook can hear, the errors the API answers, the limits and their headers |
| **Changelog** | What changed in the API, newest first |
| **Downloads** | The OpenAPI document (YAML and JSON) and a Postman collection |

![The Developer portal](dev-portal "The Developer portal: what the API is for, the guides, the Base URL, the sandbox and the downloads")

## Where to start
1. Read **Quickstart**: a test key, a token, a pipeline, a file, a run and its results, in about ten minutes, in the
   sandbox.
2. Then **Webhooks**, so the system hears back instead of asking.
3. Then **Errors**, **Idempotency** and **Rate limits and quotas**, so the system behaves well when things go wrong.

## Give a developer access
1. A workspace administrator opens **Administration & billing › Administration › Page access**.
2. Adds **Developer portal** to the developer's profile. It is never on by default.
3. The developer sees **Administration & billing › Developers › Developer portal**. Making API clients and test keys
   stays with administrators.

> **Note:** **Your API clients** in the portal shows which calls each client may make with its current scopes, and
> which need a scope it does not have. **Change its scopes** takes an administrator to the client.

## Example
Priya Singh, a developer at Summit Valley Health System, has the **Developer portal** in her profile. She follows the
**Quickstart** against the sandbox, checks under **Your API clients** that *Partner portal* has `files:write`, and
downloads the Postman collection to share with the portal's vendor.

articles.title: Upload documents and mail them in
articles.summary: Upload PDFs and images, read a file already in storage, or mail attachments to the workspace's own address; rotate it when it leaks.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Documents uploads and reads what arrived; workspace administrators turn Email-in on or off and give it a new address
articles.popular: Send documents in by email
articles.md:
**Documents › Intake** holds every way files reach the workspace. Two of its sections make **documents**: each file
you upload or mail in is read, matched to a document type and split into fields, and the values it is unsure of go to
**Review › Documents**. The third, **File drop**, stores files for pipelines without reading them; see
[The file drop](#doc-file-drop).

Whatever the channel, one file is one document, and a file the workspace already has (by any channel) is kept once.

## Upload documents
1. Open **Get data in › Documents** and choose the **Intake** tab, then **Upload**.
2. Choose **Upload documents**.
3. Drop the files on the box, or choose **Choose files**: PDF, PNG, JPEG, TIFF or BMP, up to 20 at once.
4. Choose **Upload**. The dialog then says what became of each file.

Each file is read, classified and extracted, and appears on **Documents › Documents in**. A type's values that need a
look wait in **Review › Documents**.

![The Upload section with what arrived](doc-intake-upload "Intake › Upload: Upload documents, Read a stored file, and what arrived, with a duplicate kept once")

## Read a file that is already in storage
If the file is already in one of the workspace's storage connections (a scan the copier saved to a bucket, say):

1. Choose **Read a stored file**.
2. Pick the **Storage connection**, and drop the file or name its **Folder** and file.
3. Under **Document type**, pick one, or leave it to the page: it is compared with every active type.
4. Choose **Read and extract**. The dialog shows each step: **Store the file**, **Read its pages (OCR)**, **Extract
   the fields**.

## What arrived
Under each section, **What arrived** lists the files offered by every channel, newest first:

| Column | Says |
|---|---|
| **File** | The file's own name |
| **Channel** | **Upload**, **Email**, **Form** or **Connector** |
| **From** | Who uploaded it, or the sender and subject of the mail |
| **Outcome** | **Taken**, **Duplicate** (the same file as an earlier one; no second document was made) or **Refused**, with the reason |
| **Document** | The document it became, as a link to its review screen |
| **Arrived** | When |

Filter it by channel with the list beside its title.

![Upload documents](doc-upload-dialog "Upload documents: PDFs and images, up to 20 at once")

## Mail documents in with Email-in
Every workspace can have its own address. Attachments mailed to it become documents, read and extracted as an upload
is.

1. Choose **Intake**, then **Email-in**.
2. If the workspace has no address yet, an administrator chooses **Turn on**.
3. Copy the address with the copy button and give it to whoever sends you documents: a referring clinic, a supplier's
   billing office, your own scanner.

The card says how many attachments a message may carry and how large each may be. **What arrived** shows each
attachment with the sender and subject, such as "Email from referrals@northside-clinic.example: Referral: Elena
Marsh".

![The Email-in section with the workspace's address](doc-email-in "Email-in: the address, its limits, New address and Turn off, and what arrived by mail")

## Give it a new address, or turn it off
Anyone who has the address can send to it. If it leaks, or a sender should no longer reach you, an administrator
chooses **New address**: the workspace gets a new address and the old one is shut out. Tell your senders the new one.

**Turn off** stops Email-in: mail to the address is ignored until it is turned on again.

> **Privacy:** Treat the address like a password. Give it only to senders who need it, and choose **New address** when
> it may have been shared further.

> **Note:** If the section says "Email-in is not set up on this platform", your platform has no mail domain for it
> yet. Ask your account team.

## Example
Northside Family Clinic mails Summit Valley a referral for Elena Marsh with two attachments. Both appear under **What
arrived** as **Taken**: `referral-SV-000117.pdf` becomes a **Referral** document and the scanned second page a
**Wound assessment form**. Greta Fischer in health information checks them in **Review › Documents**.

articles.title: The file drop
articles.summary: Drop files for pipelines; set the storage connection and size limit, see what arrived, and start a schedule when a file lands.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes the file drop uploads; workspace administrators set it up and change its settings
articles.md:
The file drop is for files a pipeline should work on, not documents to read: a CSV export, a batch of wound photos, an
X-ray, a spreadsheet from finance. Each file is checked, stored in the workspace's bucket, and starts every schedule set
to start when a matching file arrives. It is not read as a document.

![The File drop section](doc-file-drop "File drop: Upload, its Settings, and the newest arrivals with who uploaded them")

## Set it up (administrators)
Until it is set up, the section says **No file drop yet**.

1. Open **Documents › Intake › File drop** and choose **Set up the file drop** (or, later, **Change** under
   **Settings**).
2. Pick the **Storage connection** the files go to: one of the workspace's own. Files land under `intake/` in its
   bucket.
3. Optionally set a **Size limit (MB)** below the platform's. Empty means the platform's limit, which the dialog names.
4. Choose **Turn on the file drop** (or **Save changes**).

![File drop settings](doc-file-drop-settings "File drop settings: the storage connection and an optional size limit")

**Turn off**, in the same dialog, stops uploads after you confirm: members can no longer upload and no new file starts
a run. The files already stored stay in the bucket, and you can turn it on again later.

## Drop files
1. Drag files onto **Drop files here**, or choose **Choose files**. Several at once is fine: they are sent one by one.
2. **This session's uploads** shows each file **Queued**, **Uploading**, **Uploaded** with its SHA-256, or
   **Refused** with why. **Clear finished** tidies the list.

Choose **What the file drop accepts** to see the kinds it takes: data files (CSV, TSV, TXT, JSON, JSON Lines, XML,
YAML, Parquet), documents (PDF, Markdown, Word, Excel, PowerPoint), images (PNG, JPEG, GIF, TIFF), audio and video
(MP3, WAV, M4A, MP4) and archives (ZIP, GZ).

> **Warning:** Executables and scripts are refused whatever they are named, and a file's contents must match its
> extension. A refused file is not stored. Files are not scanned for viruses, so drop only files you trust.

## Where files land
Each file is stored as `intake/<date>/<arrival>-<file name>` in the chosen connection's bucket. **Arrivals** lists the
newest 50: **File** (with its type and the key a pipeline's read step names it by, which you can copy), **Size**,
**Uploaded by**, **Uploaded** and **SHA-256**. Files can also arrive through the API.

## Start a pipeline when a file arrives
Which files start which pipeline is set on the schedule, not here:

1. Open **Pipelines › Schedules** and the schedule (or make a new one).
2. Under **When it runs**, in **Also starts when**, turn on **A file arrives**.
3. In **Which files**, give a pattern: `*` matches any run of characters and `?` one, so `*.csv` or `wound-*.jpg`.
   Leave it blank for every file.
4. In **Files per run**, `1` starts a run per file; a larger number lets files that waited go together, up to that
   many.
5. Save the schedule.

A file that lands while a run is going waits its turn. The runs a file started are listed on each schedule.

## Example
On Ward 4B, Daniel Kim photographs a wound at each dressing change and drops the photo in the file drop. The photos land
in Summit Valley's `summit-valley-s3` bucket under `intake/`, within its 25 MB limit, and each one starts the
wound-measurement schedule set to start on `wound-*.jpg`.

articles.title: Document types
articles.summary: Add ready-made types for healthcare and finance, or make your own with its fields, line-item tables and when it is approved on its own.
articles.who: Workspace administrators make and change document types; anyone whose page access includes Document types reads them
articles.md:
A document type tells the console what one kind of document is and what to read from it: a referral, a lab result, an
invoice. Each incoming document is matched to a type and its fields are read against it. Start from a ready-made type
and change it to fit your paperwork, or make your own.

![The Document types tab](doc-types "Document types: fields, tables and rules per type, its auto-approve line, version, and what its approval starts")

## The list
| Column | Says |
|---|---|
| **Type** | Its name, with its key underneath |
| **Fields**, **Tables**, **Rules** | How many it has |
| **Auto-approve at** | How sure every value must be for a document to be approved on its own, or **Never**; **Off: every document reviewed** when the type cannot approve on its own (see [Auto-approve needs key fields](#doc-types)) |
| **Version** | The current version |
| **Kind** | **This workspace** (yours) or **Built-in** |
| **When approved, starts…** | The schedules an approved document of this type starts; see [When a document is approved](#doc-when-approved) |
| **State** | **Active** or **Inactive** |

## Add from starters
1. Open **Get data in › Documents › Document types** and choose **Add from starters**.
2. The starters are grouped by the work that reads them: **Healthcare** (Referral, Lab result, Discharge summary,
   Insurance card, Prior authorization, Patient intake form, Medication list, Consent form) and **ERP and finance**
   (Invoice, Purchase order, Contract, Receipt, Delivery note). Each says what it reads.
3. Tick the ones you receive and choose **Add**. Types you already have say **Added**.

Each one added is this workspace's own type, to change as you like.

![Add from starters](doc-starters "Add from starters: ready-made types by market, each with the fields it reads")

## Make your own type
1. Choose **New document type**.
2. Give it a **Name** and a **Key** in lower_snake_case, such as `wound_assessment`. The key cannot change later.
3. **What it is**: one sentence the model reads when it decides what a document is, such as "A wound assessment: the
   patient, the wound's site, its size in centimetres and its stage."
4. **Words on the page**: comma-separated words that appear on this kind of document, to help tell it apart.
5. **Auto-approve at**: a percentage. A document whose every value is at least this sure, with no problem, and whose
   key fields its lookups confirmed, is approved on its own. Leave it empty to send every document to a reviewer.
6. **Instructions**: anything the model should know when it reads this type, such as your own conventions.
7. Under **Fields**, add each value to read: a key, a **Label**, a type (`text`, `number`, `integer`, `money`, `date`,
   `boolean` or `choice`, with its options), **Required**, and the other words it goes by on a page (**Also written
   as**: Invoice No., Invoice #). A choice may also say how a page writes each option (**Options written as**:
   `High = H; Low = L; Normal = N`): a lab printout's `H` is then read as High, and the `H` is where High came from. Each
   word belongs to one option, and is never another option itself.
8. Under **Line-item tables**, choose **Add table** for rows such as invoice lines or lab tests: a key, a label, its
   columns, and **At least one row** if a document must have one.
9. Under **Rules**, add the checks a document must pass. See [Checks on a document](#doc-checks).
10. Choose **Save**.

![A document type open in its panel](doc-type-editor "A document type: what it is, the words on the page, the auto-approve line, and its fields")

## Change a type
Open the type and choose **Edit**. When you are done, **Save as the next version**: documents read before keep the
version they were read with, and the **Versions** list keeps every one. **Switch off** stops a type being used for new
documents; **Switch on** brings it back.

A **Built-in** type is read-only. Choose **Customise** to make your own copy: it keeps the same key, so once saved it
reads this workspace's documents in the built-in one's place.

> **Note:** A value read from a document is shown exactly as it was read, never reformatted as a number, money or a
> date, so a reviewer compares the page with what was really kept.

## Example
Summit Valley added the eight healthcare starters and the five finance ones, then made its own **Wound assessment
form** (patient, site, length and width in centimetres, stage) and a **Lab panel** with arithmetic and unusual-value
rules. Its **Invoice**, changed once, is at **v2**.

## Auto-approve needs key fields
Confidence alone never approves a document. A type approves its documents on its own only when:

1. it has an **Auto-approve at** line;
2. its **key fields** are marked: tick **Key** on each field that says who or what the document is about, such as the
   payer, the patient, the member ID or the accession number (a document's fields only, never a table's columns);
3. every key field has a **Lookup** rule against your reference data, a dataset or a CSV or JSON file in one of your
   buckets (see [Checks a document must pass](#doc-checks)).

A document is then approved on its own only when every value clears the line, nothing is wrong, and **every key
field's lookup found its value**. Otherwise it waits in review.

The type's panel says which: **Documents are approved on their own when...**, or **Auto-approve is off: every document of
this type goes to review**, with what is missing. The starters mark their key fields (the insurance card's payer and
member ID, the lab result's patient ID and accession number, the referral's patient ID and referring NPI, the intake
form's patient name, date of birth and insurance member ID); add a lookup on each to turn auto-approve on.

> **Note:** Types made before this rule keep their line, but their documents go to review until their key fields are
> marked and looked up. The list shows **Off: every document reviewed** under such a type's line.

articles.title: Checks on a document
articles.summary: Rules a document type keeps: sums and products, dates in order, patterns and check digits, duplicates, reference lists and unusual values.
articles.who: Workspace administrators add rules; reviewers see each rule's result on the review screen
articles.md:
A model can read a number perfectly and the document can still be wrong: lines that do not add up, a due date before
the invoice date, an invoice paid twice. A document type's **Rules** check each document after it is read. A rule that
fails is shown to the reviewer with your message, and a document with a problem is not approved on its own.

## Add a rule
1. Open the document type and choose **Edit**.
2. Under **Rules**, choose **Add rule** and pick its kind.
3. Pick what it checks (the fields, the table, the columns) and fill in its settings.
4. Optionally write **What a reviewer is told when it fails**.
5. Choose **Save as the next version**.

![An invoice type's rules](doc-checks "Rules: sums, dates in order, a reference list and an unusual total, each with the message a reviewer sees")

## The kinds of rule
**On the document itself**

| Rule | Checks | You give |
|---|---|---|
| **A table column adds up to a field** | The column's rows sum to a field (lines to the subtotal) | The table, the column, the field, a tolerance (0.01) |
| **Fields add up to a field** | Some fields sum to another (subtotal + tax = total) | The fields, the total field, a tolerance |
| **In every row, two columns multiply to a third** | quantity × unit price = amount, on each line | The table, the two columns, the product column, a tolerance |
| **One date is on or before another** | Invoice date on or before due date; birth before admission | The earlier date and the later date |
| **Every value has a form (a pattern)** | A value matches a pattern, such as `[A-Z]{2}[0-9]{6}` | The field (or a table column) and the pattern |
| **An ID's check digit holds** | The last digit of an ID is right | The field, and **Luhn** (cards, many account numbers) or the IBAN check |

**Beyond the one document**

| Rule | Checks | You give |
|---|---|---|
| **Not a duplicate of another document** | No other document of this type has the same values | The fields a duplicate shares (vendor and invoice number), and optionally **Within days** (all when empty) |
| **A value is in a reference list** | A value appears in a list you keep | A list name, and either a file in a bucket (CSV, TSV, JSON or JSON Lines: its storage connection, file and column) or another document type's approved data (its field) |
| **A number is not unusual for this type** | A number is not far from what approved documents of this type usually say | The number field; optionally a field to compare within (the same vendor); **Unusually high or low**, high only or low only; more than N × the median, or more than k MADs away (3.5 when both are empty); and **Applies after N approved documents** (5) |

## What the reviewer sees
On the review screen, **Rule check** lists each rule:

- a tick and **holds** when it passed;
- a cross and **fails** when it did not, with your message, and for a duplicate **Open the other document**;
- a dash and **not checked: a value it needs is missing** when a field it needs was not read.

**Before it can be approved** lists what must be fixed first, such as a required field not found on the document.

> **Tip:** A rule that fails is a question for a person, not a refusal. Write the message as what to check: "The line
> items do not add up to the subtotal."

> **Note:** In bulk review, documents whose rules fail are left out unless the workspace's review policy includes them.
> See [Review many documents at once](#doc-bulk-review).

## Example
Summit Valley's **Invoice** type keeps six rules: the line items add up to the subtotal, the due date is not before the
invoice date, subtotal and tax add up to the total, quantity × unit price = amount on every line, the PO number is in
the open purchase orders list (`finance/ap/open-pos.csv` in the finance bucket), and the total is not unusually high for
the same vendor. A supplier invoice for a PO the hospital never raised stops in review with the lookup rule failing.

articles.title: How documents are read
articles.summary: Text read from scans and photos, the document matched to a type, each value with how sure it is, and one document per file.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Documents in
articles.md:
When a file arrives, three things happen before anyone looks at it:

1. **Its pages are read.** The platform's own text recognition (OCR) reads each page, so a scan, a fax or a phone photo
   becomes text with the position of every word.
2. **It is matched to a type.** The text is compared with every active document type (its **What it is** and **Words on
   the page**). You can also pick the type yourself when you read a stored file.
3. **Its fields are extracted.** The type's fields and tables are read from the text, each value with how sure the
   reading is and where on the page it was found.

What comes out is a draft: values a person checks in review, unless every one is sure enough and the type's key fields
were confirmed by their lookups, so that the document is approved on its own (see
[Auto-approve needs key fields](#doc-types)).

![Documents in](doc-documents-in "Documents in: each document's type, fields to check, confidence and state")

## Documents in
**Get data in › Documents › Documents in** lists the recent documents. The tiles count the **Documents** of the last
30 days, the share **Auto-approved**, how many are **In review**, and **Field accuracy**, the share of values reviewers
left as they were read.

| Column | Says |
|---|---|
| **Document** | The file's own name, where it came from and its pages |
| **Type** | The type it was matched to, or **Not classified** |
| **Fields** | How many values were read, and how many are **to check** |
| **Confidence** | The least sure value |
| **State** | See below |
| **Received** | When |

Filter by type and state, or search. **Open** in a row's menu goes to its review screen; **Extract again** reads it
again, as the same type or after you fix the type.

## How sure it is
Each value has a confidence from 0 to 100 %, drawn as a bar. A value is flagged **check** when it is less sure than the
type's **Auto-approve at** line (80 % when the type has none), when a problem was found with it, or when a required
value was not found. A value a reviewer corrected counts as the reviewer's.

> **Note:** Confidence is how sure the reading is, not whether the document is true. A clear page with a wrong number on
> it reads at 100 %. That is what rules and review are for.

## The states
| State | Means |
|---|---|
| **Queued**, **Running** | Being read |
| **Unclassified** | It did not look like any active type: pick the type and choose **Extract again** |
| **Failed** | The extraction did not finish; choose **Extract again** |
| **In review** | Waiting for a person in **Review › Documents** |
| **Approved** | Approved by a reviewer |
| **Auto-approved** | Every value was sure enough, nothing was wrong, and every key field's lookup confirmed it |
| **Rejected** | A reviewer rejected it, with a reason |

## One document per file
Each file is one document. A file the workspace has received before, by any channel, is recognised by its content and
kept once: **What arrived** lists it as **Duplicate** and links the earlier document, and it is not read again. A
document of several kinds of page (a referral with a scanned clinical summary) is best sent as separate files, each
matched to its own type.

## Example
Summit Valley's `referral-SV-000117-page2-scan.pdf` is a faxed page. The text recognition reads "left foot plantar
ulcer 4 x 3 cm"; the page is matched to **Wound assessment form**; **Site**, **Length (cm)** and **Width (cm)** are read
at 91 to 92 % and **Stage** is not found at all, so all of them are flagged for Greta Fischer to check against the page.

articles.title: Review a document
articles.summary: The page beside its fields; claim it, correct a value, approve, or reject with a reason.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Review › Documents
articles.popular: Review a document
articles.md:
A document that was not approved on its own waits in **Run & review › Review › Documents** for a person: you check
the values it was unsure of against the page, correct what is wrong, and approve or reject it. Only an approved
document's values reach its type's approved data and start what its approval starts.

## The queue
**Review › Documents** lists the documents that were not approved on their own, oldest first. Filter by state (**In
review**, **Approved**, **Rejected**), type, who has claimed it (**Anyone's**, **Claimed by me**, **Not claimed**,
**Claimed by others**), how sure the least sure value is, and how long it has waited.

| Column | Says |
|---|---|
| **Document** | The file's name |
| **Type** | Its type and version |
| **To check** | How many of its values need a look |
| **Least sure** | Its least sure value |
| **Waiting since** | When it arrived for review |
| **Claimed** | Who is on it |

Choose a document to open it, or **Start reviewing** to open the first one nobody else holds.

![The document review queue](doc-review-queue "Review › Documents: what waits, how much to check and who has claimed it")

## Check and decide
The review screen shows the page on the left and the **Extracted fields** on the right.

1. Choose **Claim** so that others see you are on it. **Let go** gives it back.
2. Work down the fields flagged **check**. Choosing a field draws its box on the page; ↓ and ↑ move between fields.
   Zoom the page with − and +.
3. Correct a value by typing over it. For a table, edit the cells or choose **Add row**.
4. Read the **Rule check** and, if shown, **Before it can be approved**.
5. Choose **Save corrections** to keep your changes, or **Discard changes**.
6. Decide:
   - **Approve & next** (or press A) approves it and opens the next document.
   - **Reject** (or press R) asks **Why**, which is kept with the document; choose **Reject** again to confirm.

![A referral on the review screen](doc-review "The review screen: the page with each value's box, the fields with how sure each is, and the rule check")

On approve, the document's values go to its type's approved data (**Documents › Approved data**), and your corrections
are kept with it. **Corrections** on the screen lists each change: the field, what it was, what it is now, who changed
it and when.

![Reject this document](doc-reject "Reject: a reason is required and kept with the document")

> **Tip:** The shortcuts (A approve, R reject, ↓ next field) do nothing while you are typing in a field, so you cannot
> approve by accident.

## When you cannot decide it
- **Claimed by** someone else: they decide it; the screen is read-only for you.
- **Approved** or **Rejected** already: the screen says by whom and when, and is read-only.
- **Failed**: the extraction did not finish. Extract it again from **Documents › Documents in**.

> **Note:** What a model read is a draft. Approving it says a person checked it against the page; the approval records
> who you are.

## Example
Greta Fischer opens `referral-upload-8.pdf`, a **Referral**. **Referral date** and **Referred to** are required but
were not found, so **Before it can be approved** lists both. The page really has neither, so she does not guess: she
chooses **Reject** with the reason "No referral date or receiving service; clinic asked to resend". When the clinic's
corrected letter arrives, she checks it, and **Approve & next** puts its values in the Referral approved data.

articles.title: Review many documents at once
articles.summary: Approve or reject up to 100 documents in one decision, and the workspace's review policy that allows it.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Review › Documents decides in bulk; workspace administrators set the review policy
articles.md:
When many documents wait and they are alike (a batch of clean receipts, say), deciding them one by one is slow. Tick
them in the queue and decide them together. Each document is still decided and recorded on its own, and the console
first shows you what would happen.

## Decide several together
1. Open **Review › Documents** and filter the list to what you want to decide, for example one type and **Not
   claimed**.
2. Tick the documents, or tick the box in the header to take every one on the page that can be decided. **Select all
   matching** takes up to the first 100 that match the filters.
3. The bar at the foot says how many are selected, with **Reject**, **Approve** and **Clear**.
4. Choose **Approve** or **Reject**. A panel opens and checks what would happen: how many would be decided, grouped by
   document type, which will be skipped and why, and any that could not be checked.
5. Add a comment. It is applied to each document, and required to reject.
6. Above 25 documents, type the number back to confirm.
7. Choose the button, which says what it does: **Approve 12**. The panel then lists each document as decided, skipped or
   failed, each with a link. Choose **Done**.

![Two documents selected in the review queue](doc-bulk "Bulk review: the selected documents, and Reject, Approve and Clear at the foot")

**What is skipped:** a document someone else has claimed (theirs to decide), one already decided, and, unless the policy
includes them, one whose rules fail.

## The review policy (administrators)
Whether documents may be approved in bulk at all is the workspace's choice.

1. Open **Administration › Data policies**.
2. Under **Bulk review**:
   - **Allow bulk approve of documents**: off, documents are approved one by one.
   - **Include documents whose rules fail**: off (the default), a document with a failing rule is skipped and approved
     on its own screen. On, the failures are accepted, and the override is recorded on each document.
   - **Allow bulk approve of runs** is the same choice for pipeline runs that wait for review.
3. Choose **Save review policy**.

Rejecting in bulk is always allowed.

![The Bulk review policy](doc-review-policy "Administration › Data policies › Bulk review: runs, documents, and documents whose rules fail")

> **Warning:** A bulk approval is your decision on every document in it. Filter to the documents you have really looked
> at, and keep **Include documents whose rules fail** off unless your process says otherwise.

## Example
Summit Valley allows bulk approval of documents but not of documents whose rules fail. At month end Claire Martin
filters **Review › Documents** to **Receipt** and **Not claimed**, checks the values of the 40 listed, ticks them all,
types `40` to confirm and approves them with the comment "Checked against the card statement"; two receipts with a failing
duplicate rule are skipped, and she opens each on its own.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Documents in one decision | 100 |
| Typing the count back | Above 25 |
| Comment | Up to 500 characters; required to reject |

articles.title: Approved data
articles.summary: Each document type's dataset, one row per approved document; download it, and read it in pipelines and checks.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Approved data
articles.md:
Every document type has a dataset: one row per approved document, whether a reviewer approved it or it was approved on
its own, with a column per field. It is the clean, checked version of what came in, and what pipelines, reports and
other checks use.

![Approved data for the Referral type](doc-approved-data "Approved data: one row per approved referral, with who approved it and each field")

## Look at a type's data
1. Open **Get data in › Documents › Approved data**.
2. Pick the type in the list beside the title.
3. Each row shows:
   - **Document**: the document's number (it opens its review screen, read-only) and the type's version it was read
     with;
   - **Approved**: **By a reviewer** or **On its own**, and when;
   - a column per field, the value as approved, corrections included;
   - for each line-item table, how many rows it has.

Rows are paged; choose the page size at the foot.

## Who sees it unmasked
A document type the Data Catalog holds as **Confidential** or **Restricted** has its approved data masked for anyone who
is not its owner and has no access grant: on **Approved data**, in its CSV export, in an approved document's fields and
in Ask your data. Tagged columns are masked, and so is a person's name, email, phone number or id found in any field,
even when only one document is approved. Documents still in review are shown as they are, for the reviewer to check.

## Download it
Choose **CSV** or **JSON Lines** to download the type's whole dataset: CSV for a spreadsheet, JSON Lines for a
program.

> **Privacy:** Approved data holds what your documents say, often personal or patient data. Download it only to where
> your organisation allows that data to be, and give people page access to Approved data only when their work needs it.

## Use it in a pipeline
- The **Read documents** step reads a document type's approved data into a pipeline, so you can join it, compute with
  it, check it with a **Validate** step, write it to your storage or make a report from it.
- A pipeline can start each time a document of a type is approved, and read that document. See
  [When a document is approved](#doc-when-approved).

## Use it in a check
An **A value is in a reference list** rule can look values up in another type's approved data: an invoice's PO number
must be one of the approved purchase orders. See [Checks on a document](#doc-checks).

## Example
Summit Valley's **Referral** approved data has a row for Elena Marsh's referral, approved by a reviewer: referral
date 2026-10-18, date of birth 1959-03-14, patient ID SV-000117, the referring provider and NPI, the reason for
referral. A daily pipeline reads the Lab result approved data with **Read documents** and writes one row per test line
to a file, with the abnormal results flagged.

articles.title: When a document is approved
articles.summary: Start a pipeline each time a document of a type is approved, by a reviewer or on its own.
articles.who: Workspace administrators set the schedule; anyone with Document types sees what each type's approval starts
articles.popular: Start a pipeline when a document is approved
articles.md:
An approved document is often where work begins: a referral that should open an admission, an invoice that should be
matched to its purchase order. Set a schedule to start when a document of a type is approved, and each approval starts
a run with that document.

## See what a type's approval starts
On **Documents › Document types**, the column **When approved, starts…** names, for each type, the schedules its
approval starts, each a link to the schedule's runs. A schedule whose document start is switched off says **(trigger
off)**; one that is not active says **(schedule not active)**. **Nothing yet** means no schedule starts on it.

![The Document types list with what each approval starts](doc-types "When approved, starts…: the schedules each type's approval starts")

## Start a pipeline on approval
1. On **Documents › Document types**, in the type's row, choose **Set it on a schedule**. A new schedule opens with the
   document start on and the type picked. (Or open **Pipelines › Schedules** and a schedule of your own.)
2. Pick the pipeline the schedule runs.
3. Under **When it runs**, in **Also starts when**, make sure **A document is approved** is on.
4. In **Which documents**, pick the document type. An approved document of this type starts a run, whether a reviewer
   approved it or it was approved automatically.
5. In **Documents per run**, `1` starts a run per document. A larger number lets documents that waited for a run go
   together, up to that many, and the pipeline reads them all.
6. Save the schedule.

A document approved while a run is going waits its turn. In the pipeline, the **Read documents** step reads the
documents that started the run.

> **Tip:** A rejected document starts nothing. Only what a person (or the type's auto-approve line) passed reaches the
> pipeline, so the pipeline can trust the values it gets.

> **Note:** The schedule can start in other ways too (on a timetable, when a file arrives, when someone chooses Run now).
> The document start adds to them.

## Example
At Summit Valley, an approved **Referral** starts "Journey 1 · Referral to admission". When Greta Fischer approves Elena
Marsh's referral, the run reads it, works out her age and urgency, saves the referral as a file and sends the event that
admits her: the start of the patient's journey.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Documents per run | 1 to 50 |
| Types per document start | One type per schedule |

articles.title: Documents limits
articles.summary: File kinds and sizes per channel, how many at once, review and bulk limits, and the ranges of type and rule settings.
articles.who: Everyone
articles.md:
The limits a workspace meets when it sends documents in, defines types and reviews. Where a limit is your platform's
own setting, the screen names the number that applies to you.

## Sending documents in
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Files read as documents (Upload, Email-in, a stored file) | PDF, PNG, JPEG, TIFF or BMP |
| Upload documents | Up to 20 files at once |
| Email-in | The number of attachments a message and the size of each are shown on the Email-in card (for example up to 20 a message, 20 MB each) |
| The same file twice | Kept once, by any channel; the second is listed as **Duplicate** |
| File drop size | The platform's limit per file (the settings dialog names it), or a lower one an administrator sets |
| File drop kinds | Data, documents, images, audio and video, and archives; executables and scripts are refused |
| Arrivals listed | The newest 50 on the file drop |
| A file from a form | Sent to Document Intelligence when the form's **File upload** field says so |

## Document types and rules
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Key | lower_snake_case, unique, fixed once saved |
| Field types | text, number, integer, money, date, boolean, choice |
| Auto-approve at | Above 0 and up to 100 %; empty means never |
| Default "check" line | 80 % when a type has no auto-approve line |
| Duplicate rule, within days | 1 to 3,650; empty means all |
| Unusual-value rule | Applies after 2 to 1,000 approved documents (5 when empty); 3.5 MADs when no other setting is given |
| Reference list files | CSV, TSV, JSON or JSON Lines |
| Who may change types | Workspace administrators |

## Review
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Reject reason | Required; up to 500 characters |
| Bulk decision | Up to 100 documents; type the count back above 25 |
| Bulk comment | Up to 500 characters; required to reject |
| A claimed document | Only the person who claimed it decides it |
| Bulk approve | Only when the workspace's review policy allows it |

## Starting pipelines
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Documents per run | 1 to 50 |
| Files per run (file drop) | 1 to 50 |

articles.title: Build a form
articles.summary: Every field type, sections, required answers, placeholders and help text, a preview, and publishing so the workspace can fill it in.
articles.who: Workspace administrators build and change forms; anyone whose page access includes Forms fills in the Active ones
articles.popular: Build a form
articles.md:
A form collects the same answers the same way every time: an admission, a triage, an expense claim, a work order. Each
submission is kept, and it can start a pipeline, an approval workflow, or both. Forms are built on **Get data in ›
Forms** and filled in by the workspace's own members.

![The forms list](form-list "Forms: each form's status, its fields, what it starts and how many submissions it has")

## Make a form
1. Open **Get data in › Forms** and choose **New form**. The editor opens on **Build**, with one field to start.
2. Choose **Settings** and give the form a **Name** (up to 120 characters) and a **Description**, shown above its
   fields.
3. Back on **Build**, add fields from the **Fields** palette on the left. Each one appears on the form in the middle.
4. Choose a field on the form to set it up on the right (below).
5. Use the arrows on a selected field to move it, or the bin to remove it.
6. Choose **Preview** to see the form as members see it; nothing is sent. **Back to editing** returns.
7. Choose **Save**, then **Publish** when it is ready. A published form says **Published** and its version.

![The form builder with a field selected](form-builder "The builder: the field palette, the form, and the selected field's settings")

## The field types
| Type | For | Its own settings |
|---|---|---|
| **Text** | A short answer: a name, an MRN | — |
| **Long text** | A paragraph: a reason, notes | — |
| **Number** | A weight, an amount, a score | — |
| **Date** | A date of birth, a visit date | — |
| **Choice** | One option from a list | **Options, one per line** |
| **Checkboxes (tick all that apply)** | Every option that applies: symptoms, services wanted | **Options, one per line**, **At least** and **At most** (each optional) |
| **Yes / no** | A yes or no question | — |
| **E-mail** | An e-mail address, checked as one | — |
| **Table** | Several rows: expense lines, medicines | **Columns** (each Text, Number, Date, Choice, Yes / no or E-mail, and **Required**), **At most** N rows |
| **File upload** | A letter, a photo, a receipt | **Accepted file types**, **Largest file (MB)**, **How many files**, **Send its files to Document Intelligence** |
| **Signature** | A signature drawn in a box | — |
| **Lookup** | One of the answers another form collected | **Offers the answers of** (the form) and **Field** |

## Set up a field
- **Label**: what the person reads, up to 120 characters.
- **Key**: the answer's name in the submission file: lower-case letters, digits and `_`, starting with a letter, up to
  40. A few names belong to the submission itself and cannot be used (such as `submitted_by`).
- **Type**: change it here if you picked the wrong one.
- **Required**: the form cannot be sent without it.
- **Placeholder (optional)**: example text inside the empty box, such as `e.g. SV-000123`, up to 120 characters on one
  line. The label stays; people still see it. Text, long text, number, date, e-mail, choice and lookup fields take one.
  Left empty, the box shows a default for its type, such as "Enter case number" (greyed in the setting).
- **Help text (optional)**: a short hint shown under the field and read out with it, up to 500 characters.
- **Section (optional)**: the heading the field is shown under. See [Sections](#form-build--sections).
- **Add logic (show or require it when…)**: see [Show or require a field when](#form-logic).

> **Tip:** With **Send its files to Document Intelligence** on a **File upload** field, each PDF or image sent with the
> form also becomes a document, read and extracted against its type; the same file twice is kept once.

## Sections
A long form reads better in parts: *Patient*, *Insurance*, *This visit*. Give each field a **Section**; fields next to
each other with the same section are shown together under its heading, on the form, in **Preview** and on a share link.

1. Select the first field of the part and type its **Section**, such as `Insurance` (one line, up to 80 characters).
2. Select the next field: the box suggests the sections already used, so pick the same one.
3. Keep a section's fields together with the arrows. A field with another section (or none) between them starts the
   section again, under a second heading.

A field with no section is shown on its own, outside any heading. A section whose fields are all hidden by their rules
is not shown at all.

## Checkboxes
A **Checkboxes (tick all that apply)** field lists its options with a box each; people tick every one that applies.

- **Options, one per line**: each option once.
- **At least** and **At most** (optional): how many may be ticked, such as at most `3`. The form says it ("Tick 1 to
  3") and is not sent with too few or too many. **At least** applies once anything is ticked; tick **Required** to need
  at least one.
- The answer is the list of the options ticked, in the options' order. **Forms › Submissions** shows it as `Fever,
  Rash`, **Export CSV** joins it with `; ` (`Fever; Rash`), and the form's dataset keeps it as a list.
- In a rule ([Show or require a field when](#form-logic)), **is** `Rash` means "Rash is ticked", **is not** means it is
  not, and **is one of** means any of them is; **is answered** and **is not answered** work as for any field. **is more
  than** and **is less than** do not apply to it.

## Status
In **Settings**, **Status** is **Draft**, **Active** or **Archived**. Only an **Active** form takes submissions, and a
form needs at least one field to be Active. On the list, a row's menu (⋮) has **Activate** and **Archive**; **Show
archived** brings archived forms back into the list. Each saved change is a new version, and every submission records
the version it answered.

## Example
Summit Valley's **Admission intake** form has 15 fields and uses every field type. Among them: the patient's MRN (help text "SV- and
six digits", placeholder `e.g. SV-000123`), name, date of birth, sex and payer as choices, member ID, urgency, the
