reason for admission as long text, weight, a contact e-mail, a yes / no for allergies, the referral letter as a PDF
upload, and a drawn consent signature.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Fields in a form | 50 |
| Label and form name | 120 characters |
| Placeholder | 120 characters, one line |
| Help text | 500 characters |
| Section | 80 characters, one line |
| Checkboxes | **At least** 0 to the number of options; **At most** 1 to the number of options |
| Table | Up to 20 columns; 1 to 200 rows (20 by default) |
| File upload | 1 to 25 MB a file (10 by default); 1 to 10 files (1 by default) |
| Who may build | Workspace administrators |

articles.title: Show or require a field when
articles.summary: Show a field, or make it required, only when an earlier answer says so.
articles.who: Workspace administrators
articles.md:
Not every question applies to everyone. With logic, a field appears only when an earlier answer calls for it (the
allergy list only when the answer to "Any allergies?" is yes), or becomes required only then (a member ID unless the
patient is self-pay). A field that is not shown is not asked, and its answer is not kept.

## Add a rule
1. Open the form in the builder and choose the **Logic** tab. Each field after the first is listed with two settings.
2. Under **Show only when**, pick the earlier field it depends on; **Always shown** means no rule.
3. Pick how to compare it, then the value:

| Comparison | True when the answer… |
|---|---|
| **is** | equals the value |
| **is not** | is anything else |
| **is one of** | is one of several values, written `a, b, c` |
| **is more than** | is a larger number |
| **is less than** | is a smaller number |
| **is answered** | was given |
| **is not answered** | was left empty |

4. Under **Also required when**, do the same to make the field required only in that case; **No extra rule** means
   none.
5. Choose **Save**.

For a **Yes / no** field, the value is a choice of **Yes** or **No**. A **Table**, **File upload** or **Signature**
field can only be tested for **is answered** or **is not answered**.

You can also start from a field on **Build**: select it and choose **Add logic (show or require it when…)**. The tab's
title counts the rules, such as **Logic (2)**, and on **Build** each field with a rule says so under it.

![The Logic tab](form-logic "Logic: for each field, when it is shown and when it is also required")

![A field required only when another answer says so](form-logic-rule "On the form: Member ID, required when Payer is not Self-pay")

> **Note:** A rule can only depend on a field above the one it applies to, so the form reads top to bottom. A form
> with a single field has nothing to depend on yet: add a second field first.

> **Tip:** Check the rules with **Preview**: answer the earlier field and watch the later ones appear or become
> required.

## Example
On Summit Valley's **Admission intake**, **Member ID** is required when **Payer** is not **Self-pay**, and the
allergy list is shown only when **Any allergies?** is **Yes**. A walk-in who pays for themselves is never asked for a
member ID, and a nurse never scrolls past an empty allergy list.

articles.title: Share a form
articles.summary: Members fill in Active forms from inside the workspace; links that open one form are off until an administrator turns them on.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Forms fills in Active forms; workspace administrators make and revoke links
articles.md:
A form is shared inside its workspace: every member whose page access includes **Forms** sees its Active forms and fills
them in, signed in as themselves, so each submission says who sent it. Nothing about a form is public unless an
administrator deliberately makes a link.

## Fill in a form inside the workspace
1. Open **Get data in › Forms**. An Active form's name is a link; or choose **Fill in** in its row menu.
2. Answer the fields. Required ones are marked with an asterisk; a field's help text is under it.
3. For a **Signature**, sign inside the box and choose **Use this signature** (**Clear** starts again).
4. Choose **Submit**. The page says **Submitted**; **Fill in another** starts a fresh one.

To send a colleague straight to it, copy the address of the form's page: it opens only for a signed-in member of your
workspace whose page access includes Forms.

![The Admission intake form being filled in](form-fill "Filling in a form: each field with its placeholder and help text")

## Share by link (administrators)
For people who should fill in one form and see nothing else (a front-desk tablet, say), an administrator can make a
link. It is in the form's **Settings** tab, under **Share by link**, after the form has been saved.

1. Tick **Sharing by link is off for this workspace**; it then says **on**. While it is off, no link of this workspace opens anything;
   turning it off again stops every link at once.
2. Give the link a **Label**, such as `Front desk tablet`.
3. Pick how long it **Works for**: 1, 7, 14, 30 or 90 days.
4. Pick how many **Submissions** it takes: **No cap**, **One (single use)**, 10 or 100.
5. Tick **Only signed-in members** so that only members of this workspace, signed in, can use it. It starts unticked.
6. Choose **Make link**, then **Copy** it at once: it is not shown again.

The list of links shows each one's **Status**, how often it was **Used**, when it **Expires** and was **Last used**;
**Revoke** stops one.

![A form's Settings with Share by link](form-settings "Settings: what a submission starts, the dataset, and Share by link, off for this workspace")

> **Privacy:** A link without **Only signed-in members** opens the form for anyone who holds it. Do not use one for a
> form that asks for patient or personal data unless your organisation has approved it, and prefer **One (single
> use)** and a short **Works for**.

## Example
Summit Valley keeps sharing by link off: its forms are filled in by staff who are signed in. Rosa Alvarez, the charge
nurse, opens **Nurse triage** from **Get data in › Forms**, records a patient's vitals and pain score, and submits; the
submission is hers by name.

articles.title: What a submission starts
articles.summary: A submission can start a pipeline, an approval workflow, or both; or only be kept.
articles.who: Workspace administrators
articles.md:
A form on its own keeps what people send. In its **Settings**, a form can also start work with each submission: a
pipeline that does something with the answers, an approval workflow that asks the right people to decide, or both.

## Start a pipeline
1. Open the form in the builder and choose **Settings**.
2. Under **When submitted, start**, pick the schedule to run. **Nothing: keep the submission** starts nothing.
3. Choose **Save**.

The submission is written to the workspace inbox as JSON, and the schedule runs with it: a pipeline whose **Read
CSV/JSON/Parquet** step names no file reads it as one row, each answer a column named by its field's key. The form's
page says "Submitting starts this form's pipeline." The forms list shows the schedule under **Starts**.

## Start an approval workflow
1. In **Settings**, under **Approval**, pick a workflow. **None: no approval** asks no one.
2. Choose **Save**.

Each submission starts the workflow. Its status (**Pending**, **Approved**, **Rejected**, **Overdue**) and the stage it
is at show on **Forms › Submissions**. Workflows are built in **Approval workflows** (the **Workflow designer** link
opens it).

![A form's Settings: a pipeline and an approval workflow](form-settings "Settings: When submitted, start a pipeline; Approval: a workflow; and where its dataset is kept")

## Both
Pick a schedule under **When submitted, start** and a workflow under **Approval**. The builder's line under the form's
name says what it starts, such as `starts workflow "Patient journey"`, and the form's submissions show both the run and
the approval.

> **Tip:** Check a submission's answers in the pipeline with a **Validate** step and a data contract, so a malformed
> answer stops there with its field named. See [Data contracts](#con-contracts).

> **Note:** A file a person attaches can be sent to Document Intelligence too, with **Send its files to Document
> Intelligence** on its **File upload** field. See [Build a form](#form-build).

## How each submission went
On **Forms › Submissions**, each submission's **Status** is **Received** (kept, nothing started), **Run started** with
the run's number (a link to its run log), or **Run not started**, with the reason under **Details**. See
[Submissions](#form-submissions).

## Examples
- **Expense claim** starts the pipeline "Expense claims with receipts" and the **Expense approval** workflow: Kevin Lee's
  claim waits at **Manager approves** for Claire Martin, while the pipeline totals its lines.
- **Admission intake** starts the **Patient journey** workflow and the intake pipeline, which checks the answers against
  the `journey_intake` contract and files them by MRN.
- **Find a trial** starts only a pipeline: it searches recruiting clinical trials for the condition and city given.

articles.title: Submissions
articles.summary: What each form collected, who sent it and when, the run and the approval it started, its answers, files and signatures.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Submissions
articles.popular: See what a form collected
articles.md:
**Get data in › Forms › Submissions** shows what a form collected: who sent each submission and when, whether it
started the form's pipeline, where its approval stands, and its answers.

![The Expense claim's submissions](form-submissions "Submissions: who sent each one, the run it started, its approval and stage")

## Find a submission
1. Open **Get data in › Forms › Submissions**, or choose **Submissions** in a form's row menu.
2. Pick the form in the list at the top right.
3. Narrow the list with **State** and **Search submissions…**.

The tiles count the **Submissions** and, for a form with an approval workflow, how many are **Awaiting approval**,
**Approved** and **Overdue** (with how many were rejected).

| Column | Says |
|---|---|
| **#** | The submission's number |
| **Submitted by**, **Submitted** | Who sent it and when |
| **Status** | **Received**, **Run started** #N (a link to the run's log) or **Run not started** |
| **Stage**, **Approval** | For a form with a workflow: the stage it is at and its status, with **Open request** |
| **Details** | Where the submission is stored, or why its run did not start, or the reason it was rejected |
| **Answers** | **View** |

Next to the form's name, **Fill in** opens the form, and **Open in Analytics Studio** opens its dataset when it keeps
one.

## Read a submission
Choose **View** on its row. The answers open under it, each under its field's label:

- a **Table** answer as a table, with its columns;
- **File upload** and **Signature** answers as the files they are, each by name;
- the rest as text.

The line under the answers says which version of the form was answered; the answers are shown with that version's
fields, even if the form has changed since.

![A submission's answers](form-submission "A submission opened: the claimant and each line of the claim")

## Read an attached file as a document
On a file answer, choose **Read with Document Intelligence** to send it to be read and extracted as a document. It then
says **Being read — open Document Intelligence**. You need page access to Documents for this.

## Export
**Export CSV** downloads every submission of the form, one row each.

> **Note:** The list shows the newest 200 submissions. When a form has more, the page says so; search and the tiles
> cover the 200 shown, and **Export CSV** has every submission.

## Example
Kevin Lee has sent two expense claims. Submission 1107 started run #2014 and is **Approved**; 1103 started run #1984
and is **Pending** at **Manager approves**, waiting for Claire Martin. Opening 1107 shows his four lines: a taxi to the
Peoria clinic, parking, a lunch and a train.

articles.title: The form's dataset and Rebuild dataset files
articles.summary: A form's submissions as a dataset in Analytics, one row each, and how to write its files again when they are lost.
articles.who: Anyone with Submissions and Analytics opens the dataset; workspace administrators rebuild its files
articles.md:
A form can keep its answers as a dataset: every submission is a row you can query, chart and put on a dashboard in
Analytics, next to the rest of your data. The rows are files in the workspace's own bucket, one file per submission.

## See where its dataset is
When a form keeps a dataset:

- the builder's line under the form's name says `saves to dataset Form: <name>`;
- its **Settings** tab, under **Dataset**, says "Every submission is a row of **Form: <name>** in Analytics" with the
  storage connection and the folder the files are in;
- on **Forms › Submissions**, **Open in Analytics Studio** opens it.

Each row holds the submission's answers and, for a form with an approval workflow, its approval status, stage and the
approver's reason.

![The Dataset part of a form's Settings](form-settings "Settings › Dataset: the dataset's name, connection and folder")

## Open it in Analytics
1. Open **Forms › Submissions** and pick the form.
2. Choose **Open in Analytics Studio**. The dataset opens there, ready to query.

## Rebuild dataset files
If the files in the bucket are lost (deleted by a clean-up, or the bucket was replaced), or were written by an older
version, the submissions themselves are still kept. An administrator can write the files again:

1. Open **Get data in › Forms**.
2. In the form's row menu (⋮), choose **Rebuild dataset files**.
3. Confirm with **Rebuild files**. The dialog says where the files are written.

Each submission's file is written again from the submission as it is kept, so Analytics reads every row. No answer
changes. The menu item says **Rebuilding files…** while it works; one form is rebuilt at a time.

> **Note:** A rebuild takes the newest 1,000 submissions.

> **Warning:** The rebuild writes into the bucket of the form's dataset. If a pipeline or a person edited those files,
> their changes are replaced by the kept submissions.

## Example
Summit Valley's **Expense claim** form saves to the dataset **Form: Expense claim**, kept in the
`summit-valley-s3` bucket. When a bucket clean-up removed last month's files, the finance board showed no claims for
October. The administrator chose **Rebuild dataset files** on the form, and the board's rows came back.

articles.title: Patient intake: from the front desk to a signed summary
articles.summary: Fill in a new patient's intake (or scan a paper one), follow it in My requests, review the AI's DRAFT summary as a nurse, and read the signed Patient intake summary.
articles.who: The front desk (or the patient) fills the form; nurses in the reviewing team approve; a workspace administrator decides high-priority intakes as the senior nurse
articles.popular: Take a new patient's intake
articles.md:
A new patient's intake is typed in once, at the front desk or by the patient, on the form **New patient intake**, or
arrives as a scanned paper form. Each intake is then checked, summarised by AI as a DRAFT, reviewed by a nurse, and
kept as a signed **Patient intake summary** PDF that anyone with the report can verify. This article is for the people
who use it; the administrator who builds it follows the recipe
[Patient intake: a form in sections, an AI draft, a nurse's approval and a signed summary](#rcp-patient-intake).

> **Note:** Not yet verified end to end. This describes Riverside Health's intake as it was built on 26 October 2026,
> before its review workflow was published and before any intake had run through the whole road.

## Fill in an intake (front desk)
1. Open **Get data in › Forms** and choose **New patient intake**.
2. Work down the sections, each under its own heading: **Patient**, **Parent or guardian (patients under 18)**,
   **Emergency contact**, **Insurance**, **This visit**, **Medical history**, **Social history**, **Medicines, allergies
   and vaccines**, **Review of systems**, **Women's health**, **Care team** and **Consents and signature**.
3. The grey example text in each empty box shows the format: date of birth `e.g. 1980-04-12`, phone
   `e.g. +1 555 0100`, member ID `As on the card, e.g. PMH-448812`. It is not an answer; type over it.
4. Medicines, allergies, conditions, operations, family history and vaccines are tables: choose **Add row** for each
   one, and **Remove** to take a row out. A medicine needs its name; an allergy, what the patient is allergic to.
5. **Do you have any of these now?** is a list to tick: tick every symptom the patient has now, and leave the rest.
6. Some questions appear only when they apply. Answer **Is the patient under 18?** **Yes** and the guardian's name,
   relationship and phone appear, and are required. **Women's health** appears only when **Sex** is **Female**, and
   **Packs a day** only when tobacco is **Current**.
7. Required answers are marked. The patient (or the guardian) ticks the three consents, signs in the box with a mouse, a
   finger or a pen, and chooses **Use this signature** (**Clear** starts again). Type the **Name of the person signing**
   and the **Date signed**.
8. Choose **Submit**. The page says **Submitted** with the submission's number; **Fill in another** starts a new one.

If an answer needs attention the form is not sent: the page says so, and the field says why.

![The intake form](intake-form-fill "New patient intake: the Patient section, example text in each empty box, required answers marked")

> **Tip:** Leave a question empty rather than guessing. The summary lists what was not given under *Missing information to
> ask*, so the nurse asks the patient.

## After you submit
Each intake starts a request in the workflow **Patient intake · intake review**. Follow it in **Review › My
requests**: its state, and in **History** each step as it happens.

1. **Assess.** The answers are checked: the required ones are there, the date of birth gives a real age, the phone has at
   least 7 digits, the e-mail looks like one. The age and the BMI are worked out. Rules (not the AI) flag high-risk
   medicines (anticoagulants and antiplatelets, insulin, opioids, methotrexate, digoxin, lithium), a drug or severe
   allergy, smoking, a pregnancy, a child, and worrying symptoms (chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness or fainting,
   a fall). Then a text model drafts a summary of 4 to 6 sentences, its own flags, a suggested triage priority (high,
   medium or low) with the reasons, and the missing information to ask about.
2. **Nurse review.** The nurses' team gets an approval. A rejection, with its reason, ends the request: no summary is made.
3. **High priority.** When the suggested priority is high, a senior nurse (a workspace administrator) decides as well.
4. **The summary.** The **Patient intake summary** PDF is made, and the intake is kept as JSON beside it.

A check that fails does not stop the intake: it goes on, flagged, and the summary shows it under *Checks that failed*.

## Review an intake (nurse)
1. Open **Run & review › Review › Approvals**. The intake's approval is under your team.
2. Open it. Read the DRAFT summary, the suggested priority and why, and the flags against the patient's own answers.
3. **Approve** with a short note, or **Reject** with the reason (a reason is required). Your name, the time and your note
   are what the summary prints under *Nurse's review*.

> **Warning:** The AI's summary, flags and priority are a DRAFT to help you read the intake quickly. They are never a
> diagnosis or a triage decision: you decide, from the patient's answers.

## The Patient intake summary
The report opens in **See results › Reports › Library** as **Patient intake · S-<number>** (a typed intake) or **D-<number>**
(a scanned one). Its parts, each kept whole on a page:

- the patient: date of birth and age, sex, language, the phone **masked to its last 4 digits**, primary care and
  pharmacy, the guardian for a child, the emergency contact;
- the reason for the visit, how long, pain, height, weight and BMI;
- the **Intake summary**: the suggested priority as a red, amber or green chip, the summary, and the line *Drafted with
  AI from the patient's own answers (a DRAFT, not a diagnosis); reviewed by* the nurse *on* the date; why this priority;
- **Flags**: allergies as red chips with their reactions, high-risk medicines found by the rules, the drafted flags;
- tables of the medicines, the allergies and reactions, conditions, operations, family history and vaccines; social
  history; the symptoms ticked (positives only); women's health for a female patient;
- insurance, with the member IDs **masked**; the consents and who signed;
- **Missing information to ask**; the **Nurse's review** with the signature and the approval stamp, the senior nurse when
  there was one, and a QR code to verify the report.

The PDF is signed when it is approved with **Approve and sign**: by someone other than the person who generated it.
**Verify signature** on its page, or the QR code, says whether it holds ([Approve and sign](#rs-approve)).


## A paper form
1. Open **Get data in › Documents › Intake**, **Upload**, and choose **Upload documents** with the scanned PDF.
2. The pages are read (OCR), the document is classified as **Patient intake · New patient intake form**, and every
   section is extracted: single answers as fields, medicines, allergies, history and the symptoms ticked as tables.
3. A reviewer checks it in **Run & review › Review › Documents** and approves it.
4. If it was matched to the wrong type, open **Documents in**, choose the document's menu (⋯) › **Extract again**, pick
   **Patient intake · New patient intake form**, and check it again ([Reading documents](#doc-reading)).
5. Approving starts the pipeline **Patient intake · from documents**: the same assessment for each intake, then one
   nurse's approval for the batch (up to 5 intakes that waited together), then a summary for each.

> **Note:** Riverside Health also has the starter type **Patient intake form**. With two intake types, a scan may be
> matched to the starter: that is when you choose the type and extract again.

## Who can do what
| Person | May |
|---|---|
| Front desk (profile *Front desk*) | Fill in forms, and follow their own requests in **My requests**. Nothing else: no submissions, runs or reports |
| A nurse in the reviewing team | Approve or reject intakes in **Review › Approvals**; review scanned forms in **Review › Documents** |
| A workspace administrator | The senior nurse's decision on a high-priority intake; builds and changes the form and its workflow |
| A viewer | Nothing of the intake |
| Another workspace | Nothing: the form, its requests, runs, documents and reports are this workspace's only |

## Example
At Riverside Health the front desk takes the intake of Ingrid Castellanos, 78, who felt dizzy standing up and fell at
home last week. She takes nine medicines, warfarin among them. The rules flag warfarin as a high-risk medicine and
*polypharmacy (9 medicines)*; the DRAFT suggests **high** priority ("fall with dizziness on warfarin"). The nurse
approves with "Fall on warfarin: told the doctor; check for head injury and INR today."; because the priority is high, a
senior nurse approves too. Her signed summary shows her phone masked to its last four digits, and under *Allergies and reactions*: "No known
allergies."

articles.title: What the ETL Console does
articles.summary: Data in, build, run and review, results: the four parts of the console and where each lives in the menu.
articles.who: Everyone in a workspace
articles.md:
The ETL Console takes your organisation's data from where it is, does the work you describe, lets a person check what needs checking, and hands back finished results: reports, dashboards and answers your own systems can read. Everything happens inside your **workspace**, which holds your people, connections, pipelines, runs and bills, and nothing crosses from one workspace to another.

The menu follows that path from left to right (or top to bottom in the sidebar), so the place you need is usually the next group along.

![Home for a workspace administrator](gs-home "Home: what waits for your review, runs that need attention, the way to each part of the console, and this period's figures")

## The four parts
| Part | Menu group | What you do there |
|---|---|---|
| Get data in | **Get data in** | Connect storage, databases and APIs (**Connections**), send documents in to be read (**Documents**), and collect answers with **Forms**. |
| Build | **Build** | Describe what a run does in **Pipelines**, when it runs (**Schedules & triggers**), what a model is asked (**Prompts**), and who approves what in **Approval workflows**. The **AI Assistant** can draft a pipeline from a plain description. |
| Run and review | **Run & review** | Follow every run in **Runs**, retry what failed, and decide what waits for a person in **Review**. |
| See results | **See results** | Read **Dashboards**, ask questions in **Analysis**, make signed PDF reports in **Reports**, and convert files or transcribe recordings in **Tools**. |

A workspace administrator also sees **Administration & billing**: the people and their access, sign-in rules, data policies, the bill, settings and the API for your own systems.

## A worked example
At the fictional Summit Valley Health System a referral arrives by email. **Documents** reads its fields, Greta Fischer in health information approves them in **Review**, and the approval starts the admission pipeline. A care plan is drafted by a model and marked DRAFT until Dr. Anika Patel approves it; the discharge summary becomes a signed PDF in **Reports**, and the ward's **Dashboards** show length of stay the next morning. The whole story is told in the tour chapter.

> **Note:** Every person, patient and number in this guide is made up. A model's answer is always a DRAFT for a person to check.

## What you see depends on you
Two people in the same workspace can see different menus. A **workspace administrator** sees every page; a **workspace member** sees the pages their page access profile opens. See [Who sees what](#gs-who-sees-what).

## Where to start
1. [Sign in](#gs-sign-in) and choose your own password.
2. [Turn on two-factor sign-in](#gs-two-factor).
3. Take [a tour of the screen](#gs-tour).
4. See what [Home](#gs-home) shows you each day.

articles.title: Sign in
articles.summary: Your address and password, the one-time password of a new account, single sign-on, and what to do when you cannot get in.
articles.who: Everyone with an account in a workspace
articles.popular: Sign in for the first time
articles.md:
You sign in with the email address your administrator added you with and a password. Your workspace may also let you sign in with your company account (single sign-on), and may ask for a code from an authenticator app after the password.

![The sign-in page](gs-sign-in "Sign in: username and password, or Sign in with your company")

## Sign in for the first time
When an administrator adds you, the console emails you a **one-time password**, unless the administrator set a password and passed it to you themselves.

1. Open the console's address and choose **Sign in**.
2. Type your email address under **Username** and the one-time password under **Password**, then choose **Sign in**.
3. If your workspace requires two-factor sign-in, set it up now: see [Two-factor sign-in](#gs-two-factor--set-it-up-at-sign-in).
4. The console opens **Your profile** with the note **Choose your own password.** Type the one-time password under **Current password** and your own under **New password**. The rules under the box tick as you meet them.
5. Choose **Change password**. The emailed password stops working at once.

Until you choose your own password, every page you open brings you back to **Your profile**.

> **Tip:** Choose **Password rules** under the new password to see every rule your workspace sets, such as the minimum length and whether a symbol is needed.

## Sign in with your company
If your workspace uses single sign-on, either:
- open the sign-in link your administrator gave you and choose **Continue with** and your company's name, or
- choose **Sign in with your company**, type your **Work email** and choose **Continue**.

You then sign in at your company's own sign-in page, with your company's own two-factor sign-in. Only addresses in the email domains your administrator listed can sign in this way.

## When you cannot sign in
| What you see | What to do |
|---|---|
| Your password was not accepted | Check the address and the password. After several failed attempts in a row the account is locked for a while: wait, or ask an administrator to unlock it. |
| **Forgot your password?** | Ask your workspace administrator to reset it. You choose your own at your next sign-in. |
| **Your password has expired.** | Your workspace asks for a new password after a number of days. Choose a new one on **Your profile** to carry on. |
| **You were signed out because the console was not used for a while.** | Your workspace signs out idle sessions. You are warned a minute before. Sign in again. |
| **Your password was changed. Please sign in with the new password.** | The password changed in another session. Sign in with the new one. |

> **Note:** The lockout, the idle time and the password rules are your workspace's. Administrators set them under [Sign-in security](#sec-sign-in).

## No account yet?
**Request a workspace** on the sign-in page asks the platform's team for a new workspace for your organisation. If your organisation already has one, ask its administrator to add you instead.

## Example
Dr. Minh Nguyen, a physician at Summit Valley, receives his one-time password by email. He signs in, sets up his authenticator app because the Clinician profile requires it, saves his recovery codes, and chooses his own password on **Your profile**. From then on he signs in with his password and a code.

articles.title: Two-factor sign-in
articles.summary: Set up an authenticator app, keep your recovery codes, and what to do when you lose your phone.
articles.who: Everyone who signs in with a password; your workspace may require it
articles.popular: Turn on two-factor sign-in
articles.md:
Two-factor sign-in (the screens call it **Two-factor login**) asks for a 6-digit code from an app on your phone after your password. A stolen password alone is then not enough to get into your account.

Your workspace may require it of everyone, or only of the people on certain access profiles (clinicians, say). Where it is required you set it up at your next sign-in and cannot turn it off.

![Two-factor login on My security](gs-two-factor "My security › Two-factor login: on since, recovery codes left, New recovery codes")

## Turn on two-factor sign-in
1. Open your avatar at the top right and choose **My security**.
2. Under **Two-factor login**, choose **Set up two-factor login**.
3. Open an authenticator app on your phone (Microsoft Authenticator, Google Authenticator, 1Password, Authy or another).
4. Scan the QR code with the app, or type the **Key** shown beside it.
5. Type the 6-digit code the app shows under **Code from the app** and choose **Turn on**.
6. Save your recovery codes: choose **Copy** or **Download**. They are shown only once.

**Two-factor login** now shows **On**, the date it was turned on and how many recovery codes are left.

## Set it up at sign-in
When your workspace requires it and you have not set it up, the sign-in page shows **Set up two-factor login** after your password. Follow the same steps, then choose **I've saved them — continue** once your recovery codes are safe.

## Sign in with a code
1. Sign in with your address and password.
2. On **Two-factor login**, type the code your app shows and choose **Sign in**.

## Recovery codes
You get 10 recovery codes. Each signs you in once when your phone is not at hand: on the code step choose **Use a recovery code instead**.

- **Recovery codes left** shows how many you have; it turns amber below 3.
- To get a new set, choose **New recovery codes**, type your password and choose **Make new codes**. The old ones stop working.

## When you lose your phone
- If you still have a recovery code, sign in with it and make new recovery codes. To move to a new phone, turn two-factor off and set it up again; where it is required, ask your administrator to reset it instead.
- If you have neither, ask your workspace administrator to **Reset two-factor login** for you. Your old app and codes stop working and you are signed out everywhere; if your workspace requires two-factor sign-in, you set it up again at your next sign-in.

> **Warning:** An administrator should reset two-factor sign-in only when they are sure it is really you asking, for example by calling you on a number they already have.

## Turn it off
Choose **Turn off**, type your password and a code from the app (or a recovery code), then **Turn off two-factor login**. **Turn off** is not offered while your workspace or your access profile requires it.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Code from the app | 6 digits |
| Recovery codes | 10, each works once |
| Who may reset it for you | A workspace administrator |

articles.title: A tour of the screen
articles.summary: The menu groups, the top bar, breadcrumbs and tabs, side panels, tables, themes and the 24-hour clock.
articles.who: Everyone
articles.md:
Every page of the console has the same frame: the menu on the left, the top bar across the top, and the page itself with its breadcrumb, title and tabs. Learn it once and every part of the product reads the same way.

![The console with the Runs page open](gs-tour "1 The menu · 2 The top bar: notifications, theme, your avatar · 3 The breadcrumb · 4 The page's tabs · 5 Filters · 6 The table")

## The menu
On a wide screen the menu is a sidebar; on a narrower one the same groups sit along the top bar, and on a phone they open from the menu button.

| Group | Entries |
|---|---|
| **Home** | What waits for you, and this period's figures |
| **Get data in** | Connections, Documents, Forms |
| **Build** | Pipelines, AI Assistant, Approval workflows |
| **Run & review** | Runs, Review (with a count of what waits for you) |
| **See results** | Dashboards, Analysis, Reports, Tools |
| **Administration & billing** | Administration, Billing, Settings, Developers (administrators) |

Each entry shows a one-line hint of what it is for. **Collapse** at the foot of the sidebar folds it to icons; choose a group's icon to open the group beside it.

You see only the entries your access opens: see [Who sees what](#gs-who-sees-what).

## The top bar
From right to left:
- **Your avatar** opens the account menu: **Your profile**, **My security**, **Notifications**, **Setup guide** (this help) and **Sign out**. Under your name it shows your role.
- **The theme button** (a sun or a moon) opens the theme menu.
- **The bell** shows how many notifications you have not read; open it for the latest ones.

![The account menu](gs-account-menu "The account menu under your avatar")

## Breadcrumbs, hubs and tabs
The line above a page's title says where you are, as the menu says it: **Run & review › Runs › Latest**. Choose any step to go back to it.

Many entries are a **hub** of tabs. **Runs**, for example, has **Latest**, **By date**, **Analytics**, **Failed** and **Backfills**. Each tab is its own page with its own address, so you can bookmark it or send the link to a colleague who has the same access. A hub shows only the tabs you may open; a hub with a single tab for you shows that page without a tab strip.

## Side panels
Opening a row often slides a panel in from the right (a team, a catalog asset, a run's item) so the list stays where it was. Close it with **Close**, the cross at its top, or the Escape key.

## Tables
Most lists share the same tools:
- a search box and filters above the table; **Clear** removes them all;
- **Columns** to hide or show columns (the choice is remembered on this device);
- sorting by a column's heading;
- a pager at the foot: 50, 100, 150 or 200 rows a page.

Some lists also switch between **Table** and **Cards**.

## Themes
The theme menu offers **System** (Light or Dark, as your device is set), **Light**, **Dark**, **Ocean**, **Midnight** and **High contrast**. Your choice is kept on your account, so it follows you to any device. Until you choose one, the console uses your workspace's default theme.

![The theme menu](gs-theme-menu "The theme menu: the current theme is ticked")

![The same screen in Dark](gs-tour-dark "The Runs page in the Dark theme")

## Times and dates
Times are shown on the 24-hour clock (14:05, not 2:05 PM) and in your own device's time zone. Recent times may read as "21 min ago" or "26 Oct, 19:27". Billing counts days in your workspace's billing time zone, and its pages say which one.

> **Tip:** Keyboard users: the first Tab on any page offers **Skip to content**, past the top bar.

articles.title: Home
articles.summary: What waits for your review, the runs that need attention, the way to each part of the console, and the period's figures.
articles.who: Everyone; administrators see the whole workspace, members the schedules they made or are assigned
articles.md:
Home is the first page after you sign in. It puts what needs you at the top, then the way to the rest of the console, then how the work has gone over the period you pick.

![Home](gs-home "Home for an administrator: waiting for review, needs attention, Go to, and the figures")

## What Home shows
From the top:
1. **Waiting for your review**: how many approvals, run results and documents wait for you and your teams, how many are overdue, and **Open Review**. It reads **Nothing is waiting for your review** when you are clear.
2. **Needs attention**: recent runs in which some items failed, with the step and the items. **See failed items** opens the run; **Retry** runs only the failed items again.
3. **Get your first pipeline running**: in a new workspace, the steps to a first completed run, until one has run. **Hide this guide** puts it away.
4. **Go to**: the main parts of the console you may open, each with its one-line hint.
5. The figures: **Schedules**, **Active schedules**, **Running now**, **Last run completed** and **Last run failed**. Each tile opens the list it counts.
6. **Your bill** (administrators): this month so far and what is owed, with **Cost & usage**.
7. The charts: **Schedule status**, **Schedules by last outcome**, **Runs by day** and **Runs by hour**. Choose a cell in **Runs by hour** to see which schedules ran in that hour.

## Choose the period
Use the buttons at the top right: **Today**, **7 days**, **30 days**, **This month**, or **Custom** for your own dates. The line under the title says which days are shown and when the figures were last updated. Refresh reads them again; they also follow runs as they finish.

## What changes with your role
- A **workspace administrator** sees the whole workspace.
- A **workspace member** sees the schedules they made or are assigned (the line under the title says so), and only the cards and links their access opens. A member with no review pages sees no review card.

![Home for a reviewer](gs-home-reviewer "Home for a reviewer: two approvals waiting, and only the parts their profile opens")

> **Note:** Home has no pinned dashboards of its own. Open your boards from **See results › Dashboards**.

## Example
At 07:30 Dr. Anika Patel opens Home and sees **2 waiting for your review** (two care-plan approvals). She chooses **Open Review**, decides both, and Home reads **Nothing is waiting for your review**.

articles.title: Your profile and notifications
articles.summary: Your name, picture, position, phone and theme; your password; the bell and the Notifications page.
articles.who: Everyone
articles.md:
**Your profile** is how you appear across the console: your display name and picture show in the top bar, on approvals you decide and wherever a schedule records who assigned it. Your role and your workspace are set by an administrator and shown here for reference.

![Your profile](gs-profile "Your profile: picture, details, password and appearance")

## Change your details
1. Open your avatar at the top right and choose **Your profile**.
2. Change **Display name**, **Position** (your job title, separate from your permission role) or **Phone** (pick the country, then the number; empty removes it).
3. Choose **Save details**.

Your email address is your sign-in and only an administrator changes it.

## Add or change your picture
1. Under your portrait choose **Add picture** (or **Replace**), or drop an image on the portrait.
2. Under **Position your picture**, move and zoom it into the circle, then choose **Use this picture**.

PNG, JPEG or WebP, up to 5 MB. Location and camera details are removed from the file. **Remove** takes it away again.

## Change your password
On **Your profile** or **My security**, type your **Current password** and a **New password** that meets the rules shown under it, then choose **Change password**. You are asked for the current one too, so an unlocked screen is not enough to take the account. Changing it signs you out of your other sessions.

## Choose your theme
Under **Appearance** pick **System**, **Light**, **Dark**, **Ocean**, **Midnight** or **High contrast**. It is saved to your account (**Saved to your account**) and follows you to any device. If it could not be saved it reads **Kept on this device only**. The line beneath says your workspace's default; **Use the workspace default** goes back to it.

## Your activity
At the foot of the page, **Your activity** counts your schedules, their runs and failures over the last days and your unread notifications, and lists your recent runs with when they ran and how long they took.

## Where you are signed in
**My security** lists every session open in your name under **Where you're signed in**: the device, address, when it signed in, when it was last active and how. **End session** signs one out at once; **Sign out everywhere else** ends all but this one. Below, **Sign-in history** lists every sign-in to your account, with **Export CSV**.

![My security](gs-my-security "My security: password, two-factor login, where you're signed in and your sign-in history")

## Notifications
The bell in the top bar counts what you have not read: run outcomes, approvals, documents and alerts that are yours.

![The bell's panel](gs-bell "The bell: the latest notifications, Mark all read and View all notifications")

1. Choose the bell to see the latest. Choose one to open what it is about.
2. **Mark all read** clears the count.
3. **View all notifications** opens the **Notifications** page.

On the **Notifications** page you can filter by kind (**All kinds**), show **Unread only**, mark one read, or choose **Open** to go to its run, task or document.

![The Notifications page](gs-notifications "Account › Notifications: every notice addressed to you")

> **Note:** There are no per-person notification settings. What reaches you depends on your work: the schedules in your name, the approvals and reviews assigned to you or your teams, and the alerts that name you or your team. Your welcome email, one-time passwords and account notices go to your email address.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Profile picture | PNG, JPEG or WebP, up to 5 MB |
| The bell's panel | the latest notifications; the rest on the Notifications page |

articles.title: Who sees what
articles.summary: Why two people see different menus: their role, their page access profile and anything opened for them alone.
articles.who: Everyone; administrators set it up under Administration › Page access
articles.md:
The console shows each person only what their work needs. Two people in the same workspace can therefore see quite different menus, and the same page can show more to one than to the other. Three things decide it.

1. **Your role.** A **workspace administrator** opens every page of the workspace; page access does not apply to them. A **workspace member** opens the pages their profile gives them.
2. **Your page access profile.** A named bundle of pages, such as Reviewer, Clinician or Viewer. Members without a profile of their own get the workspace's default profile.
3. **Anything opened or withheld for you alone.** An administrator (or a delegate) can open a page or a tab for one person, for a while or until removed.

Home, **Your profile**, **My security** and **Notifications** are always open to everyone.

## Three menus side by side
![An administrator's menu](gs-menu-admin "Workspace administrator: every group")

![A reviewer's menu](gs-menu-reviewer "Reviewer profile: Forms, Runs, Review, Dashboards and Reports")

![A viewer's menu](gs-menu-viewer "Viewer profile: Runs (Analytics) and Dashboards")

| | Workspace administrator | Member on a Reviewer profile | Member on a Viewer profile |
|---|---|---|---|
| Home | Whole workspace | Their own schedules | Their own schedules |
| Get data in | Connections, Documents, Forms | Forms › Submissions | — |
| Build | Pipelines, AI Assistant, Approval workflows | — | — |
| Run & review | Runs, Review | Runs, Review | Runs › Analytics |
| See results | Dashboards, Analysis, Reports, Tools | Dashboards, Reports | Dashboards |
| Administration & billing | Administration, Billing, Settings, Developers | — | — |
| Decide approvals | Any run's review | What is assigned to them or their teams | — |

The Reviewer and Viewer columns show the profiles of the same names in this guide's example workspaces. Your workspace's profiles are whatever your administrators made: see [Page access profiles](#adm-access-profiles).

## What happens at a page you may not open
A page your access leaves out is off your menu. If you follow a link to it, the console says **… isn't part of your access** and offers **Request access**, which goes straight to your administrators' notifications. Hiding a page is only a courtesy: the server refuses the data behind it whatever the browser shows.

## Check what someone sees
Administrators can see a member's menu before they change anything:
- on **Administration › Page access**, choose **Check a person** and pick the member; or
- open the person on **Administration › Users**: **What they can see** lists their menu.

## Why my menu changed
- An administrator moved you to another profile, or opened or withheld a page for you.
- Something opened for you for a number of days has run out.
- Your workspace is managed by our team: an **Activity** tab appears for administrators.

Your menu follows the change from your next sign-in or when your session refreshes.

articles.title: Glossary
articles.summary: The words the console uses, A to Z, each in plain words with where to read more.
articles.who: Everyone
articles.popular: What does a word in the console mean?
articles.md:
The words the ETL Console uses, in plain words. A word in **bold** is the console's own label. Where an article says
more, the meaning links to it.

## A
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Access delegate** | A member an administrator allows to grant some pages and tabs to some people, for a set time. Everything they grant is recorded. See [Delegates](#adm-delegates). |
| **Active** | Switched on: an active schedule runs, an active pipeline or workflow may be started. Inactive ones keep their history. |
| **AI answers** | A run's tab listing each call it made to a model: the prompt, how long it took and the tokens it used. |
| **AI Assistant** | A conversation in which you describe a pipeline in plain words and the assistant proposes its steps. See [Design a pipeline with the AI Assistant](#ai-assistant). |
| **Alert rule** | A rule under **Settings › Alerts** that raises an alert when something needs attention, such as a failed run, and tells people or a webhook. |
| **API client** | One of your systems as the customer API knows it: an id, a secret, its scopes and where it may call from. See [API clients](#dev-clients). |
| **API collection** | A saved set of requests to another system's API, with its address, sign-in and variables, for pipelines to call. See [Make an API collection](#con-api-collections). |
| **Approval** | A person's decision, approve or reject, on a run, a document, a report or a workflow step. |
| **Approval step** | A step in the middle of a pipeline that pauses the run until reviewers decide. See [Approval steps inside a run](#apr-approval-steps). |
| **Approval workflow** | A designed sequence of approvals, tasks, conditions and pipeline runs that a request walks through. See [Design an approval workflow](#apr-workflows). |
| **Approved data** | The values of approved documents, kept as rows that pipelines can read. See [Approved data](#doc-approved-data). |
| **Asset** | In Report Studio, a logo, image, signature or stamp a report may place. In the Data Catalog, a dataset, file or document type it lists. |
| **Attempt** | One go at a run. Retrying a failed run makes its next attempt; the run's page lets you switch between attempts. |

## B
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Backfill** | Running a schedule once for each period of a past range, to fill a gap or catch up. See [Backfills](#trg-backfills). |
| **Brand profile** | A report's look in one place: header, footer, colours and logo, so every report matches. |
| **Bucket** | A storage container (for example on S3) that holds the workspace's files and the files runs write. |
| **Bulk approve** | Approving or rejecting several items at once, after seeing what will happen to each. See [Decide many at once](#apr-bulk). |

## C
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Calls at once** | An AI or Call API step's setting: how many calls it makes at the same time. |
| **Check by hand** | A page a step read with low sureness, sent to a person to check beside its image. |
| **Condition** | A workflow step that sends a request one way or another depending on a value, such as a care plan's risk. |
| **Connection** | How the workspace reaches a storage bucket, a database, an API or a connector. See [Connect your storage](#con-storage). |
| **Connector** | A ready-made connection to a known service. |
| **Cost & usage** | The Billing tab that shows the month so far as the invoice will read it. |
| **Cron** | A timetable written as five fields: minute, hour, day of the month, month, day of the week. Read in server time (Chicago). |

## D
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Dashboard** | A board of tiles over your pipelines' results, re-run each time it opens. See [Read a dashboard](#dash-boards). |
| **Data Catalog** | The list of the workspace's datasets, files and document types, what they hold and which fields are sensitive. See [The Data Catalog](#dash-catalog). |
| **Data contract** | What a record must look like: its fields, their types and which are required. Steps and the API check records against it. See [Data contracts](#con-contracts). |
| **Data level** | How sensitive a piece of data is (Sensitive, Internal or Public); it decides which models may see it. See [Which models may see which data](#ai-data-levels). |
| **Data policies** | The workspace's rules for its data: which models see each level, how long things are kept, whether bulk approve is allowed. See [Data policies](#sec-data-policies). |
| **Dataset** | A table of rows a run made or a form kept, which dashboards and analyses read. |
| **Document** | A file read into fields against a document type. |
| **Document type** | What a kind of document holds and how to read it: its fields and checks. See [Document types](#doc-types). |
| **DRAFT** | The mark on a model's answer: a draft for a person to check, never a decision. |
| **Due time** | When a task or approval should be decided; past it the task is overdue. |

## E
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Email-in** | The workspace's own email address: attachments mailed to it become documents. |
| **Environment** | An API collection's set of variables, such as its base address, for one place it calls. |
| **Event** | A message from one of your systems that something happened, such as a lab result is ready. See [Events and event routes](#dev-events). |
| **Event route** | What an event type starts in the workspace: a pipeline's run or a workflow request. |
| **Extraction** | Reading a document's fields, with how sure the reading is of each. |

## F
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **File drop** | Dropping files into the workspace inbox, where they can start pipelines. See [The file drop](#doc-file-drop). |
| **Form** | Fields people fill in; a submission can start a pipeline, a workflow or both. See [Build a form](#form-build). |
| **Frequency** | How often a schedule runs: minutes, hourly, daily, weekly, monthly or a cron expression. See [Reference](#gl-reference--schedule-frequencies). |

## G
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Generate report** | The step, or the action, that makes a report from a template and data. Every generate is a new version. |

## I
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Inbox** | The workspace's storage place where dropped and uploaded files land, and where a file can start a run. |
| **Item** | One thing a run works on, such as a photo, a document, a recording or a patient, with how it went at each step. See [The Items view](#run-items). |
| **Items** | A run's tab listing its items, to find a failed one and retry only those. |

## K
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Kept outputs** | What a run's steps kept (rows and files), which a retry reuses and which retention removes in time. |

## L
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Lead** | The member of a team who may add and remove its members. See [Teams](#adm-teams). |
| **Library** | **Reports › Library**: every report and all its versions. |
| **Log** | A run's tab with every line its steps wrote, every try included. |

## M
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Managed workspace** | A workspace whose pipelines and connections our team builds; its build screens are read-only for its own people. See [The managed service](#sec-managed). |
| **Managed session** | The recorded session in which our team works inside a managed workspace. |
| **Manager** | The person a member reports to; a workflow can send tasks or overdue work to them. |
| **Map** | A drawing of steps and how they connect: a run's **Map** tab, or an approval workflow's map. |
| **Masked** | A sensitive value hidden from someone whose access does not let them read it ("Masked for you"). |
| **Meter** | A count of something billed as it is used, such as runs, model tokens or pages read. |
| **Missed** | A run status: its time passed while nothing was running to take it. |
| **Model connection** | How the workspace reaches a model, hosted or on your own machines. See [Your models](#ai-models). |
| **My requests** | The requests you started, where each stands and its history. See [Start and follow a request](#apr-my-requests). |

## N
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Notification** | A notice in the bell; **Notifications** lists them all. |

## O
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **OCR** | Reading text from page images; the step **Read text from pages** does it and says how sure it is. |
| **Out of office** | A period in which a colleague stands in for you and may decide your tasks, each decision recorded "for" you. See [Out of office](#adm-out-of-office). |
| **Outputs** | A run's tab with the files it kept, each with **View** and **Download**. |

## P
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Page access** | Which pages and tabs a member may open; administrators open every page. See [Page access profiles](#adm-access-profiles). |
| **Page access profile** | A named set of pages and tabs, such as Clinician or Viewer, given to members. |
| **Page limit** | The most pages one report may have, 300 unless the workspace set fewer. |
| **Parameter** | A value a run is started with, such as a record number, that its steps read. See [Placeholders and run parameters](#pl-placeholders). |
| **Pass on** | Handing one task to a colleague, with a note; the history records it. |
| **Pipeline** | What a run does: the steps that read, check, transform, ask a model and write. See [What a pipeline is](#pl-overview). |
| **Placeholder** | A name in double braces, such as `{{mrn}}`, filled in from the row or the run. |
| **Platform administrator** | Our team's role across every workspace; works in a workspace's data only inside that workspace. |
| **Prompt** | The saved instructions an AI step sends to a model, with its answer's shape. See [Write and test a prompt](#ai-prompts). |

## Q
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Queue** | A run status: due and handed to the engine, not started yet (the run's page says **Queued**). |

## R
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Rate card** | The prices the workspace's usage is billed at, kept in versions with effective dates. |
| **Report** | A finished PDF and HTML document made from a template and data, with every version kept. |
| **Report Studio** | Where reports are designed, made, approved and signed: **See results › Reports**. See [Report Studio at a glance](#rs-overview). |
| **Request** | One case walking through an approval workflow, with its details and history. |
| **Retention** | How long each kind of data is kept before it is removed. See [Retention](#sec-retention). |
| **Retry** | Running a failed run again from its failed step, or only its failed items. See [When a run or a step fails](#ts-runs--retry). |
| **Review** | **Run & review › Review**: everything waiting for a person, with one count on the menu. See [Review](#apr-review-home). |
| **Role** | How much a person may do: workspace member, workspace administrator or platform administrator. See [Reference](#gl-reference--roles). |
| **Run** | One execution of a pipeline, with its steps, items, outputs and log. See [A run's page](#run-page). |
| **Run now** | Starting a schedule's run at once, by hand. See [Run now and Run with](#trg-run-now). |
| **Run pipeline** | A step, in a pipeline or a workflow, that runs another pipeline and can wait for its answer. See [Call another pipeline](#pl-run-pipeline). |

## S
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Sandbox** | A separate test workspace for your systems' test keys; nothing there is billed. See [The sandbox and test keys](#dev-sandbox). |
| **Schedule** | When a pipeline runs: on a timetable, only when started, or when something arrives. See [Run a pipeline on a timetable](#trg-schedules). |
| **Scope** | What an API client may do, such as `runs:write`. |
| **Sensitive** | The data level for personal, health or confidential data. |
| **Signature** | In Report Studio, a person's approval applied to a PDF, which **Verify signature** checks; also a signature image placed in a report. |
| **Skip** | A run status: passed over on purpose, or because the last run was still in flight (the run's page says **Skipped**). For a step: it did not run because an earlier step failed. |
| **Source** | A named place a pipeline reads from. See [Sources and connectors](#con-sources). |
| **Standing in** | Deciding a colleague's task while they are out of office; the task shows **Standing in for** them. |
| **Step** | One action of a pipeline, such as Read S3, Validate or Generate report. See [Every step at a glance](#step-glance). |
| **Sub-item** | A part of an item, such as one page of a document, listed under it. |
| **Submission** | One filled-in form; **Forms › Submissions** lists them. See [Submissions](#form-submissions). |

## T
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Tab** | One page of a menu entry with several, such as **Runs › Failed**; page access may grant tabs one by one. |
| **Task** | A workflow step for a person or a team to do and mark done, such as filling the triage form. |
| **Task Registry** | **Settings › Task Registry**: every task a step can run, and whether it is available here. |
| **Team** | A group of people that work can be sent to; whoever is free picks it up. See [Teams](#adm-teams). |
| **Template** | A report's design, made once and filled with data each time; published versions never change. |
| **Test sample** | Data kept with a template or pipeline for trying it out. |
| **Tile** | One chart, figure or table on a dashboard (also called a widget). |
| **Timeout** | The most seconds one try of a step may take. |
| **Trigger** | What starts a pipeline other than its timetable: a file, a document approved, a form, an event or a workflow. See [Three ways to start a pipeline](#pl-start). |
| **Tries** | How many times a step is tried before it fails. |

## V
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Verify signature** | Checking a report's PDF, or a file someone sent you, is intact and one of the workspace's approved reports. |
| **Version** | A saved state of a pipeline, workflow, template or report; earlier versions are kept. See [Save, versions and history](#pl-versions). |
| **Void** | A report version marked as no longer stood behind, with a reason; it stays, and every copy served says VOID. |

## W
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Webhook** | A call the platform makes to one of your systems when something happens, such as a run completed. See [Webhooks](#dev-webhooks). |
| **Workspace** | Your organisation's space in the console: its people, connections, pipelines, runs and bills; nothing crosses between workspaces. See [Your workspace](#adm-workspace). |
| **Workspace administrator** | The role that sets up a workspace: people, access, connections, pipelines, settings and bills. |
| **Workspace member** | The role that runs, reviews and reads, within the pages their profile opens. |

articles.title: Reference
articles.summary: The menu, the schedule frequencies, the roles and what a run's status means, to look things up.
articles.who: Everyone; what you see in the menu depends on your role and page access
articles.md:
The console's menu, the ways a schedule can repeat, the three roles and the run statuses, in one place.

## The menu
The menu is grouped by the job you are doing: get data in, build, run and review, see the results, then
administration and billing. Each entry with several pages opens them as tabs. You see the entries and tabs your role and
your page access open; the table below is the menu as it is for you now.

<!-- widget: menu-map -->

![The menu](gl-menu "The menu of a workspace administrator: Home, then Get data in, Build, Run & review, See results, Administration & billing")

> **Note:** Hiding a page from the menu is a courtesy: the page itself, and the data behind it, are refused to anyone
> who may not open them. See [Who sees what](#gs-who-sees-what).

## Schedule frequencies
A schedule **On a timetable** repeats in one of six ways. Pick it under **How often** on the schedule's page; the
timetable then reads as a sentence, such as "Every 1 day at 02:00, starting 5 Oct 2026".

| How often | Repeats | Also set |
|---|---|---|
| **Minutes** | Every N minutes, from a start time | The start date and time |
| **Hourly** | Every N hours, from a start time | The start date and time |
| **Daily** | Every N days, at a time | The time and start date |
| **Weekly** | Every N weeks, at a time | **On these days**: one or more weekdays |
| **Monthly** | Every N months, at a time | The day of the month, or the start date's day |
| **Advanced (cron)** | When a cron expression says | The expression; the start date and time may be left blank |

![How often on a schedule's page](gl-frequencies "How often: the six frequencies, the timetable as a sentence, and the optional end")

- **Repeat every** (the N) is a whole number, 1 or more.
- **Ends** is optional: the schedule still runs on the day it ends.
- A cron expression has five fields, minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week, and is read in server time (Chicago).
  The field offers three examples:

| Expression | Means |
|---|---|
| `0 3 * * *` | 03:00 every day |
| `*/15 * * * *` | every 15 minutes |
| `30 8 * * 1-5` | 08:30 on weekdays |

> **Tip:** A schedule can also be **Only when started** (from **Run now**, or when a workflow starts it), and either
> kind can add **A file arrives** or **A document is approved** as a way in. See
> [Run a pipeline on a timetable](#trg-schedules).

## Roles
A person's role decides how much they may do, and whether page access applies to them.

| Role | Opens | Can change |
|---|---|---|
| **Workspace member** | The pages on their page access profile (or the workspace's default profile); with no profile and no default, every page; plus any page opened for them alone | Only what those pages allow: running, reviewing, reading |
| **Workspace administrator** | Every page of the workspace; page access does not apply | People, connections, pipelines, policies and settings, and the bills |
| **Platform administrator** | Every workspace (the platform's own team) | Everything; a workspace's data only from inside that workspace |

What a member may open is set under **Administration › Page access**. See [Page access profiles](#adm-access-profiles)
and [Add a person and choose their role](#adm-people).

## Run statuses
Every run has one status. Lists show it as a pill; the run's own page says it in full, as in the second column.

| In lists | On the run's page | Means |
|---|---|---|
| **Queue** | Queued | Due and handed to the engine; not started yet |
| **Start** | Starting | Being picked up; its first step is about to run |
| **Running** | Running | Its steps are running and reporting progress |
| **Completed** | Completed | Finished, and whatever it produced has been written |
| **Failed** | Failed | Stopped with a reason; the page says which step and why, and it can be retried from that step |
| **Interrupted** | Interrupted | Stopped before it finished: cancelled, or it stopped responding |
| **Skip** | Skipped | Passed over on purpose: by a person, or because the schedule's last run was still in flight |
| **Missed** | Missed | Its time passed while nothing was running to take it, so a gap in the history is never silent |

A completed run whose results wait for a person reads **Completed · waiting for review**, then **Completed · approved**
or **Completed · rejected**; a run paused at an Approval step reads **Running · waiting for approval**. See
[Run statuses](#run-statuses).

## Kinds of failure
**Runs › Failed** sorts each failure into one kind, to show where to look:

| Kind | Where to look |
|---|---|
| **The data** | A row, a file or a contract: the data the run was given |
| **A service it called** | Another system, an API or a service the step depends on |
| **Timed out or stopped responding** | A step's time limit, or a slow system |
| **Too large for memory or a limit** | A row, size or call limit |
| **Its settings** | The pipeline's or the step's settings |
| **Rejected by a reviewer** | An Approval step's decision |
| **Closed by a person** | Someone stopped it |
| **Other** | Anything else; read the message |

See [When a run or a step fails](#ts-runs).

articles.title: What a pipeline is
articles.summary: Steps in order, each reading the step before or a step you name; a run; and what a run leaves behind.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Pipelines can see them; a workspace administrator builds and changes them
articles.md:
A pipeline is one unit of work your workspace does again and again: where it reads, what it does to the rows, who
checks them and where the results go. You describe it once as a list of **steps**; every time it runs, the steps run
in that order on that run's data.

A pipeline on its own does nothing. A **schedule** says when it runs: on a timetable, when a file, form, document or
event arrives, or only when someone presses **Run now**. One pipeline can have several schedules.

## Steps run in order

Each step does one job, such as **Read S3**, **Filter**, **Join**, **AI prompt** or **Generate report**. A step reads
rows and passes rows on:

1. The first step reads the pipeline's source, usually a file, an API, a database or approved documents.
2. Every later step reads **the latest output before this step**, unless you choose another earlier step in its
   **Reads** box. A **Join** or **Append** step also names the other steps it brings in.
3. Output steps (**Save File**, **Upload to bucket**, **Generate report**, **Send webhook** and the others) pass the rows
   on unchanged, so a pipeline can write in several places.

The builder groups the steps into stages so a long pipeline stays readable: **Read** (where the rows come from),
**Check**, **Transform**, **AI**, **Review** (the run waits for a person) and **Write** (where the results go).

## The run

A run is one go of the pipeline. While it runs, each step's output is kept as a dataset that the next steps read and
that you can open on the run's page. When the last step finishes the run is **Completed**; if a step fails, what
happens next depends on that step's **If it fails** setting (by default the run fails). A run always uses the version of
the steps that was current when it started, so saving a change never alters a run in progress.

## What a run leaves behind

- **Outputs**: files kept with the run (a CSV, a PDF, a report), objects written to your buckets, and rows sent to other
  systems.
- **Step datasets**: each step's rows, kept for the hours set in the pipeline's **Keep datasets (hours)** (24 unless you
  change it).
- **Items**: when a pipeline works one file, recording or document at a time, the run lists each of them with how it went
  at every step.
- **A review**, when the pipeline's settings ask for one: the results wait until a person approves them.

![The Pipelines list in Summit Valley Health System](pl-list "Build › Pipelines: each pipeline with its steps, schedules, last run and data sensitivity")

## Read the Pipelines list

1. Open **Build › Pipelines**. The **Pipelines** tab lists every pipeline of the workspace.
2. Each row shows **Steps** (how many; **Legacy** for an older pipeline that has none), **Schedules** (how many run it),
   **Last run** with its status, **Data** (its sensitivity, and **Reviewed** when its results wait for a review) and
   **Status**.
3. Use the search box (id, name, topic or pipeline), **Only mine** and the **Table** / **Cards** switch to find one.
4. Open the arrow beside a row to see **Schedules that run this pipeline**, or **Schedule it** when none does.
5. Click the name to open the pipeline. The **⋮** menu has **Edit**, **Duplicate** and **Delete**.

> **Note:** **Delete** is not offered while a schedule still runs the pipeline ("In use"). Move or delete those schedules
> first.

## Example

Summit Valley Health System's **Bed occupancy by ward** reads the day's census file, counts beds and occupied beds per
ward, works out the occupancy percentage, sorts the wards, uploads the result for the bed board and sends a notice when
there were no census rows. Its daily 06:00 schedule runs it; a manager can also press **Run now**.

## Limits

| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Steps in one pipeline | 50 |
| How long a run's step datasets are kept | 1 to 720 hours (24 by default) |
| Who builds and changes pipelines | A workspace administrator |
| Who sees them | Anyone whose page access includes Pipelines |

articles.title: Three ways to start a pipeline
articles.summary: Describe it to the AI Assistant, add the steps yourself, or copy an existing pipeline.
articles.who: A workspace administrator (New pipeline); the AI Assistant needs it in your page access
articles.popular: Start a new pipeline
articles.md:
**New pipeline** offers three starting points side by side. Whichever you choose, you end in the same step builder,
and nothing runs until a schedule or **Run now** starts it. A schedule, triggers and a review come after the pipeline is
made.

![The three ways to start a new pipeline](pl-new "New pipeline: describe it to the AI Assistant, add steps yourself, or copy an existing pipeline")

## Describe it to the AI Assistant

Use this when you know what the pipeline should do but not which steps make it.

1. Open **Build › Pipelines** and choose **New pipeline**.
2. Under **Describe it to the AI Assistant**, write in **What should it do?** what to read, what to work out and where
   the results go, for example: "Every night read the new lab result files, keep the abnormal results, save them and tell
   the physicians."
3. Choose **Open the AI Assistant**. The assistant drafts the steps and draws them as a flow beside the chat.
4. Select a step in the flow to see what it does and fill in its settings. Ask in the chat to change the flow; the
   drawing changes with it.
5. Choose **Create pipeline**. Check the **Name**, the **Pipeline id** (upper case, digits and _, unique in the
   workspace) and when it **Starts**. Tick **Create without schedule: it runs only when you press Run now** if you do not
   want the timetable the assistant proposed yet.
6. Choose **Create pipeline** in the dialog. Afterwards the flow offers **Run now**, **Schedule** and **Open in step
   builder**.

> **Note:** Nothing is saved until you press **Create pipeline**. If you change the flow afterwards, the button reads
> **Update pipeline** and saves the change as a new version; it never makes a second pipeline.

> **Tip:** The AI chapter says more: [Design a pipeline with the AI Assistant](#ai-assistant).

> **Warning:** The assistant's design is a draft. Check every step and its settings before you run it on real data.

## Add steps yourself

Use this when you know the steps, or want to start from sample rows.

1. In **New pipeline**, under **Add steps yourself**, type a **Name** (for example "Readmission risk (daily)").
2. Leave **Advanced: event source** as it is unless an older system starts this pipeline with a message.
3. Choose **Create and add steps**. The pipeline opens on its **Steps** tab, empty. See
   [the builder](#pl-builder) and [Test with sample](#pl-try).

## Copy an existing pipeline

Use this to make a variant of a pipeline that already works.

1. In **New pipeline**, under **Copy an existing pipeline**, choose the **Pipeline to copy**.
2. Change **Name of the copy** (it starts as the original's name with "(copy)").
3. Choose **Copy it**. The steps are copied into a pipeline of its own, so a change to one never changes the other.
4. The copy starts **Inactive**. Change what you need, save, then set its **Status** to **Active** on the **Details** tab.

> **Warning:** **Duplicate** in a pipeline's **⋮** menu on the list is not the same: the duplicate keeps using the
> original's steps, so saving steps in one changes both. For an independent copy, use **Copy an existing pipeline**.

## Example

Summit Valley's analyst copies **Bed occupancy by ward** as "Bed occupancy by ward (ICU only)", adds a **Filter** step
for the ICU wards and a tag on the **Settings** tab, and saves. The original pipeline and its 06:00 schedule are not
touched.

## Limits

| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| A pipeline's name | 120 characters |
| What should it do? | 4,000 characters |
| Who may start one | A workspace administrator; a platform administrator first opens the workspace |

articles.title: The step builder
articles.summary: Add, move and remove steps; each step's settings panel; the flow map and folding stages; the YAML and JSON views.
articles.who: A workspace administrator; some steps (Call API, Read runs, Run pipeline, Send webhook, Upload to bucket) only an administrator may add
articles.md:
The step builder is where a pipeline's steps are put in order and set up. Open a pipeline from **Build › Pipelines**:
its page shows the pipeline's name, status and version, **Schedule** and **Run now** at the top, an overview strip, and
the tabs **Details**, **Steps**, **Settings**, **Schedules**, **History**, **YAML** and **JSON**.

The overview strip reads left to right in the order a pipeline is set up: **Source**, **Steps**, **Review**,
**Outputs** and **Schedule & triggers**. Each part says **Set**, **Optional** or what is missing ("Add a Write step: a
file, a bucket, a PDF or a webhook"); click a part to go where it is set.

![The step builder with the steps grouped by stage](pl-builder "A pipeline's Steps tab: the overview strip, the steps in stages, Test with sample and Add step")

## Add a step

1. Open the pipeline's **Steps** tab.
2. Click **Add step from the Task Registry…** and type part of a step's name, such as "filter" or "report". The steps
   are grouped as **Read**, **Process** and **Output**; one marked **(disabled)** cannot be added here, and its hint says
   why.
3. Pick the step. It is added at the end and its settings panel opens.
4. Fill in the settings and choose **Apply**. The step is in the draft; nothing is saved yet.

> **Tip:** Which steps **Add step** offers is set for the whole workspace in **Settings › Task Registry**, not per
> pipeline.

## Fill in a step's settings panel

Click a step's name (or its pencil) to open its panel on the right.

1. **Key**: lower case letters, digits and _. It names the step's rows and is what a later step's **Reads** chooses.
2. **Name**: what the run's timeline calls the step. Blank: its key.
3. **Reads**: **The latest output before this step**, or an earlier step by its key.
4. **Task settings**: the step's own settings, as a form. **Edit as JSON** shows the same settings as text; **Edit as
   form** goes back. Each step's settings are described in the Step reference, for example [the Read steps](#step-read).
5. **How it runs**: **Tries** (1 means no retry), **Seconds between tries**, **Timeout (seconds)** and **If it fails**
   (**Fail the run**, **Continue with the next step** or **Skip the rest and complete**). Blank fields take the step's
   own defaults and then the pipeline's [run defaults](#pl-settings--run-defaults).
6. Choose **Apply** to keep the changes in the draft, or **Cancel**.

![A step's settings panel](pl-step-panel "The Measure image step's panel: key, name, what it reads and its task settings")

## Move or remove a step

- Drag a step by its handle, or focus the handle and press the up and down arrow keys.
- Or use the step's **up** and **down** arrows.
- The bin removes the step from the draft.

After a move, problems found earlier are cleared: choose **Validate** again to see what is still wrong.

## The flow map

Choose **Flow** (beside **List**) to see the steps as a map: each step a box with its first settings, the arrows where
its rows really come from (the step before, the step it reads, a join's other side), the run's start before it.

- Click a box to open that step's panel.
- A step with problems is marked red; a step not saved yet is dashed.
- The arrows beside the stage buttons draw the map **top to bottom** or **left to right**; the zoom buttons fit and
  enlarge it.

### Fold the stages

A pipeline of more than 12 steps opens with its stages folded: each run of steps of one stage is one box, such as
"Transform · 3 steps".

1. Click a stage button (for example **Transform 3–5**) to open or fold that stage.
2. **Collapse all** folds every stage; **Expand all** opens them.
3. Clicking a folded box opens it.

The builder remembers in your browser whether you last chose **List** or **Flow**.

![The flow map with folded stages](pl-flow "A 20-step pipeline in the Flow view, its stages folded")

## The YAML and JSON views
