The **YAML** and **JSON** tabs show the same definition as the builder, as text: its steps with their keys, tasks,
settings and how they run, its run parameters and its settings.

1. Open **YAML** (or **JSON**) to read or copy the whole definition.
2. You may edit the text. **Validate** and **Save** read it; leaving the tab applies it to the builder.
3. If the JSON is not valid, the builder keeps the steps it had and says why.

![The definition as YAML](pl-yaml "The YAML tab: the same definition as the builder")

## Example

Summit Valley's **Journey 7 · Wound photo** pipeline has 11 steps in five stages: read the photo the run was started
for, take the MRN from the file name, measure the wound against the ruler, ask the vision model for a DRAFT
description, join the patient's last visit, work out the change in area, keep the result, wait for the wound-care team's
approval, and make one report per photo.

## Limits

| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Steps in a pipeline | 50 |
| Tries for one step | 1 to 10 |
| Seconds between tries | 0 to 3,600 |
| A step's timeout | 1 to 86,400 seconds |

articles.title: Try a pipeline before you rely on it
articles.summary: Put sample rows first, check the pipeline with Validate, run it once and read each step's result.
articles.who: A workspace administrator
articles.popular: Test a pipeline on sample rows
articles.md:
Before a pipeline reads real data on a timetable, try it on a few rows you write yourself, let the console check the
whole definition, and run it once to see what every step made. Nothing here changes the data the pipeline will later
read.

## Put sample rows first

1. Open the pipeline's **Steps** tab and choose **Test with sample**.
2. In **Sample rows**, write the rows as a JSON list, each row an object of column and value (text, a number,
   true/false or null). The box starts with two example rows, or with the rows a sample step already holds.
3. Choose **Use these rows**. A **Sample rows** step is put first in the draft (or the existing one is filled) and the
   console checks the pipeline at once.

```Sample rows for a pipeline
[
  { "mrn": "SV-000917", "condition": "heart failure" },
  { "mrn": "SV-000918", "condition": "copd" }
]
```

![The Test with sample dialog](pl-sample "Test with sample: rows the steps run on, in place of the pipeline's source")

> **Warning:** The **Sample rows** step is a real step of the draft. Once the pipeline works, remove it (or put the real
> **Read** step first) before you save the version a schedule will run.

> **Tip:** A **Call API** step's panel shows **What the first call sends** from these sample rows, so you can check the
> request body before any call is made.

## Check the pipeline

Choose **Validate** in the save bar at the foot of the page. The platform checks every step's settings, the keys,
what each step reads and the pipeline's settings, the same checks a save makes.

- "The definition is valid." means it would save and run as written.
- Otherwise the bar says how many problems there are, each step with a problem shows a red **Problems** pill and its
  messages under its name, and a problem with the pipeline's settings shows beside that field.
- A problem the console cannot place on a step is listed at the top of the tab.

## Run it once and read each step

1. Choose **Save & run now** at the top of the page (it reads **Run now** when there is nothing to save). Unsaved changes
   are saved first: a run always runs the saved steps.
2. If no schedule runs the pipeline yet, **Run now** gives it an on-demand schedule (it runs only when started) and runs
   it.
3. A panel opens on the run: each step with its status, how long it took, its rows in and out, the datasets it made
   (their row counts and columns), any error, and **Show log** for its log lines.
4. Open the run's own page (from **Run & review › Runs**) to see each step's rows, the outputs and the items.

> **Note:** A pipeline with more than one schedule asks which one to run.

## Example

Summit Valley's **Synthetic cohort generator check** starts with **Sample rows** (20 synthetic patients), checks them
against the registry contract with **Validate**, and keeps the result with **Save File**. The team builds the real
pipeline on these rows first, then swaps the first step for **Read CSV/JSON/Parquet**.

## Limits

| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Rows in a Sample rows step | 1,000 |
| Who may run Validate and Save | A workspace administrator |
| Runs started this way | Billed like any run |

articles.title: Save, versions and history
articles.summary: What a save makes, the version history, which version a run uses, and how to go back to an earlier design.
articles.who: A workspace administrator saves; anyone who can open the pipeline sees its history
articles.md:
Every save of a pipeline's steps makes a new **version**. A run uses the version that was current when it started, so
you can change a pipeline while it runs, and every run can later be traced to the steps it used.

## Save the pipeline

1. Make your changes on any tab: **Details**, **Steps**, **Settings**, **YAML** or **JSON**.
2. The save bar at the foot of the page says whether there are unsaved changes. **Discard** puts everything back as
   saved; **Validate** checks the draft first (see [Try a pipeline](#pl-try--check-the-pipeline)).
3. Choose **Save**. The platform checks the definition again; when it is valid, the steps are saved as the next version
   and the version pill beside the pipeline's name (**v3**, for example) moves on.
4. If the save is refused, the problems are shown on their steps, as **Validate** shows them, and nothing is saved.

> **Note:** A pipeline made before steps existed runs as its **legacy** step: its payload, sent to the worker that reads
> its topic. Adding a step replaces it, and once saved every schedule of that pipeline runs the steps instead.

## Read the version history

1. Open the pipeline's **History** tab.
2. **Versions** lists each saved version with when it was **Saved** and **By** whom. The current one is marked
   **Current**.

![The version history of a pipeline](pl-history "History: each save of the steps is a version")

## Go back to an earlier design

The **History** tab lists the versions; it does not compare two of them side by side or restore an older one with a
button. To undo a change:

1. Before you save, choose **Discard** in the save bar to drop unsaved changes.
2. After you save, change the steps back (on the **Steps** tab, or paste the earlier definition you kept from the
   **YAML** tab) and save again. The result is a new version with the earlier design.

> **Tip:** Before a large change, copy the **YAML** tab's text somewhere safe. It is the whole definition, and pasting
> it back and saving restores it exactly.

To see what changed between two runs, open the schedule's **Items** tab and tick two runs to compare them (see [a schedule's items](#run-schedule-items)): the
comparison shows each step's differences and what changed in the pipeline between them.

## Example

Summit Valley's **Journey 7 · Wound photo** has three versions, v1 to v3, each saved by the workspace administrator
within a few minutes while the pipeline was built. Its schedule's runs from before the last save still name the version
they ran, so a wound report made by v2 can be told apart from one made by v3.

## Limits

| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Versions kept | Every saved version |
| Who saves | A workspace administrator; in a workspace our team manages, the pipeline is read-only to you |

articles.title: Pipeline settings
articles.summary: Reviews and who reviews, one by one, data sensitivity, tags, how long outputs are kept, the default timeout and what a failed step does.
articles.who: A workspace administrator
articles.md:
A pipeline's **Settings** tab holds what applies to all its steps: where the first step's input comes from, the run
parameters, the defaults every step inherits, the data's sensitivity and tags, and whether a person reviews the results.
They are saved with the steps, as part of the same version.

![The Settings tab of a pipeline](pl-settings "Settings: source, run parameters, run defaults and data sensitivity")

## Source

**Source** says where the first step's input comes from when no **Read** step says. Leave it at **Default (none: the
first step makes its own rows)** for almost every pipeline: its first step reads a file, an API, a database or
documents. **The task payload: one row, a column per tag** is for a pipeline whose run is handed a record, for example
by a form, an event or the API.

## Run parameters

What a run may be given: by **Run with…**, by a backfill or through the API. A scheduled run takes the defaults. See
[run parameters](#pl-placeholders--run-parameters).

## Run defaults

| Setting | What it does | Blank |
|---|---|---|
| **Keep datasets (hours)** | How long a run's step outputs are kept, 1 to 720 | 24 |
| **Default timeout (seconds)** | The time limit for each try of a step that sets none, 1 to 86,400 | 600 |
| **If a step fails** | What happens when a step that does not say fails: **Fail the run**, **Continue with the next step** or **Skip the rest and complete** | Fail the run |

A step's own panel can say otherwise under **How it runs**. Some steps have a longer time limit of their own (for
example **Transcribe audio** and **Read text from pages**, two hours); see [the steps at a glance](#step-glance).

## Data sensitivity and tags

1. Under **Data sensitivity**, choose **Public**, **Internal** or **Sensitive**. Patient data (PHI) is **Sensitive**. The
   workspace's data policy for that level decides which models the pipeline's steps may use and how long a run keeps its
   files.
2. Under **Tags**, type short words separated by commas, such as "research, pilot". A rate card may price a tag's
   pipelines at a price of their own.

The **Data** column of the Pipelines list shows the sensitivity, or **Not set**.

## Review: whether a person approves the results

1. Under **Results need review by**, tick **Our team**, **The customer (through the API)**, or both. A run's results then
   start as waiting for review. Your team approves or rejects them on the run's page or in **Review**; the customer
   decides through the API from its own portal.
2. Tick **Requires individual review (never approved or rejected in bulk)** when every result must be looked at on its
   own. Each run's review, and each request of this pipeline's **Approval** steps, then has to be decided one by one:
   bulk approve and bulk reject skip them.
3. Who is asked, and the reminders, are set in **Approval workflows › Pipeline run review**. The workflow for **Approval**
   steps inside the run is **Approval workflows › Pipeline step approval**.

![The Review settings of a pipeline](pl-review "Review: who must approve the results, and whether they are decided one by one")

> **Note:** The run's review waits on the whole run's results after the last step. An **Approval** step pauses the run in
> the middle until its reviewers approve. A pipeline can use either or both; see [Approval](#step-people).

## Example

Summit Valley's **Journey 8 · Chest X-ray triage** marks its results for review by **Our team**, with the Radiology team
asked, and **Requires individual review**: a radiologist opens every draft finding on its own, and none can be approved
in bulk with others. Its data sensitivity is **Sensitive**.

## Limits

| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Keep datasets | 1 to 720 hours |
| Default timeout | 1 to 86,400 seconds |
| Who changes settings | A workspace administrator |

Which steps **Add step** offers is switched on and off for the whole workspace in **Settings › Task Registry**, not
here.

articles.title: Placeholders and run parameters
articles.summary: {{date}}, {{run}}, a row's columns and run parameters: what each fills in, and where it can be used.
articles.who: A workspace administrator writes them; they fill in every run

where.label: Build › Pipelines › a pipeline › Steps and Settings

articles.popular: Use the run's date in a file name
articles.md:
A **placeholder** is a name in double braces, such as `{{date}}`, written in a step's text setting. Each run fills it
in: the day, the run's number, a value from the row, or a value the run was given. One pipeline can then write a new
file every day, name a report after its patient, or read only the period it was started for.

An unknown placeholder is left as written, so a typing mistake shows in the result instead of vanishing.

## The run's placeholders

| Placeholder | Fills in |
|---|---|
| `{{date}}` | The day the run started, as 2026-10-26 (Chicago time) |
| `{{time}}` | The time the run started, as 061500 (hours, minutes, seconds) |
| `{{run}}` | The run's number |
| `{{attempt}}` | Which try of the run this is |
| `{{step}}` | The step's key |
| `{{job}}` | The schedule's number |
| `{{pipeline}}` | The pipeline's id |
| `{{rows}}` | How many rows the step has (where a step has rows) |

## A run started for files or documents

| Placeholder | Fills in |
|---|---|
| `{{input_key}}`, `{{input_name}}` | The file the run was started for: its key in your storage, and the key's last part |
| `{{input_count}}`, `{{input_keys}}` | How many files a run took, and their keys joined by commas |
| `{{document_count}}`, `{{document_ids}}` | How many approved documents started the run, and their ids |
| `{{document.field}}` | A field of the first document, such as `{{document.patient_name}}`; also `{{document.id}}` and `{{document.file_name}}` |

In a run that no document started, `{{document_count}}` is 0 and the document placeholders are empty.

## A row's columns

Where a step works row by row, `{{column}}` is that row's value: `{{mrn}}`, `{{file_stem}}`. Where a step fills a
setting once for the whole step (a notice's title, an approval's title), the first row's values are used.

## Run parameters

Run parameters are values a run is given. Declare them on the pipeline's **Settings** tab, under **Run parameters**:

1. Choose **Add a parameter**.
2. Give it a **Name** (lower case letters, digits and _, starting with a letter), a **Type** (**Date**, **Date and
   time**, **Text**, **Number**, **Yes or no** or **Choice**), a **Label** people see, a **Default**, whether it is
   **Required**, and for a choice its **Choices** (separated by commas).
3. Save. Steps read the value as `{{param.name}}`.

| Placeholder | Fills in |
|---|---|
| `{{param.name}}` | The run's value for that parameter, or its default |
| `{{run.date}}` | The day the run is for, in the workspace's billing time zone; for a backfill, the period's day |
| `{{run.windowStart}}`, `{{run.windowEnd}}` | The start and end of the run's period |

A scheduled run takes the defaults. **Run with…**, a backfill and the API may give other values; see
[Run now and Run with…](#trg-run-now).

![Two run parameters declared on a pipeline](pl-parameters "Run parameters: a from and a to date, read by the steps as {{param.from}} and {{param.to}}")

## Where placeholders work

Placeholders fill in the text settings that say so in their hint ("{{date}} and the other run placeholders are filled
in"). The main ones:

| Step | Settings that take placeholders |
|---|---|
| Read CSV/JSON/Parquet | **File** |
| Read S3 | **Prefix** |
| Read API | **Variables** |
| Read documents | **Approved from**, **Approved to** |
| AI prompt | **Variables** |
| Call API, Enrich | **Variables** |
| Run pipeline | **Parameters** |
| Approval | **Task title**, **What to check**, **Fields** |
| Convert file | **Output key** |
| Save File | **File name** |
| Upload to bucket | **Object key** |
| Generate report | **Report name**, **Period** |
| Render PDF | **Title**, **Header fields**, **Watermark**, section titles and notes |
| Send Notification | **Title** |
| Send webhook | **Fields** |

```A daily file name
ops/beds/census-{{date}}.csv
```

```One file per row, named from the row
insights/{{file_stem}}.json
```

> **Note:** A row's values fill a key's name but cannot add folders to it.

## Example

Summit Valley's **Consent forms by date range** declares two **Date** parameters, `from` and `to`. Its **Read
documents** step reads consent forms approved from `{{param.from}}` to `{{param.to}}`, so a records officer can press
**Run with…** and count the forms of any month.

## Limits

| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Run parameters on one pipeline | 20 |
| A text parameter's value | 500 characters, one line, no `{{` |

articles.title: Call another pipeline with a Run pipeline step
articles.summary: Use another pipeline's answer inside a pipeline, once or once per row, and how deep a chain may go.
articles.who: A workspace administrator (Run pipeline is an administrator's step)
articles.md:
A **Run pipeline** step calls another pipeline of the same workspace with parameters, waits for its run to end and
takes its answer as rows. Build a piece of work once (a patient lookup, a risk score) and use it from several pipelines,
instead of copying its steps into each.

Each call is a run of its own: it shows in **Runs** under the called pipeline, with its own steps and outputs, and it is
billed like any run.

## Add a Run pipeline step

1. Open the calling pipeline's **Steps** tab and add **Run pipeline** from **Add step**.
2. **Pipeline**: choose the schedule of the pipeline to call. It must be one of this workspace's, active, and built from
   steps.
3. **Call**: `once` makes one call for the step, its parameters filled from the run and the first row; `each` makes one
   call per input row.
4. **Parameters**: the called pipeline's parameters by name, filled from the row and the run, such as `{{mrn}}`,
   `{{param.region}}` or `{{run.date}}`. They are checked against what the called pipeline declares, as **Run with…**
   checks them.
5. **Answer from**: `final` takes the called run's last output; or name the key of one of its steps.
6. **Fields**: the answer's columns to keep (a column, or a column holding JSON and a dot path into it, such as
   `summary.risk`), each with an **As** name. None: every column.
7. Choose **Apply**, then **Save**.

## What the step gives back

- With `once`: the called run's rows, at most **At most rows** of them (10,000 by default); the step warns when there
  were more.
- With `each`: the input rows, each with its call's first answer row and four columns about the call: its run id,
  status, ok and error, named with the **Column prefix** (`called_` by default: `called_run_id`, `called_status`,
  `called_ok`, `called_error`).

**When a call does not complete**: `fail` fails the step; `continue` (with `each`) keeps the row with its status and
error, so a later **Filter** can pick out the failed calls.

## From an approval workflow

An approval workflow can run a pipeline too, with a **Run pipeline** step of its own, and wait for it before the next
person decides. See [From an approval workflow](#trg-workflow).

## Example

A Summit Valley care-coordination pipeline reads the patients due a visit tomorrow, then calls **Journey 9 · Care-plan
draft** once per patient (`each`, parameter `mrn` = `{{mrn}}`), keeping the draft's `risk` field as `care_risk`. A
**Filter** then keeps the patients whose draft risk is High for the nurse's list.

## Limits

| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Calls one step may make (`each`) | **At most calls**: 20 by default, up to 100; an input needing more fails before any call |
| How deep a chain may go | 3 calls deep (A calls B calls C calls D); a pipeline already in the chain cannot be called again |
| Rows taken from the answer (`once`) | **At most rows**, 10,000 by default |
| Time limit of the step | 3,600 seconds unless its panel says otherwise |
| Who may add it | A workspace administrator |

articles.summary: Set up the workspace for the journey, mail a referral in, have a person check it, and let the approval start the admission pipeline.
