- **Raise the limit**: for a workspace administrator, opens Report size.

## Retention
How long report files stay is the class **Reports** of the workspace's retention policy, set in **Administration ›
Data policies** ([Retention](#sec-retention)). After the days you set, retention removes:

- the files of versions a newer version replaced, and
- the frozen data no kept version uses.

It **never** removes a report's current version, any approved or signed version, a version waiting for approval,
templates, assets or brand profiles. A removed version keeps its record and reads **Removed by retention**.

To see what would go before anything is removed: in **Reports › Settings › What retention would remove**, set **Older
than (days)** (365 by default) and choose **Preview**. Nothing is removed there.

## Other limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Pages in one report | 300 by default; up to 2,000 with the platform's agreement |
| A report's output file | 50 MB |
| Components in a template | 500 |
| Generating | 30 a minute a person; previews 30 a minute |
| Download links | work for five minutes |

articles.title: What reports cost
articles.summary: Which report actions are billed, how they show in Cost & usage, and what is never billed.
articles.who: Workspace administrators read Billing
articles.md:
Report Studio is billed by what it makes, on the workspace's rate card, and shows in **Billing › Cost & usage** like
everything else ([How usage is counted](#bill-usage)).

| What you do | How it is counted |
|---|---|
| Generate a report version (by hand or from a pipeline) | one **Documents converted** per version; Cost & usage names the template and the pages, and a pipeline's version counts towards that pipeline's cost |
| A job retried after a failure | billed once |
| The AI designer's proposals | AI usage (tokens) on the workspace's model connection ([What AI costs](#ai-costs)) |
| Report files kept | storage, measured nightly, like any file |
| Previews, checks, Verify signature, reading the Library | not billed |
| A job that failed and made no version | not billed |

## See what reports cost
1. Open **Billing › Cost & usage**.
2. Look for **Documents converted** under the meters; **Line by line** shows each version's line with the template's
   name.
3. For a pipeline's reports, open **Cost by pipeline** and the pipeline: its reports are part of its cost.

> **Tip:** One report per row makes one version per row, so a pipeline that makes eighteen statements a run is eighteen
> documents a run. Use **At most reports** to cap it while you try it.

articles.title: Report Studio troubleshooting
articles.summary: The messages you may meet — a missing field, over the page limit, a missing picture, a refused approval — and what to do.
articles.md:
When a report cannot be made, **no version is made** and the version before it is unchanged: a failed job never
replaces anything. The report's page and the job say why.

## "'primary.x' is not in this data"
The template reads a field the data does not have, and nothing is filled in for it.

- **Fix:** choose **Fix field mapping** and match the field to what the data calls it; or add the field to the
  pipeline's output and run the pipeline again; or, in the template, make the field optional or change the binding.

## Required field missing
In **Data and mapping**, a required field reads **Missing**. A missing value is never filled in for you: pick the
source field the data has, or a newer run that has it.

## Over the page limit
The report would have more pages than the workspace's limit. See [Retention and page limits](#rs-limits--over-the-limit):
make one report per row, lower a table's rows, export the data as CSV, or ask a workspace administrator to raise it.

## A picture is missing
An **Image from data** reads a file that is not there, or that you may not open (pictures are read as the person
generating). Check the file exists in **Analysis › Files**, then generate again. The component's settings say whether a
missing picture prints a placeholder or nothing.

## You cannot approve
- You generated the version: someone else approves it.
- It is not the current version: approve the newest one.
- You lack **Approve and sign reports** in your page access: ask a workspace administrator.

## "Someone saved this draft since you opened it"
Two people edited the same draft. **Reload** to take theirs, or **Save as a copy** to keep yours as a new template.

## The AI assistant says "Not available here now"
The workspace has no active model connection, or data policies keep this data from the model. See
[Your models](#ai-models).

## Too many at once
Past 30 generates or previews a minute you are asked to wait a few seconds. A pipeline making many reports at once
queues them; nothing is lost.

## The signature reads "validity unknown" in Adobe Reader
Expected while the platform uses its test certificate: use **Verify signature** on the report's page.

articles.title: Follow runs
articles.summary: Runs › Latest, By date, Analytics, Failed and Backfills, what each is for, and who sees which runs.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Schedules or Runs by date; Analytics, Failed and Backfills each have their own page access
articles.popular: Find a run and see how it went
articles.md:
Every time a pipeline runs, the console records a **run**: when it was queued, started and ended, what started it, its
steps, its items and what it made. **Run & review › Runs** is where you follow them, in five tabs.

![Runs › Latest](run-latest "Run & review › Runs › Latest: narrow the runs on the left; the bars show when they ran")

## The five tabs
| Tab | What it is for |
|---|---|
| **Latest** | Every schedule's newest runs. Narrow them on the left by **When**, **Status**, **Pipeline** and **Started by**; the bars show when they ran |
| **By date** | Every run in a date range (**Today**, **7 days**, **30 days**, **This month**, **Custom**): waiting, running and finished |
| **Analytics** | How the runs measure up: success rate, durations, outcomes by day, and **Pipeline health**, worst first |
| **Failed** | Every failed or timed-out run, grouped by error pattern, with where it failed and why (see [When something fails](#run-failures)) |
| **Backfills** | A schedule run once for each day of a past range, a few at a time, with its progress |

![Runs › By date](run-by-date "Run & review › Runs › By date: every run of the last seven days, with its status counts")

## Find a run
1. Open **Run & review › Runs**. **Latest** opens first.
2. On the left, pick **When** (Today, Since yesterday, Last 7 days, Last 30 days), then tick a **Status**, a **Pipeline** or
   how the run was **Started by** (Schedule, Run now, File arrived, Document approved, Form submitted, Backfill,
   Workflow, Called by a pipeline, API). The numbers beside each say how many runs match.
3. Type a run number or a word of its message in **Search run id or message**.
4. **Charts** shows or hides the bars; **Columns** chooses the table's columns.
5. Click the run number to open the run's page (see [A run's page](#run-page)).

Each row shows the run, its schedule and pipeline, when it was queued, started and ended, the duration, the
[status](#run-statuses), how many items are done (**1 of 1 done**) and the run's last message, such as *11 of 11 step(s)
completed*.

> **Tip:** A schedule's own runs are on the schedule: **Build › Pipelines › Schedules & triggers**, open the schedule and its
> **Runs** tab, beside **Items**. **Ask about this schedule** answers questions such as when it runs next or why it failed.

## Read Analytics
**Run analytics** covers a range (**Today** to **90 days**, or **Custom**) and can be narrowed to some pipelines, schedules,
outcomes or owners. It shows the runs, how many failed, the success rate and the median duration; the **Outcome mix**;
the **Duration spread**; **Runs by day**; and **Pipeline health**: each pipeline with its runs, completed, failed,
interrupted, skipped and missed, its success rate, median and slowest time, and a state such as *Failing* or *Unreliable*.

## Backfills
A backfill runs a schedule once for each day of a past range, a few at a time. Start one from the schedule's **⋮** menu,
**Backfill…**. **Runs › Backfills** lists each with its range, how many at once, its progress (*25 of 25*) and its state;
filter by **Open**, **Failed**, **Completed** or **Cancelled**. The failed days of a backfill are retried from the backfill.

## Who sees which runs
- A workspace administrator sees every run of the workspace.
- A member sees the runs of the schedules that are theirs.
- A reviewer also sees the runs they are asked to review, and the runs whose Approval steps went to them, so the link in
  their task opens the run.
- A viewer whose page access has neither Schedules nor Runs by date sees no runs.

Reading a run is not changing it: retrying, running again and deciding stay with the run's owner and the administrators,
and with the reviewers for their own decisions.

## Example
On a Monday morning, Rosa Alvarez (charge nurse, Ward 4B) opens **Runs › Latest**, ticks **Failed** and the pipeline
*Journey 11 · Daily progress and threshold alerts*, and opens any run that did not complete. Claire Martin (controller)
uses **Analytics** to see which finance pipelines failed this week, such as *Bank statement matching*.

articles.title: A run's page
articles.summary: The run's summary and Next steps, and its tabs Steps, Map, AI answers, Items, Outputs and Log; viewing a PDF, JSON or table; downloading.
articles.who: Anyone who may read the run (see Follow runs); deciding and retrying stay with its owner, the administrators and its reviewers
articles.md:
A run's page says everything about one run: what it did step by step, what it made, and what is left for a person to do.
Open it from any list of runs by its number, from a task in Review, or from a notification.

![A run's page, its Steps tab](run-page "A run's page: the header and its links, the summary strip, the tabs, and the Steps table")

## The top of the page
- The **title** names the run and its schedule, with one status, such as *Completed*, *Completed · waiting for review* or
  *Running · waiting for approval* (see [Run statuses](#run-statuses)).
- The links under it: **All runs of this schedule**, the **Pipeline**, the **Dashboards** the run feeds, and, for an
  administrator, **What this run cost**.
- The **summary strip**: **Started**, **Ended**, **Duration**, **Started by** (*By hand*, *Its timetable* or *A trigger*),
  **Steps** done, **Rows in → out** and, for an administrator, its **Cost**. A failed run's message is under it in words.
- **Next steps** appears when the run waits for a person: its review, or an Approval step. Those who may decide approve or
  reject there (see [Review a run's results](#apr-run-review) and [Approval steps inside a run](#apr-approval-steps)).

## The tabs
| Tab | What it shows |
|---|---|
| **Steps** | Each step in order: its status, when it started, how long it took (the slowest is marked), **Rows in → out**, its output and its own log lines |
| **Map** | The run drawn as its steps, sized by time or rows |
| **AI answers** | Each model answer of the run's AI steps, with the prompt, version, time and tokens; only when the pipeline has AI steps |
| **Items** | Each file, document, recording or row the run worked on, one by one; only for a pipeline that works item by item (see [The Items view](#run-items)) |
| **Outputs** | Every file the run kept or wrote, by step |
| **Log** | Every log line: search, filter by level and step, jump to the **Previous error** or **Next error**, copy or download what is shown |

The tab is part of the page's address, so a link to a run's **Outputs** opens on its outputs.

> **Tip:** While a run is still running, the Log follows it, checking every five seconds. **Timing** on the Log shows
> where the run waited between entries.

## View a file, or take it away
1. Open the **Outputs** tab. Files are grouped by the step that made them, with their type, size and where they are kept
   (*With the run · until* a date, or the bucket and folder they were written to).
2. Choose **View** to look at a file in place:
   - a PDF opens in the PDF viewer;
   - a JSON file opens formatted, with a **Table** view one click away;
   - a table (CSV, JSON lines, Excel, Parquet) opens as a table.
3. Choose **Download**, or from **⋮** download a table **as CSV, JSON or JSONL**, **Visualise** it as a chart, or copy its
   bucket path or file name.

On the **Steps** tab, a step's output has its own download button beside it.

![The PDF a run made, open in the viewer](run-outputs-pdf "Outputs › View: the report the run made, in the PDF viewer")

> **Note:** A file kept *with the run* expires after the time the pipeline or the workspace's data policy sets (24 hours
> unless they set another). Once it has expired it shows **Expired** and can no longer be downloaded; files a run wrote to
> your own buckets stay there.

## Example
Run #2042 of *Journey 7 · Wound photo* took 21 seconds: 11 of 11 steps, one photo in and one row out. On **Steps**,
*Vision model: DRAFT description* was the slowest at 15 seconds, and *Wound care approves the measurement* shows
*Approved by Sam Harper*. **Outputs** holds the wound result as JSON in the clinical bucket and the one-page wound report
as a PDF.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Rows drawn in the table viewer | 500 (the rest are in the download) |
| Formatted JSON drawn | 200,000 characters (the rest is in the download) |
| Files kept with the run | 24 hours unless the pipeline or the data policy sets another |

articles.title: The Items view
articles.summary: One item per file, document, recording or row; sub-items; an item's data and files; text read beside the page image; acting on many at once.
articles.who: Anyone who may read the run; retrying items and Send to review are for those who may open the schedule
articles.popular: Open one item of a run
articles.md:
A pipeline that works **item by item** (each photo, document, recording or patient) keeps a record for every item: how it
went at each step, its data and its files. The run's **Items** tab lists them, so you can find the one that failed, see
why, and retry only that one.

![The Items tab of a run](run-items "A run's Items tab: the summary, the filters and search, and one row per item with a column per step")

## Read the list
- The **summary** at the top: how many **Items** the first step found, how many are **Done** and **Failed**, the
  **Duration** (about how long an item took) and the **Files made**.
- The filters **All**, **Done**, **Failed** and **Running**, each with its count, and **Check by hand** when a step that
  reads text from pages marked pages it was unsure of.
- **Search an item, or a value like risk = High**: an item's name, or a value of any field.
- One row per item: its name and folder, its status (*Done*, or *Failed at* the step), and a column per step with
  **View** for that step's data. **Columns** chooses the fields shown; **Download CSV** takes the list.
- A row with **sub-items** (a document's pages, for example) opens them with **Show the pages of** the item.

> **Privacy:** A value the Data Catalog holds as sensitive shows as **Masked for you** unless your access lets you read it.

## Open one item
1. Choose **Open** on the item's row.
2. The panel shows the item's **Steps for this item**: each step's status and time, **Why it failed** for a failed item,
   and **Data at each step** (**View the data at** a step, **Copy** it).
3. **Files for this item** lists what each step kept for it, such as the page images, with **View** and **Download**.
4. For a scanned page, **Page image beside the text read** shows the page and the text the step read side by side, and how
   sure it was.
5. **Previous item** and **Next item** move through the list; **All runs of this item** finds the item in the schedule's
   other runs; **Retry this item** runs a failed item again from the step it failed at.

![One item open](run-item-panel "An item's panel: its steps, its data at each step and the files kept for it")

**Earlier versions** lists the item's attempts (*Attempt 2 · Done · current*, *Attempt 1 · Failed · earlier*) when it was
retried.

Some steps are made once for the whole run (a report of all rows, say): they show **Made once for the run**. A step that
did not run for an item because an earlier one failed shows **Not run: an earlier step failed**.

## Act on many items at once
1. Tick the items, or tick the page and choose **Select all N matching** to take every item the filter and search find,
   on every page.
2. The bar at the foot of the list offers:
   - **Retry N failed**: only the failed ones of the selection, each from the step it failed at;
   - **Download zip**: each item's files in a folder of its own;
   - **Export CSV**: the selected rows;
   - **Send to review**: ask **A team** or **A role** to check them, with **What to check**; they get one task in
     **Review › Approvals**.
3. **Clear the selection** with the close button.

![Items selected, with the bar](run-items-selected "Three failed items selected: Retry failed, Download zip, Export CSV and Send to review")

> **Tip:** **Retry failed items** above the list retries every failed item at once. The steps before are reused, not run
> again, and the items that are done are left as they are; a report already made for an item is kept.

## Sensitive pipelines
A pipeline marked sensitive in its settings has a person's details masked for anyone the data policy masks them for
(names, emails, phone numbers, ids, addresses): in every item's values, its data at each step, the compare, the CSV,
the zip's `item.json` and the run's outputs, from its very first row. An item's name stays visible (its file name, or
the id column that names it, such as a record or patient id), so you can still find it and tell items apart.

The files such a pipeline keeps (a saved file, an item's files, a report's PDF) are its real output and are not masked:
viewing, previewing or downloading them needs the **Download sensitive files** permission on the person's access
profile (**Administration › Page access**). Without it you see each file's name, size and type, and a lock in place of
**Download**. Workspace administrators always have it.

## Example
Daniel Kim drops four wound photos; one is too dark to measure. The run's **Items** shows *4 items, 3 done, 1 failed at
Measure*. Sam Harper opens the failed item, reads **Why it failed**, has the photo taken again, and chooses **Retry this
item**: only that photo is measured again.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Items in one zip | 200 |
| Rows per page | You choose the page size at the foot of the list |

articles.title: Find an item across runs, and compare two runs
articles.summary: A schedule's Items tab finds an item or a value in every run, newest first; tick two runs to compare them field by field.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Schedules and who may open the schedule
articles.md:
The [Items view](#run-items) shows one run's items. A schedule's **Items** tab looks across all its runs: where did this
patient's record go, which runs found *risk = High*, and what changed between yesterday's run and today's.

![A schedule's Items tab](run-schedule-items "A schedule's Items: every run that processed an item, newest first, with its pipeline version and status")

## Find an item
1. Open **Build › Pipelines › Schedules & triggers**, open the schedule, and choose its **Items** tab (beside **Runs**).
2. In **Find an item**, type an item's name or a value, such as `risk = High` or a record number.
3. Pick the dates (**7 days**, **30 days**, **90 days**, **All time** or **Custom**) and, if you want, a status:
   **Done**, **Failed** or **Check by hand**.
4. Each row is one run that processed a matching item: the **Run** and how it started, the **Item**, **When**, the
   **Pipeline version** it ran, its **Status** and the **Report** made for it, if any. Click the item to show only that one.

> **Tip:** From an item's panel in a run, **All runs of this item** opens this list for that item.

## Compare two runs
1. Tick **Compare** on two rows.
2. **Compare two runs** opens below the list: the item's fields side by side, what changed between the two runs, and
   what changed in the pipeline between them, so you can tell a change in the data from a change in the steps.
3. Values masked for you in both runs stay masked; a value that changed only in letter case says so.

![Two runs compared](run-compare "Compare two runs: the item's fields in each run and what changed")

## Compare two attempts of one run
A run that was retried keeps each attempt. On the run's **Steps** tab, pick **Attempt 1**, **Attempt 2** and so on to see
each attempt's steps: a step that was not run again says **Reused from attempt** and the number.

## Example
Marcus Owens (Revenue cycle) wants to know why claim *SVH-1* keeps failing. On *Compare two runs and retry in bulk* he opens
**Items**, finds *SVH-1* in three runs, all *Failed at The partner (503 until fixed)*, and compares the two latest. The
comparison reads *Nothing changed in the data both runs kept* and *Both runs ran pipeline version 1: any change is the
data's, not the pipeline's*. The fault is the partner's service, not the data or the steps.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Runs compared at once | Two |
| Which pipelines | Only pipelines that work item by item have items |

articles.title: When something fails
articles.summary: The message in words, Runs › Failed grouped by error, retry from the failed step, retry only the failed items, retry several runs at once.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Runs › Failed reads it; retrying is for the run's owner and the workspace administrators
articles.popular: Retry only the failed items of a run
articles.md:
A run that fails stops with a reason. The console says which step failed and why, in words, and lets you retry from that
step once the cause is fixed: the steps before it are not run again.

## Read why it failed
- The run's page shows the message under its summary, and the **Steps** tab marks the failed step: *Fix the cause, then
  retry: the steps before it are not run again.*
- For a pipeline that works item by item, the **Items** tab shows which items failed and at which step; open one for
  **Why it failed** (see [The Items view](#run-items)).
- **Run & review › Runs › Failed** lists every failed or timed-out run in a range, with its **Failing step**, its
  **Error** and its **Kind**.

![Runs › Failed](run-failed "Runs › Failed: the error patterns, most frequent first, above the failed runs")

## Failed runs, grouped by error
1. Open **Run & review › Runs › Failed** and pick a range (**Today**, **7 days**, **30 days**, **This month**, **Custom**).
2. **Error patterns** groups the same error with its numbers, names and ids set aside, most frequent first, with how many
   schedules it touched and when it was first and last seen. Pick a pattern to list only its runs.
3. Narrow the list on the left by **Pipeline**, **Schedule**, **Failing step**, **Error kind** or **Day**. The kinds say
   where to look: *The data*, *A service it called*, *Too large for memory or a limit*, *Rejected by a reviewer*, *Other*.
4. Click a run for its panel: the failing step, the schedule, the attempt, the times and the error in full, with
   **Open the run** and the retry buttons.

![A failed run's panel](run-failed-panel "A failed run's panel: where it failed, why, and how to retry it")

## Retry a run
- **Retry from the failed step**: the steps before it are reused (**Steps reused**) and the run goes on from where it
  stopped, as a new attempt of the same run.
- **Run again from the start**: every step runs again on the pipeline as it is now, and its work is billed again.

Before anything happens, the console reads what a retry would do and says where it would start. A retry can be refused,
with the reason: the pipeline changed before the failed step (run it again from the start), an input file changed since
the run read it, the kept outputs of the steps before it expired, another run of the pipeline is in flight, or the run is
part of a backfill (retry its failed days from **Runs › Backfills**).

> **Note:** A run that stopped responding is closed as *Interrupted*, not failed: run its pipeline again rather than
> retrying it.

## Retry only the failed items
On the run's **Items** tab, **Retry failed items (N)** runs only the failed items again, each from the step it failed at.
The items that are done are left as they are, and a report already made for one is kept. To retry some of them, tick them
and choose **Retry N failed** in the bar.

![A run whose items all failed at one step](run-failed-items "A run's Items tab: 30 items failed at the eligibility call, with Retry failed items")

## Retry several runs at once
1. On **Runs › Failed**, tick the runs (or the page).
2. Choose **Retry from failed step** in the bar.
3. The panel lists what will be retried and what will be skipped, with each reason, before you confirm. Each run is retried
   on its own, as if one by one.

## Compare two attempts
A retried run keeps each attempt. On its **Steps** tab, pick **Attempt 1** or **Attempt 2** to see what each did; a step
that was not run again says **Reused from attempt 1**. To compare two runs item by item, use the schedule's **Items** tab
([Find an item across runs, and compare two runs](#run-schedule-items)).

## Example
The census file for 12 October arrived late, so that day's backfill run of *Late census feed alert* failed at its first step:
*No object at summit-valley-s3/ops/beds/late/census-2026-10-12.csv*. The alert rule told the IT team. When the file arrived,
the administrator retried the failed day from **Runs › Backfills**, and the run completed.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Runs retried in one bulk retry | 100 |
| Who may retry | The run's owner and the workspace administrators |
| A backfill's runs | Retried from the backfill, not one by one |

articles.title: Runs at once and big data
articles.summary: One run of a schedule at a time, workflow requests in parallel, backfills a few at a time, calls at once, and large files.
articles.who: Workspace administrators set schedules, backfills and step settings; anyone who may read the runs follows them
articles.md:
Several pipelines can run at the same time, and one pipeline can work on a very large file. A few rules keep that safe and
predictable: a schedule never runs over itself, calls to a model or another service are capped, and a step that would
need too much says so before it starts.

## One run of a schedule at a time
A schedule starts a new run only when its last run has finished. A **Run now** or a trigger that comes while a run is
still queued, starting or running is refused with the reason: *A job can't be run while its last run is still in flight*.
A timetable slot that comes while the last run is still working is recorded as **Skipped**, so nothing is lost silently.

The exception is an approval workflow: requests that each run the same pipeline (one patient's journey and another's, say)
run side by side, each its own run.

## Backfills, a few at a time
A backfill runs a schedule once for each day of a past range, with as many at once as you set when you start it (*3 at
once*). **Runs › Backfills** shows each one's progress, and its failed days are retried from there.

## Calls at once
A step that calls something for every row (an AI prompt, a transcription, an API call, a report per row) asks one after
another unless its **Calls at once** says more. The workspace's calls together are capped too, so one busy pipeline does
not hold up the others, and a busy service is backed off. See [AI in pipelines](#ai-steps).

## Big files
- Ordinary steps (read, check, transform, join, aggregate, save) work through files of hundreds of thousands or millions
  of rows. The run's **Steps** tab shows **Rows in → out** for each step, so you can see where rows were dropped.
- A step that calls a model or a service row by row has an **At most rows** (or **At most calls**) setting. An input
  larger than that fails before any call is made, with a message that says to filter, batch, or call once.
- A failure because of size shows the error kind *Too large for memory or a limit* on **Runs › Failed**.

![A run over a large file](run-big "A run's Steps: rows in and out of each step of a large daily file")

> **Tip:** Filter and aggregate first, and call a model only on what is left: Summit Valley's daily appointment file has
> about 110,000 rows, but only tomorrow's 240 appointments are sent on, one call each.

## Example
Summit Valley's *Four runs at once* starts four ward reports together. The first starts; the others, of the same schedule,
are refused while it is in flight and are started again in turn, so the four complete one after another. Ten patients'
journeys, by contrast, run side by side, because each is its own workflow request.

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Runs of one schedule at a time | One (requests of an approval workflow excepted) |
| Calls at once in one step | 8 |
| At most rows of an AI prompt step | 500 |

articles.title: Run statuses
articles.summary: What Queued, Starting, Running, Completed, Failed, Interrupted, Skipped and Missed mean, and the review and approval words beside them.
articles.md:
Every run has one status. Lists show it as a coloured pill with its own mark, so two statuses of the same colour still look
different; the run's page adds what waits for a person.

## A run's status
| Status | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Queued** | Due and handed to the engine; not started yet |
| **Starting** | Being picked up; its first step is about to run |
| **Running** | Its steps are running and reporting progress |
| **Completed** | Finished, and whatever it produced has been written |
| **Failed** | Stopped with a reason. The run's page says which step and why; it can be retried from that step |
| **Interrupted** | Stopped before it finished: cancelled, or it stopped responding. Counts against the success rate like Failed; run the pipeline again rather than retrying it |
| **Skipped** | Passed over on purpose: by a person, or because the schedule's last run was still in flight |
| **Missed** | Its time went by while nothing was running to take it, so a gap in the history is never silent |

## What waits for a person
The run's page puts what is left after the status:

| Shown as | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Completed · waiting for review** | The run finished; its results wait until someone approves them in **Review** |
| **Completed · approved** | The results were approved and count |
| **Completed · rejected** | The results were rejected; they do not count, and the pipeline can be run again |
| **Running · waiting for approval** | The run is paused at an Approval step until its reviewers decide |

Only a completed run waits for review: a failed run has no results to approve.

## An item's status
In the [Items view](#run-items) each item is **Done**, **Failed** (*Failed at* the step), **Running**, or **Check by hand**
when a step that reads pages was unsure of one.

## Where the statuses are counted
- **Runs › Latest** and **By date** count runs by status; tick one to narrow the list.
- **Runs › Analytics** counts completed, failed, interrupted, skipped and missed for each pipeline, and its success rate.
- **Runs › Failed** lists the failed and timed-out runs, grouped by error (see [When something fails](#run-failures)).

articles.title: Sign-in security
articles.summary: The workspace's password rules, lockout, idle sign-out and two-factor rule, single sign-on, and the history of every sign-in.
articles.who: Workspace administrators
articles.popular: Set the workspace's sign-in rules
articles.md:
**Sign-in security** decides how people sign in to your workspace: how strong a password must be, what happens after failed attempts, when idle sessions end, whether a code from an authenticator app is needed, and whether people sign in with their company account. Below the rules, the page lists every sign-in to the workspace.

Every field left empty follows the platform's default, shown greyed in the box. Password rules apply from each person's next password change or reset; the rest from their next sign-in.

![Sign-in rules](sec-sign-in-rules "Sign-in rules: Passwords, Lockout and Sessions, with the rules in force at the top right")

## Set the workspace's sign-in rules
1. Open **Administration › Sign-in security**.
2. Under **Passwords**, set what you need:
   - **Minimum length** (8 to 128 characters);
   - **Upper-case letter**, **Lower-case letter**, **Digit**, **Symbol**: **Required** or **Not required**;
   - **Remember earlier passwords**: a new password may not be any of the last N (0 to 24; 0 is off);
   - **Maximum age**: days before a change is owed (0 is never).
3. Under **Lockout**, set **Lock after** (3 to 20 failed attempts in a row, passwords and codes alike) and **Lock for** (1 to 1,440 minutes). Administrators are told of a lock and can unlock under **Users**.
4. Under **Sessions**, set **Sign out after** (5 to 720 minutes without activity; people are warned a minute before) and **Require two-factor login**.
5. Choose **Save rules**. **Use the platform's defaults** clears your own values.

The list at the top right, **Rules in force**, says in words what applies now. Every password is also checked against commonly used passwords and the person's own sign-in name.

## The platform's defaults
Unless your workspace sets its own, these apply today:

| Rule | Default |
|---|---|
| Minimum length | 12 characters |
| Upper-case, lower-case letter and digit | Required |
| Symbol | Not required |
| Remember earlier passwords | 5 |
| Maximum age | 0 (never) |
| Lock after | 5 failed attempts |
| Lock for | 15 minutes |
| Require two-factor login | No |

## Two-factor sign-in for everyone, or for some
- **Require two-factor login: Required** makes everyone who signs in with a password set up an authenticator app at their next sign-in.
- To require it of some people only (clinicians, say), leave it off here and tick **Require two-factor sign-in** on their [access profile](#adm-access-profiles--require-two-factor-sign-in-on-a-profile).

**Administration › Users** shows who has it on (**2FA on**, **2FA off**).

## Single sign-on
With single sign-on people sign in with their company account, and their company's own two-factor sign-in applies. Both **OpenID Connect** (Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace, Okta) and **SAML 2.0** (ADFS, Okta, Entra ID) work.

![Single sign-on](sec-sso "Single sign-on: protocol, the provider's details, email domains and new people")

1. Under **Single sign-on**, choose **OpenID Connect** or **SAML 2.0**.
2. Type the **Name on the sign-in button** (for example "Summit Valley (Microsoft)").
3. For OpenID Connect, type the **Issuer**, the **Client (application) id** and the **Client secret**, and register the **Redirect URI** shown with your provider. For SAML, **Upload metadata** (or paste it) from your provider, check the **Identity provider entity ID**, **Single sign-on URL** and **Signing certificate**, then register our entity ID and reply address (or **Download our metadata**) with your provider.
4. Under **Email domains**, list your company's domains. Only those addresses sign in this way.
5. Under **New people**, choose **Only people already added under Users**, or **Add them at their first sign-in, as a workspace member** with **Their access profile**.
6. Choose **Save single sign-on**, then **Test the issuer** (OpenID Connect) or **Test sign-in** (SAML).
7. Tick **On: people can sign in this way** and save again.

The section's **How to connect …** notes walk through Entra ID, Google, Okta and ADFS. **This workspace's sign-in link** is the address to give people; on the sign-in page they can also use **Sign in with your company**. The client secret is stored encrypted and never shown again.

## Sign-in history
Every sign-in to the workspace, successful or not: **When**, **Person**, **Outcome**, **Method**, **Reason**, **Address** and **Device**. Search by name or address, filter by outcome and method, and choose **Export CSV**. Each person sees their own on **My security**.

![Sign-in history](sec-history "Sign-in history, with its filters and Export CSV")

## Limits
| Setting | Range |
|---|---|
| Minimum length | 8–128 characters |
| Remember earlier passwords | 0–24 |
| Maximum age | 0–3,650 days |
| Lock after | 3–20 attempts |
| Lock for | 1–1,440 minutes |
| Sign out after | 5–720 minutes |
| SAML signing certificates | up to three, during a rollover |

## Example
Summit Valley keeps the platform's password rules and lockout, signs people out after 30 minutes idle, and requires two-factor sign-in on its Clinician profile rather than for everyone. Single sign-on is not set up yet.

articles.title: Your data stays yours
articles.summary: How workspaces are kept apart, what our team can see and when, and what the console never does with your data.
articles.who: Everyone; workspace administrators read the records
articles.md:
Your workspace's data belongs to your organisation. The console keeps it apart from every other workspace, opens it to our staff only in a recorded session, and does not write to your own systems.

## Workspaces are kept apart
- Every person belongs to one workspace, and every page, list, search and export reads only that workspace's data.
- The separation is enforced on the server, not only on the screen: a request for another workspace's data is refused, whatever the browser sends.
- Inside the workspace, each member reads only the pages their access opens, and sensitive columns are masked for people without access (see [Data policies](#sec-data-policies)).

## What our team can see, and when
The platform's own administrators look after the service as a whole: the workspaces, their requests, service health and billing. On their own sign-in they see **no** workspace's data: its pipelines, runs, files, documents, reports, forms and connections open only inside the workspace.

To work in your workspace, a staff member must be granted it and then open a **managed session** (**Work in this workspace**). During that session:
- a bar across their screen names your workspace and says every change and every data read is recorded;
- everything they change, and every piece of data they open, export or download, is written to a record you can read on **Administration › Activity** ([Our team's activity](#sec-managed--our-teams-activity));
- they leave with **Exit**, and their session's access ends.

## What the console never does
- It never writes to your databases. A database connection is read-only.
- It does not delete files a pipeline delivered to your own storage: they are yours and stay, even when the run's own copy expires.
- A downloaded report is a signed link that works for five minutes, for the person who asked.

## Where to check
| You want to know | Look at |
|---|---|
| What our staff did in the workspace | **Administration › Activity** |
| Who signed in, and how | **Administration › Sign-in security › Sign-in history** |
| Who changed whose access | **Administration › Page access › Changes** |
| How long each kind of data is kept | **Administration › Data policies › Retention** |

> **Privacy:** Keep real patient data out of a workspace until your organisation has agreed how it will be handled. See [Working with health data](#sec-health-data).

articles.title: The managed service
articles.summary: What changes when our team builds your workspace for you, what you can still do, and how to read our team's activity.
articles.who: Workspace administrators read the activity; the platform's team switches the mode
articles.md:
Some customers have our team build their pipelines, schedules and connections for them. Such a workspace is **managed by our team**; the others are **self-managed**. The platform's team switches a workspace between the two, and can switch it back.

## What changes in a managed workspace
- The build screens (pipelines, connections, forms, the Task Registry and others) are read-only for your own people, with the note **Managed by our team**: "Our team builds and changes this workspace's …, so they are read-only here. Contact your account team to request a change."
- Your administrators still manage **people and access**, sign-in rules and data policies, run pipelines with **Run now**, review and approve, and read every result and bill.
- Our team builds in a recorded managed session.
- **Administration › Activity** is always on your administrators' menu.

![The note on a build screen](adm-managed-banner "In a managed workspace the build screens are read-only for your own people")

In a self-managed workspace your administrators build everything themselves. **Activity** appears there too once our team has acted in the workspace, and stays, so a workspace that goes back to self-managed keeps its history.

## Our team's activity
**Administration › Activity** (**Our team's activity**) lists every change our team made in your workspace and every data they opened, exported or downloaded, newest first.

![Our team's activity](sec-team-activity "Our team's activity: when, who, what they changed or read")

| Column | What it shows |
|---|---|
| **When** | Date and time, to the second |
| **Staff member** | Who, with their sign-in address |
| **Change or read** | What they did. **Read** marks data they opened, exported or downloaded; **Builder** marks a change to what the workspace builds |
| **Service** | The part of the platform that recorded it |

Filter by **Every staff member** and by changes or reads; **Load older** goes further back.

## Example
For one week Summit Valley is managed while our team builds its population-health pipelines. Its administrators keep running the admission pipeline with **Run now** and approving discharges; each evening Jordan Reyes reads **Our team's activity** to see what was built and which run outputs our staff opened while testing.

articles.title: Data policies
articles.summary: The three data levels, which models may see each, masked columns, how long run files are kept, and bulk review switches.
articles.who: Workspace administrators change them; members who use the AI Assistant can read the policy
articles.popular: Choose which models may see sensitive data
articles.md:
**Data policies** says, for each level of data, which models may see it, how long a run keeps its working files and whether the AI Assistant may change things with it. The same page holds the workspace's **Bulk review** switches and its **Retention**.

![Administration › Data policies](sec-data-policies "Data policies: Sensitive, Internal and Public, each with its model rule and settings")

## The three levels
| Level | What it is | Default model rule |
|---|---|---|
| **Sensitive** | Personal, health or confidential data | **Local only** |
| **Internal** | The workspace's everyday data; a call is internal when nothing says otherwise | **Any model** |
| **Public** | Data anyone may see: published figures, open datasets and APIs | **Any model** |

Until you save a level, its defaults apply and the page says **Not saved yet — these are the defaults**. A prompt declares its level, a pipeline may declare one in its settings, and an API collection or a data contract has one of its own. A call's level is the highest level known of it.

![How a call's level is decided](sec-level-rule "How a call's level is decided")

## Choose which models may see sensitive data
1. Open **Administration › Data policies**.
2. In the **Sensitive** column, under **Model rule**, choose:
   - **Local only**: only models running on your own machines; the data never goes to a hosted provider;
   - **BAA-signed hosted, or local**: local models, and hosted models only on a connection marked as covered by a signed Business Associate Agreement;
   - **Any model**.
3. Under **Allowed models**, tick connections or single models to narrow it further. None ticked: any model the rule allows.
4. Set the other rows if you need to:
   - **Keep run files**: days (1 to 3,650) a run keeps this level's working copies; blank means the pipeline's own (24 hours unless it sets another);
   - **AI write tools**: whether the AI Assistant may run pipelines, create PDFs, save or delete files and call APIs that change data (it still asks first). Off for Sensitive by default;
   - **Minimum-fields warning**: reminds whoever builds a step to send a model only the fields it needs.
5. Choose **Save policy**. **Use the defaults** puts a level back.

More on the model rules: [Which models may see which data](#ai-data-levels).

## Masked columns
Columns marked sensitive in the **Data Catalog** (patient identifiers, names, contact details) are masked for anyone without access: in the catalog, in Analytics Studio, on dashboards and in their exports, and in Ask your data.
- Open a dataset or file in **See results › Analysis › Data Catalog** and choose **Scan for sensitive data**, or mark columns by hand.
- A person who needs the values opens the asset, types **Why you need it**, picks **For** (1, 7, 30 or 90 days) and chooses **Request access**. A workspace administrator decides in **Review**.

![A masked asset in the Data Catalog](sec-masked "For a researcher, the medical record number is marked Sensitive and the asset's values are masked")

## Sensitive files
Masking changes what a screen shows, not the files a sensitive pipeline keeps. Viewing or downloading those files (a
saved file, an item's files, a report's PDF) needs **Download sensitive files** on the person's access profile; without
it they see the file's name, size and type and a lock. See [The Items view](#run-items--sensitive-pipelines).

## Bulk review
Whether reviewers may approve many runs or documents in one decision. Each item is still decided and recorded on its own, and rejecting in bulk is always allowed.
- **Allow bulk approve of runs**: off, runs are approved one by one.
- **Allow bulk approve of documents**, and under it **Include documents whose rules fail** (off by default: such a document is skipped and approved on its own screen; on, the failures are accepted and the override is recorded on each).

Choose **Save review policy**. A pipeline can still require individual review in its own settings.

![Bulk review](sec-review-policy "Bulk review: the switches for runs and documents")

## Example
Summit Valley keeps Sensitive on **Local only**, so its clinical prompts run on its own local models. Its Researcher profile sees the columns marked sensitive, such as the medical record number, masked; Dr. Hana Ito requests 30 days' access for an approved study and an administrator decides.

articles.title: Retention
articles.summary: How long run outputs, logs, files, documents, reports and records are kept, the daily removal pass, previews, confirmation and legal holds.
articles.who: Workspace administrators
articles.md:
**Retention** sets how long each kind of your workspace's data is kept. Once a day, after 02:00 (Chicago time), a pass removes what is older than its days, in small batches, and records what it removed. Set the days your own record-keeping policy requires.

Retention starts **Off**: nothing is removed and every kind shows **Forever** until you set days and turn it on.

![Retention](sec-retention "Retention: each kind of data, how long it is kept, the last pass, and legal holds")

## The kinds of data
| Data | What it covers |
|---|---|
| **Run outputs and datasets** | The datasets and files each run made, its result records and its AI answers. The run itself and its manifest (names, rows, bytes) stay. |
| **Run logs** | Each run's log lines and its steps' logs. The run, its steps and their counts stay. |
| **Uploaded files** | Files sent in through the API, and their stored copy in the workspace's inbox. |
| **Documents** | Each document's extraction (fields, corrections, decisions, its approved row), its page images and the original file. |
| **Form submissions** | Each submission's answers, its files, and its copy in the inbox. |
| **AI conversations** | AI Assistant conversations and their messages, tool runs and prompt test runs, pinned ones included. |
| **Notifications** | Bell notices, read or not. |
| **Reports** | Report Studio files that a newer version replaced, and frozen data no kept version uses. Each report's current version and every approved or signed version stay. |
| **Analytics copies and cache** | Bounded by the platform: copies kept to 4 GB a workspace and query results for 10 minutes, both rebuilt from your sources. |
| **Audit records** | File downloads and previews, what retention removed, and the policy's own history. Never less than the platform's minimum (2,190 days). |

A run's **working files** are a different thing: how long a run keeps them for its next steps is set per data level under **Keep run files**, or per pipeline (24 hours by default).

## Set retention
1. Open **Administration › Data policies** and scroll to **Retention**.
2. Choose **Edit retention**. Under **Keep for (days)**, type the days for each kind; empty keeps it forever.
3. Tick **Remove data older than its days** to turn retention on.
4. Choose **Preview these days**: **If saved, a pass now removes** shows, for each kind, what a pass would remove with those days. Nothing is removed by a preview.
5. Choose **Save retention**. The next daily pass applies it; **Run now** on the Retention section starts one at once.

**Preview** on the section itself counts what a pass would remove with the days already saved (**Would remove now**).

## Safety catches
- **Needs confirmation**: if a pass would remove more than a set share of one kind in one go, it pauses that kind. **Confirm** (with the count) lets it go ahead.
- **Legal holds**: **Place a hold** on the whole workspace, a pipeline or one run with a reason. While a hold is on, nothing in its scope is removed. **Release** ends it. Placing and releasing are recorded.
- **History** lists every pass: when, how it started, what it removed.
- Issued invoices and billing records are never removed by retention. Files a pipeline delivered to your own storage are yours and stay; their record in the run is marked expired.

## Example
Summit Valley keeps run logs 90 days and notifications 30 days, previews the effect first, and places a legal hold on the "Patient journey" pipeline while a complaint is open, so none of its runs' outputs are removed until the hold is released.

articles.title: Audit: who did what
articles.summary: Where the console records sign-ins, access changes, approvals, report downloads, retention and our staff's activity.
articles.who: Workspace administrators; each person sees their own sign-ins
articles.popular: Find out who changed someone's access
articles.md:
The console records who did what as it happens. There is no single audit page: each record lives next to the thing it is about, where the people who look after that thing will find it.

## Where each record is
| What | Where | What it says |
|---|---|---|
| Sign-ins | **Administration › Sign-in security › Sign-in history**; each person's own on **My security** | When, who, outcome, method (password, code, recovery code, single sign-on), reason, address, device. **Export CSV** |
| A person's account | Their page on **Administration › Users** › **Activity** | Recent sign-ins and account changes, who last edited it |
| Access changes | **Administration › Page access › Changes** | Every page or tab opened or withheld, profile moves, delegations, two-factor rule changes: when, who, for whom, until when, why |
| Approvals and reviews | The request's history in **Review**; each run's and document's own page | Who approved, rejected or asked for changes, with their comment; a stand-in shows as "(for …)"; a bulk decision is recorded on every item |
| Reports | A report's **Activity** tab in **Reports** | Created, generation requested, version made, failed, downloaded, archived |
| Retention | **Data policies › Retention › History** | Every pass, what it removed; every legal hold placed and released |
| Our staff | **Administration › Activity** | Every change our team made, and every data they opened, exported or downloaded |
| File downloads and previews | Kept as audit records | Never removed before the platform's minimum of 2,190 days |

## Find out who changed someone's access
1. Open **Administration › Page access**, scroll to **Grant pages and tabs** and choose **Changes**.
2. Read down to the person: **Who** made the change, **What** it was, the **Page or tab**, **Until** and **Why**.

A delegate's changes show with the delegate's name, and the delegation itself (**Delegated access**, **Ended a delegation**) with the administrator's.

## Find out who approved something
Open the item in **Review** (or the run or document) and read its history: each step, who decided, when, and their comment.

## Find out who downloaded a report
Open the report in **Reports › Library** and choose its **Activity** tab. Each download is listed with its time.

> **Tip:** For a periodic access review, export **Sign-in history** and read **Changes** for the period; the reasons typed with each grant and delegation are there for that purpose.

## Example
Summit Valley's quarterly access review: Jordan Reyes exports the sign-in history for the quarter, reads **Changes** for every tab opened for one person (Dr. Patel's week of ward cover, with its reason and its end date), and checks **Our team's activity** for the week the workspace was managed.

articles.title: AI and your data
articles.summary: Which models see your data, why every model answer is a DRAFT, what is sent to a model, and what the AI Assistant may change.
articles.who: Everyone who uses AI steps, prompts or the AI Assistant; administrators set the rules
articles.md:
The console uses AI models to read documents, describe images, summarise, draft and answer questions. You decide which models may see which data, a person checks what a model says before it is used, and the AI Assistant asks before it changes anything.

## Which models see your data
- Models run through your workspace's **model connections** (**Settings › Model connections**). A connection to a model running on your own machines is **local**; others are hosted.
- Your **data policy** gives each level of data a model rule: **Local only**, **BAA-signed hosted, or local**, or **Any model**. **Sensitive** data starts as **Local only**: it never goes to a hosted provider until an administrator says otherwise.
- A call's level is the highest level known of it: the prompt's declared level, and in a tool run every API collection it has read. A call is internal when nothing says otherwise.

See [Which models may see which data](#ai-data-levels) and [Your models](#ai-models).

## Every model answer is a DRAFT
A model can be wrong. In the console a model's answer is a draft for a person to check:
- a pipeline can hold its results for review, so a person approves or rejects them in **Review** before they are used;
- documents read with low confidence go to **Review › Documents**;
- a report is approved and signed by a person.

> **Warning:** Do not let a model's answer reach a patient, a payment or a record without a person approving it.

## What is sent to a model
Only what the step or prompt sends: its instructions and the fields or files it is given. Send only the fields the task needs; the **Minimum-fields warning** reminds whoever builds a step to do so. Columns masked for a person stay masked in Ask your data and on the dashboards they open.

## What the AI Assistant may change
The AI Assistant can design and run pipelines for you. Its **write tools** (running pipelines, creating PDFs, saving or deleting files, calling APIs that change data) are set per data level under **AI write tools**, off for Sensitive by default, and it still asks before it uses one.

## Example
At Summit Valley every model is local, and Sensitive stays **Local only**. The wound-photo step describes each photo as a DRAFT; Sam Harper, the wound specialist, approves or corrects every measurement in **Review** before it reaches the patient's report.

articles.title: Working with health data
articles.summary: The controls the console gives you for patient data, starting with synthetic data, and what remains your organisation's to decide.
articles.who: Workspace administrators, and everyone who handles patient data
articles.md:
The console is built for healthcare data work and gives you controls for it: who opens what, how people sign in, which models may see sensitive data, which columns are masked, what a person must review, how long data is kept, and a record of who did what. How you set them is your organisation's decision.

> **Note:** Meeting your organisation's privacy and regulatory obligations depends on how you configure and use the console. The console does not by itself make a workspace compliant with any law or standard.

## Start with synthetic data
Build and try your pipelines with **synthetic** or **de-identified** records first. Move to real patient data only when your organisation has agreed how it will be handled, and who may see it.

Everything in this guide is synthetic: the Summit Valley Health System, its people, its patients (such as Elena Marsh), their records, images and numbers are made up. Some examples call public, keyless APIs or use public research images; none hold real patients' data.

## The controls, and where they are
| Control | Where | Article |
|---|---|---|
| Only the pages each person's work needs | **Administration › Page access** | [Page access profiles](#adm-access-profiles) |
| Strong sign-in, two-factor for clinicians | **Administration › Sign-in security**, a profile's **Require two-factor sign-in** | [Sign-in security](#sec-sign-in) |
| Sensitive data on local models only | **Administration › Data policies** | [Data policies](#sec-data-policies) |
| Patient identifiers masked for people without access | **Data Catalog** › **Scan for sensitive data** | [Masked columns](#sec-data-policies--masked-columns) |
| A person checks every model answer | Review on the pipeline; **Review** | [AI and your data](#sec-ai) |
| Data kept only as long as needed | **Data policies › Retention** | [Retention](#sec-retention) |
| A record of who did what | Sign-in history, Changes, Activity | [Audit](#sec-audit) |
| Our staff's access recorded | **Administration › Activity** | [The managed service](#sec-managed) |

## A checklist before real patient data
1. Profiles give each group only the pages it needs; the default profile is the narrowest (a Viewer).
2. Two-factor sign-in is required of administrators and clinicians.
3. Sensitive stays on **Local only**, or only on hosted connections your organisation has agreed in writing to use for it.
4. Every dataset and file with patient identifiers is scanned and its sensitive columns marked.
5. Pipelines that use a model hold their results for review.
6. Retention is set to your record-keeping policy, and previewed first.
7. Someone reads the access changes and sign-in history on a regular schedule.

> **Privacy:** Send a model only the fields it needs, and never paste patient details into a place that does not need them, such as a pipeline's name, a team's description or a reason field.

articles.title: Alerts: be told when something needs you
articles.summary: Alert rules for failed runs, missed schedules, slow runs, waiting reviews and retention; who is told and how; an alert opening, and resolving by itself or by hand.
articles.who: Workspace administrators
articles.popular: Get told when a run fails
articles.md:
An **alert rule** watches the workspace for one kind of trouble and, when it happens, opens an **alert** and tells the
people you chose: by the bell in the top bar, by mail, or by your webhooks. The alert stays open until the trouble
clears (it then resolves by itself) or someone resolves it.

## Start with the recommended rules
In a workspace with no rules yet, choose **Add the recommended rules**. It adds five, each telling the administrators
by the bell:

| Rule | Watches for | How bad |
|---|---|---|
| *A run failed* | A run fails | Warning |
| *Failures in a burst* | 3 or more runs of a pipeline fail within 15 minutes | Critical |
| *A schedule missed its slot* | A schedule's slot is skipped, missed or overdue | Warning |
| *A run is slower than usual* | A run takes over twice its pipeline's usual time | Warning |
| *A review is waiting too long* | A review or approval waits longer than 4 hours | Warning |

Change or remove any of them afterwards.

## Make a rule
1. Open **Administration & billing › Settings › Alerts** and choose **New rule**.
2. **Watch for**: **Runs failed**, **A schedule missed its slot**, **A run is slower than usual**, **A review is
   waiting too long** or **Retention needs attention**. The line under it says what to do when it fires.
3. Give it a **Name**.
4. Set when it fires: **Failed runs** and **Within (minutes)** for failed runs; **Slower than (× the usual p95)** for
   slow runs; **Waiting longer than (minutes)** for reviews.
5. **Schedule**: one schedule, or **Every schedule of the workspace**.
6. **How bad**: **Warning** or **Critical**.
7. **Tell them by**: **The bell**, **Mail**, **Webhooks**.
8. **Who hears of it**: **Administrators**, **Every other member**, **And these teams:**.
9. **Quiet hours** (optional): **Hold mail during quiet hours**, from and until. Mail waits until they end, then goes
   if the alert is still open. The bell and webhooks are not held.
10. Leave **On** ticked and choose **Save the rule**.

![A rule](set-alert-rule "New alert rule: what it watches, when it fires, how bad, how and whom it tells, and quiet hours")

> **Tip:** A "slower than usual" rule needs at least five completed runs of the pipeline in the last 30 days to know
> what usual is.

## Read the alerts
The left of the page lists the **Alerts**, open first, with **All** and **Open**. Each shows its title, what happened,
its kind, since when, how many times it was seen, and when it resolved: *cleared by itself* or *by a person*. An open
alert also says **What to do**.

- **Open** goes to what it is about, such as the failed run.
- **Resolve** closes it by hand, once you have dealt with it.

The right lists the **Rules**, grouped by what they watch: each one's sentence (**When**), whom it **Tells**, its
**Quiet hours**, when it **Last fired**, and its **On** switch. Its ⋯ menu has **Change**, **Mute for** an hour, 8
hours, a day or a week (its alerts are still recorded, nobody is told), **Unmute** and **Remove**.

![Alerts](set-alerts "Alerts: an alert that opened and cleared by itself, and the workspace's rules")

## Alerts to your own tools
A rule with **Webhooks** ticked sends `alert.opened` when it fires and `alert.resolved` when the alert clears, to every
webhook that subscribes to them, so an on-call tool can open and close its own incident. See
[Webhooks](#dev-webhooks).

## Limits
| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Rules in a workspace | 50 |
| Resolved alerts kept | 30 days |
| Mute | An hour, 8 hours, a day or a week |

## Example
At Summit Valley Health System, the rule *Census feed failed* watches every schedule for a failed run and tells the
administrators and the IT team by the bell. At 06:00 the census file had not arrived, the run of *Late census feed
alert* failed and the alert opened. When the file landed and the run was retried from the failed step and completed,
the alert resolved: *cleared by itself*.

articles.title: Model connections, Tool Registry and Task Registry
articles.summary: What a workspace administrator can switch on and off: the models prompts run on, the tools the AI Assistant may use, and the tasks pipeline steps may run.
articles.who: Workspace administrators; the Tool Registry also opens to members whose page access includes Prompts
articles.md:
Three pages under **Settings** decide what the workspace's AI and pipelines may use. Each says, for every row, what it
is, whether it is on here, and who set it. Something our team has **Blocked** for the workspace shows locked, with who
blocked it and why; it cannot be switched on from the workspace.

## Model connections
A **model connection** is where prompts run: a provider, its key, a default model, and two caps that keep a schedule
from running up a bill. One connection is the workspace's **Default**: a prompt that names none runs on it.

On a connection you can:
- **Test connection**, to check the key and see the models the provider lists.
- **Make active** or **Make inactive**; **Set as default**; **Edit connection**; **Delete connection**.
- Set its caps under **Edit connection**: **Calls in flight** (at most this many calls at once through the key; the
  rest wait in order) and **Daily token budget** (once the day's runs reach it, a step fails before any call is made;
  blank means no cap).
- Read its **Usage · last 30 days**, its runs by day, its **Recent runs** and the **Prompts on this connection**.

Keys are encrypted and never sent back to the browser. How to connect a model, and which data may go to which model,
is in [Your models: model connections](#ai-models).

![Model connections](set-model-connections "Model connections: the workspace's default connection, its caps, its models and its usage")

## Tool Registry
The **Tool Registry** lists the only operations the **AI Assistant** may ask for. Each tool calls a part of the
platform, checks the person's own role, and is logged on the run; a tool that writes asks the person first.

- Each row shows the **Tool**, what goes in and comes out, the **Permission** it needs, whether it **Asks first**, and
  when it was **Last used**.
- Narrow the list by kind (**Reads**, **Writes**), by state (**Enabled**, **Off**, **Blocked**), or search.
- Untick **Enabled** to switch a tool off for the workspace; **Reset** puts it back to its default. **Recent changes**
  lists who switched what.

## Task Registry
The **Task Registry** lists every task a pipeline's steps can run (**Read S3**, **Aggregate**, **AI prompt**,
**Approval** and the rest), what it does, its kind, what goes in and comes out, how many **Pipelines** use it and how
many runs they had this month. Every existing pipeline is listed too, as a **Legacy** task, edited on its own page.

- Untick a task under **In this workspace** to switch it off for the workspace. A task switched here says **Switched
  here**, with who set it; switching it back to its default undoes that.
- A count of pipelines opens the list behind it.
- **Recent changes** lists who switched what.

![Task Registry](set-task-registry "Task Registry: every task a step can run, how many pipelines use it, its runs this month and its switch")

> **Warning:** Check a task's **Pipelines** count before you switch it off: those pipelines have a step that runs it.

## Example
Summit Valley Health System runs only local models: one connection, *Local Ollama*, is the default, with **Calls in
flight** at 1. Its administrator switches off the assistant's tools that write to the store systems, so the AI Assistant
in that workspace can read them but never change them.

articles.title: Configuration values, home pages, task groups and topics
articles.summary: A short reference for the values and secrets pipelines read at run time, the home pages and groups a task can name, and the Kafka connections and topics.
articles.who: Workspace administrators
articles.md:
Four short lists under **Settings** hold things pipelines name rather than contain: a value or a secret, a web
address, a group label, a broker and its topics. Keeping them here means they are written once and changed in one
place.

## Configuration values
**Configuration values** are values and secrets a pipeline reads when it runs, per workspace: a bucket name, a
database password. A pipeline's settings name an entry instead of holding it:

```A configuration value and a secret, as a pipeline names them
${config:BUCKET_NAME}
${secret:DB_PASSWORD}
```

The real value is fetched when the run starts; the pipeline's settings and its logs only ever carry the reference.

![How a pipeline names a value](set-values "Configuration values: how a pipeline names a value or a secret, and which settings must hold a secret")

1. Choose **New value**.
2. Pick the **Workspace** (only its pipelines can use the entry), type the **Key** (capital letters, digits and
   underscores, a letter first, up to 64 characters), and pick the **Kind**: a value or a secret.
3. Type the **Value**, or the **Secret**, and a **Description**.
4. Save. The figures at the top count the **Values**, the **Secrets** and those **In use**; **Used by** names the
   pipelines that reference each one.

> **Warning:** A secret is stored encrypted and never shown again, not here and not to anyone. To change it, type a
> new one.

A setting whose name looks like a credential (password, secret, token, API key, access key, private key, client
secret) must hold a `${secret:…}` reference. A pipeline that writes the credential itself there, or names a key the
workspace does not have, is refused when it is saved.

## Home pages
**Home pages** are web addresses a task can name as its home page: where a person goes to see what the task feeds
(a report site, a partner's portal). Choose **New home page**, give it a **Name** (what a task's list shows, unique in
the workspace), its **Address** and a **Description**, then pick it on a task.

## Task groups
**Task groups** are labels that group tasks together. Choose **New task group**, give it a **Name** and, if you like,
a **Value** and **Description**; a task then picks it in its **Group** field. **Used by** shows the tasks in each.

## Kafka & Topics
**Kafka & Topics** shows, live, the message brokers your pipelines publish through: whether they answer, whether your
topics exist, who reads each topic and how far behind they are.

- With no connection of its own, the workspace publishes through the platform's default broker, and the page says so.
- Choose a connection on the left to see its **Topics**, **Consumer groups** and **Connection**; **Recheck** reads them
  again. A topic nobody reads says **No consumer**.
- **New connection** adds a broker of your own; **Add topic** adds a topic. Secrets are encrypted and never sent back
  to the browser.

## Example
Summit Valley Health System keeps its finance bucket's name as `${config:FINANCE_BUCKET}` and its store database
password as `${secret:STORES_DB_PASSWORD}`. When the database password changed, the administrator typed the new secret
once, and every pipeline that reads the store systems used it from the next run.

articles.title: Appearance and themes
articles.summary: The six themes, the workspace's default theme an administrator sets, the theme each person picks for themselves, and dashboards' chart themes.
articles.who: Everyone picks their own theme; a workspace administrator sets the workspace's default
articles.md:
The console comes in six themes. Each person can pick the one they like; a workspace administrator can set the one
everyone else opens in.

## The themes
| Theme | What it is |
|---|---|
| **System** | Light or Dark, as your device is set |
| **Light** | The console's own, on white |
| **Dark** | Neutral dark |
| **Ocean** | Calm blue and teal on light |
| **Midnight** | Deep navy with teal accents |
| **High contrast** | Black on white, strongest edges |

## Pick your own theme
- In the top bar, open the theme button (the sun or moon) and pick one. It changes at once.
- Or open **Your profile** from the account menu and pick it under **Theme**. When the workspace has a default, the
  profile says so, with **Use the workspace default** to go back to it.

Your choice stays yours, whatever the workspace's default is.

## Set the workspace's default
1. Open **Administration & billing › Administration › Appearance**.
2. Under **Default theme**, pick one. **System (no default)** leaves each device's own light or dark.
3. The page says *Not saved yet* and which theme; **Undo** puts it back.
4. Choose **Save default**.

People who have chosen a theme keep theirs; everyone else opens in the new default from their next sign-in.

![Appearance](set-appearance "Appearance: the workspace's default theme, with the six themes to choose from")

![The console in Dark](set-appearance-dark "The same page in the Dark theme")

## Dashboards' chart themes
Dashboards' charts follow the console's theme, light or dark. A board's editor can also give the whole board a chart
theme of its own, and a widget can override it in its **Chart settings**. Their colours are held to a 3 : 1 contrast
against the card in light and dark. See [Build and edit a dashboard](#dash-build--the-boards-chart-theme).

## Example
Summit Valley Health System's default is **Light**, the theme of its printed reports. The night charge nurses on
Ward 4B pick **Dark** for themselves in the top bar, and Dr. Okafor picks **High contrast** on his profile. Neither
choice changes anyone else's.

articles.title: Help in the console
articles.summary: The help centre and how to search it, links to an article, the Developer portal for developers, and whom to ask when the help does not answer.
articles.who: Everyone
articles.md:
Help is in three places: this **help centre** for everyone who uses the console, the **Developer portal** for the
developers who connect your systems, and the people to ask when neither answers.

## Open the help centre
1. Open the account menu (your name, top right) and choose **Setup guide**. The help centre opens.
2. Type in the search box: every article is searched, its steps included. **Clear search** goes back.
3. Or **Browse by topic**: you see the topics for the pages you can open. Each topic starts with **Start here**, its
   common questions, and its articles in order.
4. **Popular how-tos** and **What's new** are on the front page; **Read the whole guide** puts every article on one
   page, to read through or print.
5. **Back to console** returns you to where you were.

![The help centre](set-help "The help centre: search every article, and browse the topics for the pages you can open")

> **Tip:** Every article has its own address (for example `/docs#set-alerts`). Copy it from your browser to point a
> colleague straight to the steps.

## For developers: the Developer portal
The API's guides, its reference with a call to copy for each, samples in curl, Python and Node.js, the event and
problem types, the changelog and the downloads are in **Administration & billing › Developers › Developer portal**.
See [The Developer portal](#dev-portal).

## When the help does not answer
- **Something you cannot open or change** (a page, a tab, a button greyed out): ask your workspace administrator.
  Page access, teams and roles are theirs.
- **A run that failed**: open it from **Run & review › Runs › Failed**; the failing step says why, and most failures
  can be retried from that step.
- **A bill, a limit, the sandbox, the billing time zone, a model or a service**: your workspace administrator asks
  your account team.
- **Something that looks broken**: note the page's address, what you did and when (to the minute, in your time zone),
  and send it to your workspace administrator. A screenshot helps, as long as it shows no patient or personal data.

> **Privacy:** Never paste a secret, a password or a patient's details into a support message.

## Example
Rosa Alvarez, charge nurse at Summit Valley Health System, cannot find the **Approve** button on a care plan. She
searches the help centre for *approve*, reads that her page access decides what she may decide, and asks the
workspace administrator, who adds her to the right team.

articles.title: Read steps: where the rows come from
articles.summary: Read CSV/JSON/Parquet, Read S3, Read API, Read Database, Read documents, Read runs and Sample rows.
articles.who: A workspace administrator adds steps; Read runs is an administrator's step

where.label: Build › Pipelines › a pipeline › Steps › Add step

articles.md:
A **Read** step brings rows into the pipeline. Most pipelines start with one; a pipeline may have several (a file and
a reference list to join to it). Each Read step below lists its settings by the names on its panel. Settings left blank
take the default shown.

Unless their panel says otherwise, **Read CSV/JSON/Parquet**, **Read S3**, **Read API** and **Read documents** are tried
three times on a passing error (a busy or briefly unreachable service), and **Read Database** twice.

![The Read S3 step's settings](step-read "Read S3, set to read only the remittance files written since the last run")

## Read CSV/JSON/Parquet

**What it does.** Reads one file from one of the workspace's buckets as rows: CSV, JSON, JSON Lines or Parquet.

**When to use it.** A daily extract, a reference list, a file whose name you know (or can build from the date).

**Settings.**

- **Bucket**: one of the workspace's storage connections, by its alias. Leave **Bucket** and **File** empty to read the
  file the run was started for (a file that arrived in the inbox, or a form's submission).
- **File**: the object's key. Placeholders such as `{{date}}` are filled in.
- **Format**: `auto` (by the key's extension), `csv`, `json`, `jsonl` or `parquet`.
- **CSV delimiter** (`,`), **CSV has a header row** (on; off names the columns c1, c2, …), **JSON rows at** (a dot path
  such as `data.items`; empty for the whole file).
- **At most rows**: stop after this many. **Only these columns**: read only these, in this order; a wide file's other
  cells are never read.

**Example.** Summit Valley's **Bed occupancy by ward** reads `ops/beds/census-{{date}}.csv`: each morning, that day's
census. **General-ledger journal validation** reads the JSON Lines file that arrived in the inbox.

**Limits.** CSV cells arrive as text (later steps convert them). Time limit 600 seconds.

## Read S3

**What it does.** Lists the objects under a prefix of a bucket (one row per object, with its key and size), or reads all
of them as rows.

**When to use it.** A folder that fills up: hourly feed files, recordings, photos. Its list is also what the file steps
(**Transcribe audio**, **Convert file**, **Split pages**) work through, one file each.

**Settings.**

- **Bucket** (required) and **Prefix**: only objects whose keys start with it; placeholders are filled in.
- **Read as**: `list` (one row per object) or a format (`auto`, `csv`, `json`, `jsonl`, `parquet`) to read each object's
  rows, each row with `_source_key`.
- **At most objects**: 100 unless you say.
- **The run's own files first**: a run started for files (an inbox arrival) reads those files instead of the prefix;
  any other run reads the prefix. So one pipeline serves an inbox trigger and a schedule.
- **Which objects**: `all`, or `last_run`: only the objects written since this schedule's last completed run, oldest
  first. A failed run moves nothing on, so its files come again.
- The CSV and JSON settings of **Read CSV/JSON/Parquet** apply when it reads rows.

**Example.** **ADT feed: hourly admissions, discharges and transfers** reads `ops/adt/` with **Which objects** `last_run`,
so each hourly run reads only the new files.
