articles.summary: Each approved document of a type starts a run; read that document's fields in the pipeline.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Schedules & triggers
articles.md:
When a document of a type is approved, by a reviewer or automatically, it can start a run. The pipeline then reads that
document's fields straight away: a referral becomes an admission request, a lab report becomes rows of results.

## Make a schedule start when a document is approved

1. Open the schedule in **Build › Pipelines › Schedules & triggers**, or make a new one.
2. Under **Also starts when**, tick **A document is approved**.
3. **Which documents**: choose the document type. Any approved document of it starts a run, whether a reviewer approved
   it or it was approved automatically.
4. **Documents per run**: 1 makes each document its own run. More: documents that waited for a run go together, up to
   this many, and the pipeline reads them all.
5. Save. **What you will get** says "Also when a document of … is approved".

A document approved while a run is going waits its turn.

![A schedule started by approved referrals](trg-document "A document is approved: each approved Referral starts a run")

## Read the documents that started the run

Put a **Read documents** step first and leave its **Document type** empty: it reads the documents whose approval
started this run, one row each with its id, status, approval and the type's fields. Steps can also use
`{{document_count}}`, `{{document_ids}}` and the first document's fields as `{{document.field}}`.

> **Tip:** The same pipeline can also run on a timetable and read every approved document since the last run: give
> **Read documents** a **Document type** and set **Which approved documents** to `last_run`.

## Example

Summit Valley's referrals arrive by Email-in, are read by **Documents**, and are checked by Greta Fischer's team. Each
approved **Referral** starts **Journey 1 · Referral to admission**: it reads the approving document, checks it against
the referral contract, works out the patient's age and urgency, and tells the platform the admission was accepted.

## Limits

| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Document types per schedule | One |
| Documents per run | 1 to 50 |

articles.title: Start a pipeline when an event arrives
articles.summary: Event routes say which pipeline or workflow each of your event types starts when your systems send it.
articles.who: A workspace administrator sets up event routes; your systems send events with an API client that has events:write
articles.md:
Your own systems can tell the platform that something happened: a lab result was created, a device took a reading, a
patient was admitted. Each such message is an **event** with a type, such as `lab.result.created`, and its data. An
**event route** says what an event type starts: a pipeline's run, or a workflow request.

An event of a type no route takes is refused, so nothing runs by accident.

## Add an event route

1. Open **Administration & billing › Developers › API Clients** and scroll to **Event routes**.
2. Choose **New event route**.
3. **Event type**: letters, digits and `.` `_` `:` `-`, such as `order.received`.
4. **Starts**: **A pipeline's run** (then choose the **Pipeline**) or **A workflow request** (then type the **Workflow
   key**).
5. **Data contract (optional)**: the name of a data contract the event's data must meet.
6. Leave **Active** ticked, and choose **Add route**.

Use **Change** to point a route elsewhere or switch it off, and **Remove** to delete it.

![The event routes of Summit Valley](trg-events "Event routes: each event type and what it starts")

## What the pipeline receives

The event's data is the run's record. Give the pipeline's **Source** (on its **Settings** tab) the setting **The task
payload: one row, a column per tag**, so the first step reads it as one row, and check it with a **Validate** step
first.

## Send an event

Your system sends the event to the platform's API with an API client that has the `events:write` scope. The request
and its answers are described in the Developer portal (**Developers › Developer portal**), with samples.

## Example

Summit Valley's partner lab, Northgate Labs, sends `lab.result.created` each time a result is ready. The route starts
**Journey 6 · Lab results from the partner lab**, which validates the result, flags abnormal and critical values,
keeps the file and tells the physicians at once when a value is critical. The **HomeLink devices** client sends
`device.reading` the same way.

## Limits

| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| An event type | 128 characters |
| Who sets up routes | A workspace administrator; in a workspace our team manages they are read-only to you |
| API calls | The per-client and per-workspace limits shown on API Clients |

articles.title: Start a pipeline from your own systems (the API)
articles.summary: Your portal or system starts a run with a record, files and parameters, then reads its status, steps and result.
articles.who: A workspace administrator makes the API client; the client needs the runs:write scope to start runs
articles.md:
The platform's API lets your own systems do what **Run now** does, without a person: a partner portal starts a run for
each lab record it receives, a hospital system starts a run when a patient is discharged. The console stays your
administrators' tool; the API is how your systems reach the platform.

## Before you start

1. A workspace administrator makes an **API client** for the system on **Administration & billing › Developers › API
   Clients**, with only the scopes it needs: `pipelines:read` to list the pipelines it may start, `runs:write` to start
   them, `runs:read` to follow them, `files:write` to upload files for them.
2. The client's secret is shown once. The system exchanges its id and secret for a token that lasts 15 minutes.

## Start a run

The system sends `POST /v1/pipelines/{pipelineId}/runs` with, as it needs:

- **record**: the data for the run, checked against the pipeline's input contract when it has one;
- **files**: the ids of files it uploaded first with `POST /v1/files`;
- **parameters**: values for the pipeline's run parameters, by name (see [run parameters](#pl-placeholders--run-parameters));
- **reference**: its own id for this work, echoed back.

It sends an `Idempotency-Key` header with each start. Sending the same key again within 24 hours returns the first run
instead of starting a second one, so a retry after a network error is safe.

```Start a run (the request line)
POST /v1/pipelines/{pipelineId}/runs
```

## Follow the run and read its result

| Request | Answers |
|---|---|
| `GET /v1/runs/{runId}` | The run's status (queued, running, completed, failed, skipped or interrupted), times (UTC) and review status |
| `GET /v1/runs/{runId}/steps` | Its steps, in order |
| `GET /v1/runs/{runId}/outputs` | The files it received and made, and its review |
| `GET /v1/runs/{runId}/result` | A completed run's final rows: at most 100 rows and 16 KB, masked by the workspace's data policy |
| `GET /v1/runs/{runId}/items` | Each file, document or row it worked one by one |

The full reference, with samples and a sandbox for testing without touching real pipelines or the
bill, is in the Developer portal.

## Example

Northgate Labs' system starts **Partner starts a run through the API** with three lab records, one request each, each
with its own `Idempotency-Key`. Every run validates the record, flags abnormal values, keeps the file and makes a
report; the partner's script then reads each run's status, steps and outputs back.

## Limits

| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| A token | 15 minutes |
| Calls | The limits per client and per workspace shown on API Clients; past them the API answers 429 with a time to wait |
| A run's result through the API | 100 rows and 16 KB |
| An Idempotency-Key | Remembered 24 hours |
| Runs started this way | Billed like any run |

articles.title: Start a pipeline from an approval workflow
articles.summary: A workflow's Run pipeline step runs a schedule with the request's values, waits for it, and keeps fields of its answer for later decisions.
articles.who: Anyone who may change approval workflows; the change takes effect when the workflow is published
articles.md:
An approval workflow moves a request from person to person: a task here, an approval there, a condition that decides
the way. A **Run pipeline** step in it runs a pipeline at that point, with the request's values as the pipeline's
parameters, and can wait for the run before the next person is asked. The answer's fields are then on the request, for a
condition or an assignee to use.

## Add a Run pipeline step to a workflow

1. Open **Build › Approval workflows** and choose the workflow.
2. Choose **Add a step** (or **Add after** on a step) and pick **Run pipeline**.
3. **Schedule to run**: the schedule of the pipeline to run. A schedule **Only when started** is the usual choice.
4. **Parameters**: each parameter the pipeline declares, with its value from the request by name (`{{subject.mrn}}`) or
   an earlier step's kept value (`{{registration.patient_id}}`). Empty: the pipeline's default. A parameter the pipeline
   does not declare is marked **Not declared**, and publishing refuses it.
5. Tick **Wait until the run ends, its approvals included** to hold the workflow until the run is over. Off: the next
   step starts as soon as the run is queued.
6. With waiting on, **Keep how it ended as** names the outcome, such as `registration`. A condition after the step reads
   `registration.ok`, `registration.status` (Completed, Failed, TimedOut) or `registration.message`; **Add a condition on
   it** puts one right after.
7. Tick **Keep values from its answer** to keep fields of the run's answer: **From** **Its final output** or a step,
   **Keep** (**The first row's fields**, **The rows (up to 100)**, **How many rows**, or each field's sum, lowest,
   highest or average), and the **Fields** to keep (a JSON column's field by a dot, such as `summary.age`).
8. Publish the workflow. Requests already running keep their version.

![A Run pipeline step in an approval workflow](trg-workflow "The Patient journey workflow: its first step runs the registration pipeline with the patient's MRN and waits for it")

## Example

Summit Valley's **Patient journey** workflow starts when an admission is accepted. Its first step runs **Journey 4 ·
Registration: eligibility then patient record** with `mrn` = `{{subject.mrn}}`, waits for it and keeps the outcome as
`registration`. The next step, **Registered?**, sends a patient who is not eligible to the self-pay counselling team
and everyone else to nurse triage. Later steps run the care-plan draft and the discharge summary the same way, before
Dr. Anika Patel approves.

## Limits

| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Values kept from an answer | Up to 16 KB; masked columns stay masked |
| Rows kept | Up to 100 |
| Each run it starts | A run of its own, billed like any run |

articles.title: Backfills: run a schedule for each day of a past range
articles.summary: Pick the dates and the period, see what will run and what it may cost, start it, and follow, pause or retry it.
articles.who: Anyone who may run the schedule; the cost estimate is shown to workspace administrators

where.label: Build › Pipelines › Schedules & triggers › a schedule's ⋮ › Backfill…

articles.popular: Rerun a pipeline for last month
articles.md:
A **backfill** runs a schedule once for each day (hour or week) of a past range, a few at a time: to fill the history a
new pipeline missed, or to rebuild a month after a fix. Each run is told which period it is for, so the pipeline reads
that period's data.

## Make the pipeline period-aware

A backfill run gives its period to the steps as `{{run.date}}` (the day), `{{run.windowStart}}` and
`{{run.windowEnd}}`. Use them where the pipeline chooses its data, for example a **Read S3** prefix of
`remits/{{run.date}}/` or a **Read Database** query `WHERE ordered_at >= '{{run.windowStart}}'`. A pipeline that only
reads "today" gives every period the same data.

## Start a backfill

1. Open **Build › Pipelines › Schedules & triggers**, open the schedule's **⋮** menu and choose **Backfill…** (or
   **Backfill…** at the top of the schedule's editor). The schedule must be active.
2. Under **Range**, pick the **Dates** (**7 days**, **30 days**, or a range), and **One run per**: **Day**, **Hour** or
   **Week**. Days are counted in the workspace's billing time zone.
3. Under **How it runs**, choose **At once**: how many of its runs are in flight together (1 to 4). The schedule's own
   runs keep going beside them.
4. Tick **Run again the periods that already have a completed run**, or leave it off to skip them.
5. If the pipeline has run parameters, set their values under **Parameters**: every run of the backfill takes them.
6. Read the **Preview**: how many periods **will run**, how many are **already done, skipped**, each period's date, and
   the **Cost estimate** (from what this pipeline's runs were billed in the last 30 days).
7. Choose **Start** (it reads, for example, **Start: 14 days**). The backfill opens in **Runs › Backfills**.

![A backfill's settings and preview](trg-backfill "Backfill…: the range, one run per day, two at once, the parameters and the preview")

## Follow a backfill

Open **Run & review › Runs › Backfills**. Each backfill shows its schedule, range, periods and how many at once, a bar
of how many are done, failed and running, its status and when it will end. Show **Open**, **All**, **Failed**,
**Completed** or **Cancelled** ones.

On a running backfill you can **Pause** and **Resume**, **Retry failed** periods, or **Cancel** it. The history button
opens the schedule's runs.

![The Backfills page](trg-backfills "Runs › Backfills: each backfill's range, progress and status")

## Example

Summit Valley's revenue cycle team added **Denials by month (backfill a quarter)** in October and needed the earlier
days. They backfilled 1 to 25 October, one run per day, three at once: 25 runs, all completed, each reading that day's
remittance folder with `{{run.date}}`, while the daily runs of other schedules carried on.

## Limits

| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| Periods in one backfill | 366 |
| Runs at once | 1 to 4 (2 by default) |
| Open backfills in a workspace | 3 at a time (the platform may set another number) |
| Runs of a backfill | Billed like any run |

articles.title: When a run or a step fails
articles.summary: How to read a failure, and what to do about a missing file, a step that timed out, a busy model, a run that is still going and a quiet day.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Runs reads failures; retrying is for whoever may run the schedule
articles.popular: Find out why a run failed and retry it
articles.md:
A run that fails always says where and why. This article shows where to read that, and the fixes for the failures
people meet most often in runs and steps. The messages are quoted as the console shows them; a part in angle brackets
or a number is filled in for your run.

## Read a failure
1. Open **Run & review › Runs › Failed**. **Error patterns** groups the same error with its numbers, names and ids set
   aside, most frequent first, and names the kind of failure: **The data**, **A service it called**, **Timed out or
   stopped responding**, **Too large for memory or a limit**, **Its settings**, **Rejected by a reviewer**, **Closed by
   a person** or **Other**. Pick a pattern to list its runs.
2. Open a run. Its **Steps** tab marks the failed step in red with its message under the step's name, and says above the
   list: "Failed at step N <name>. Fix the cause, then retry: the steps before it are not run again."
3. The steps after a failed one read "Skipped: step <name> failed and its on-error is fail." Nothing is wrong with them;
   they did not run.
4. The **Log** tab has every try, for example "Try 1 of 2 failed: timed out after 5 s".

![Runs › Failed with its error patterns](ts-failed-runs "Runs › Failed: each error pattern, how often it came back and what kind of failure it is")

## Retry
- **Retry from step N** runs the run again from the failed step, as a new attempt of the same run. The steps before it
  are not run again: their kept output is reused, and the page says "Reused from attempt 1".
- **Run again from the start** runs every step again.
- A run that works item by item offers **Retry failed items** on its **Items** tab: only the failed items run again,
  each from the step it failed at.
- A run made by a backfill says "Part of backfill #N: retry failed days from the backfill." Open the backfill with
  **Open backfill #N** and retry its failed days there.

> **Tip:** Fix the cause first. A retry with nothing changed usually fails the same way, and each attempt is a run that
> is billed.

## When a retry is refused
Retrying several failed runs at once (tick them in **Runs › Failed**) shows what will happen to each first; one that
cannot be retried is skipped with its reason:

| Reason shown | What to do |
|---|---|
| The run is not failed (already retried, or running again) | Nothing: it is being dealt with |
| Another run of the pipeline is in flight | Wait for it to finish |
| The pipeline is not active | Make the pipeline active, or leave the run |
| The workspace is paused | Ask your administrator |
| The pipeline changed before the failed step: run it again from the start | Use **Run again from the start** |
| An input file changed since the run read it | Run it again from the start, so every step reads the new file |
| The kept outputs of the steps before it expired | Run it again from the start |
| Part of a backfill: retry failed days from the backfill | Open **Runs › Backfills** and retry the failed days there |

## A missing file: "No object at"
**The message:** `No object at summit-valley-s3/ops/beds/late/census-2026-10-12.csv.`

**Why:** the step reads a file that is not there: it has not arrived yet, it is in another folder, or its name is not
what the step expects (a date in the name is the usual suspect).

**Fix:** check the bucket under **See results › Analysis › Files**. When the file arrives, use **Retry from step 1**.
If the file is often late, move the schedule later, or let an arriving file start the pipeline instead (see
[Start a pipeline when a file arrives](#trg-file)).

![A run that failed on a missing file](ts-missing-file "The census file was not there: step 1 failed, steps 2 and 3 were skipped")

> **Note:** A file that is not there is not the same as nothing new. A scheduled read that finds no new files since
> the last run does not fail; see [Nothing new to do](#ts-runs--nothing-new-to-do).

## A step that timed out
**The message:** `timed out after 5 s`, on the step, and on each try in the log: `Try 2 of 2 failed: timed out after 5 s`.

**Why:** the step took longer than its **Timeout (seconds)**. A partner system that answers slowly is the usual cause.

**Fix:** open the pipeline, select the step and, under **How it runs**, raise **Timeout (seconds)** (1 to 86,400 a
try) or give it more **Tries** (1 to 10) and **Seconds between tries** (0 to 3,600). Then **Retry from step N**.

![A step that timed out on both tries](ts-timeout "A slow partner: the step allows 5 seconds and was tried twice")

## The AI service is busy
**The messages:** `Row 3: the AI service is busy (still busy after 4 tries)`, or the model's own answer such as
`Row 3: HTTP 429: …`.

**Why:** the model connection was answering other calls. The step waits and tries again by itself before it gives up,
and with **Calls at once** above 1 it also sends fewer calls at a time.

**Fix:** retry later, or lower **Calls at once** on the AI step. A workspace administrator can see what the model
connection allows under **Settings › Model connections**. When the console cannot reach the AI service at all, the
step says `The AI service could not be reached, so the step did not run.`

## A run that is still going
**The message:** `A job can't be run while its last run is still in flight ('Queue', 'Start', 'Running').`
A retry says instead: `Another run of this pipeline is still in flight; one runs at a time. Retry once it has finished.`

**Why:** one run of a schedule at a time. A scheduled run that comes due while the last one is still going is recorded
as **Skip**.

**Fix:** wait for the running one to end (**Runs › Latest** shows it), then run or retry.

## Too many rows, columns or bytes
**The messages:** `… has more than 50,000 rows, the most a step holds.`, `… has 240 columns; a step holds at most
200.`, or `… is 60,452,588 bytes; a step reads or writes at most 52,428,800.`

**Why:** a step holds at most 50,000 rows, 200 columns and 1,000,000 cells, and reads or writes a file of at most
50 MB, unless the platform set other limits for your workspace.

**Fix:** make the input smaller before it reaches the step: split the file, filter or aggregate earlier, or select only
the columns you need.

## Nothing new to do
A scheduled read of "only the files since the last run" that finds none is not a failure. The log says
`0 object(s) written since the last completed run read …`, the later steps run on no rows, and the run is
**Completed**. A step set to **Skip the rest and complete** under **If it fails** ends the run **Completed** when it
fails, with the steps after it marked skipped: "… completed; stopped after <name> failed (skip_rest), N skipped."

## Learn more
- Files, photos, recordings and conversions: [Files and media](#ts-files).
- Calls to other systems: [Connections and APIs](#ts-connections).
- The statuses: [Run statuses](#run-statuses); backfills: [Backfills](#trg-backfills).
- More questions: [Frequently asked questions](#ts-faq).

articles.title: Files and media
articles.summary: A photo that cannot be measured, a file that will not convert, and a recording with nothing to transcribe.
articles.who: Anyone whose page access includes Runs reads the messages; changing a step's settings is for whoever may edit the pipeline
articles.md:
Steps that work on files (photos, documents to convert, recordings) meet files that are dark, broken or empty. Each of
these steps has a setting that says what to do then: fail the step, skip that file, or keep its row with the reason.
Choose it before the run, and one bad file never costs you the others.

| Step | Its setting | Choices |
|---|---|---|
| Measure image | **When a photo cannot be read** | `fail` the step, `skip` the row, or `null`: keep it with the sizes empty and the reason in the note (the default) |
| Convert file | **When a file fails** | `fail` the step (the default), `skip` the row, or `null`: keep it with no result, the reason in `convert_error` |
| Transcribe audio | **When a file fails** | `fail` the step (the default), `skip` the row, or `null`: keep it with the transcript empty, the reason in `transcribe_error` |

## A photo that cannot be measured
**The messages:**
- `Row 4: The file is not a png or jpg image.` The file is not a readable photo: broken, or another format.
- `"wound-17.tif" is not a png or jpg image.` The key names a file of another type.
- `The row has no image key.` The column that should name the photo is empty for that row.
- In the note column, `no ruler found: not measured`. The photo is readable, but no ruler was found in it (a photo too
  dark, or taken without the ruler), so nothing was measured. This is not an error: the row is kept and its sizes are
  empty.

**Fix:** replace the photo in the bucket with a readable png or jpg, with the centimetre ruler in view, then on the run's
**Items** tab choose **Retry failed items**: only the photos that failed run again, from the step they failed at. With
**When a photo cannot be read** set to `null`, the run completes and warns "2 photo(s) could not be read: their sizes
are empty."

![A run whose photo could not be measured](ts-photo "Attempt 1: the measuring step failed on row 4; attempt 2, after the photo was replaced, completed")

> **Note:** The step measures with code against the ruler, never with a model. A model may describe the photo in a
> later step; its description is a DRAFT for a person to check.

## A file that will not convert
**The messages** (each starts with the file's name, or "Row N"):
- `Conversion failed — the file may be corrupt or password-protected: …` A damaged file, or one with a password.
- `Conversion timed out after N seconds and LibreOffice was restarted. A very large document can take longer than
  that: split it, or convert a smaller part.`
- `'xyz' isn't a supported input format.` or `Can't convert a spreadsheet to 'pptx' — valid targets are: …`
- `'letter' has no extension, so its format is not known.`
- `The converter is busy: 4 conversion(s) running and 6 waiting. Try again in a minute.`

**Fix:** open the file on your own computer; save a damaged or password-protected file again without the password; pick
a target the message lists; give the file its extension. For a busy converter, retry a minute later. With **When a file
fails** set to `skip`, the run completes, and its log counts the files converted and those that failed and were
skipped.

## A recording with nothing to transcribe
**The messages:**
- `The recording is silent or nearly silent (98% of it below -50 dBFS) -- there is nothing to transcribe.`
- `No speech was found in this recording -- there is nothing to transcribe.`
- `The recording is only 0.30 seconds long -- at least 0.5 seconds of audio is needed.` (the first number is the
  recording's)
- `The recording is 5.2 hours long, over the 4-hour transcription limit. Split it and transcribe the parts.`
- `The recording is distorted throughout (60% of samples clipped) -- it cannot be transcribed reliably.`
- `This file could not be read as audio -- it may be damaged, or not really the type its name says.`

**Why:** the transcriber checks a recording before it transcribes it, and refuses one it cannot hear anything useful in.
The limits are those of the transcriber: at least half a second, at most 4 hours, unless the platform set others.

**Fix:** check the recording plays and has speech; record again, or split a long one. To keep the other recordings of a
run going, set **When a file fails** to `null`: each refused file keeps its row with `transcribe_status` failed and the
sentence above in `transcribe_error`, so a later step can filter them out or send a notice.

> **Tip:** When the transcriber is busy, the step waits and asks again by itself, and the log says so: "The
> transcriber is busy (…); <file> waits N s and asks again (try N of M)."

## Learn more
- Retrying and reading a failure: [When a run or a step fails](#ts-runs).
- Documents and reports: [Documents, forms and reports](#ts-documents).

articles.title: Connections and APIs
articles.summary: Too many calls refused up front, a call the other system refused or answered wrongly, a blocked address, and a record the API's contract refused.
articles.who: Workspace administrators set up Call API steps and API collections; developers read the API's answers

where.label: Get data in › Connections › API collections

articles.md:
A pipeline that calls another system depends on that system's answers, and the API that other systems call depends on
what they send. These are the messages you see on either side, and what to do about each.

## Too many calls
**The message:** `The input has 1,000 rows; Call API makes at most 300 calls (At most calls). Put a filter, a limit or
an aggregate before it, send them in batches, or call once.`

When the step sends rows in batches: `The input has 9,000 rows: 9 calls of 1,000 rows; Call API makes at most 5 calls
(At most calls). Raise Rows per call (at most 1,000), or put a filter, a limit or an aggregate before it.`

**Why:** **At most calls** (100 unless the step says otherwise, never more than 500) protects the other system and your
bill. The step counts the calls it would make **before it sends any**, so nothing was sent and no call was billed.

**Fix:** what the message says: filter, limit or aggregate the rows before the step; set **Send** to batches and raise
**Rows per call**; send once; or raise **At most calls** if the other system allows it. Then **Retry from step N**.

![Call API refused before sending](ts-too-many-calls "The step needed 1,000 calls and allows 300: it failed before making any")

> **Note:** On the run's **Items** tab such a run lists every row as a failed item, because none was sent. Retrying them
> fails the same way until the step or its input changes.

## A call the other system refused
**The message:** `Call 5 of 30 was not ok: HTTP 503: The API answered HTTP 503. (When a call is not ok: fail; set it to
continue to branch on api_ok instead).`

The reason after "not ok:" is one of:
- `HTTP 503` or `HTTP 404: …`: the other system answered with an error status.
- `no answer`: it did not answer at all.
- `the answer's json.status is denied, not eq approved`: it answered, but the step's **Ok only when** condition did not
  hold.

**Why:** the other system refused the call, was down, or answered something the step treats as not ok. In **Runs ›
Failed** this kind of failure is grouped as **A service it called**.

**Fix:**
1. Read the run's **Log**: each call's status and the first characters of its answer, "Call 5 of 30: HTTP 503, …".
2. If the other system was down, **Retry failed items** (or **Retry from step N**) once it is back: only the calls that
   failed are sent again.
3. If some refusals are normal (a patient not found, say), set **When a call is not ok** to `continue`. Each row then
   carries `api_status`, `api_ok` and `api_error` (the prefix is the step's **Column prefix**), the run warns "3 call(s)
   were not ok; their rows carry api_error.", and a later Filter step can send those rows elsewhere.

## A blocked address
**The message:** `The API request was blocked: …` (in a collection's own test, `The call was blocked: …`).

**Why:** the console only calls addresses it is allowed to reach. A private address (a server inside your network) is
refused unless the platform's operator has listed it.

**Fix:** use the API's public address. If it must be a private one, ask your platform administrator to allow it. See
[What the console may call](#con-addresses).

## The API refused a record (422)
When your own system starts a run or sends an event through the customer API, the record is checked against the
pipeline's or the event's data contract **before** anything is stored. A record that does not meet it is answered
`422 Unprocessable Content`, and no run is made.

| What was sent | The answer's detail |
|---|---|
| A run's record | The record does not meet the pipeline's input contract. |
| An event | The event's data does not meet its contract. |
| A run with no record, for a pipeline that needs one | `record`: this pipeline's runs take a record meeting its input contract |

The answer lists each field that failed by its path, such as `record.loinc` or `data.loinc`, with the reason.

**Fix:** correct the field the answer names and send again. If the contract itself cannot be read for a moment, the
answer is 503: "The pipeline's input contract cannot be read right now. Try again in a moment."

## Learn more
- Data contracts inside a pipeline: [Documents, forms and reports](#ts-documents--a-row-that-does-not-hold-to-its-contract).
- Retrying: [When a run or a step fails](#ts-runs).
- Setting up calls: [Make an API collection](#con-api-collections), [Test a request](#con-api-test); the customer API:
  [Start a run and read it back](#dev-runs).

articles.title: Documents, contracts and reports
articles.summary: A row that does not hold to its data contract, the same document twice, a report over the page limit, a missing picture or field, and too many reports at once.
articles.who: Anyone who reads runs, documents or reports; raising the page limit is a workspace administrator's
articles.md:
Documents, data contracts and reports each check what they are given before they act on it. When a check says no, the
message says which file, row, field or limit, and usually what to do.

## A row that does not hold to its contract
**The message:** `1 of 3001 row(s) do not hold to gl_journal v1; row 3001: $.debit: must have a minimum value of 0`

**Why:** a **Validate** step checks each row against a data contract (the columns, their types and their rules). Its
setting **Rows that do not hold** is `fail`, so the first bad rows stop the step; the message names the contract and
its version, how many rows broke it, and the first problems of the first bad row. The steps after it are skipped, so
nothing is summed or written from data that did not pass.

**Fix:** correct the row in the source file (here, a debit below 0) and run again. If bad rows are expected and should
not stop the run, set **Rows that do not hold** to `drop` (leave them out) or `flag` (keep them, with `_valid` and
`_errors` columns, for a later step to sort out).

![A run stopped by its data contract](ts-contract "One journal line of 3,001 broke the contract: the run stopped at the check, the sums were skipped")

> **Note:** The customer API checks a record against a pipeline's input contract before it makes a run. See
> [The API refused a record](#ts-connections--the-api-refused-a-record-422).

## The same document twice
**The message:** `The same file as "referral-upload-8.pdf" (Uploaded by Summit Valley admin); no second document was
made.` The upload dialog shows the file as **Already here** with the first document's number, and sums up
"1 document(s) made · 1 already here · 0 refused."

**Why:** the console keeps one document per file: the same file uploaded or mailed again is recognised and not read a
second time, so it is not extracted twice.

**Fix:** nothing to fix; open the first document. If the first read had failed, the second is read: "The same file as
"…", whose earlier read had failed: it is read again."

## A report over the page limit
**The message:** `The report lays out to 412 pages; this workspace's reports are at most 300 pages. Narrow the data,
lower a table's maxRows or a repeat's maxItems, make one report per row, or split it into several reports.` It ends with
who may raise the limit:
- "Your administrator can raise this workspace's limit up to N pages in Report Studio › Settings."
- "Only the platform administrator can raise this workspace's limit."
- "N pages is the most the platform allows."

**Why:** every page counts toward the workspace's limit for one report (300 unless its administrators set fewer), a long
table's pages too. A report over it is not made.

**Fix:** the failed job and the report's page offer the way out that applies: **Make one report per row**, **Lower the
table's rows** or **Export the data as CSV**, and for a workspace administrator whose limit it is to raise, **Raise
the limit**. The message's "Report Studio › Settings" is **See results › Reports › Settings** in the menu. In a pipeline, the Generate report step says `The report was not made (FAILED, LIMIT_EXCEEDED):
…`; with **When the checks refuse it** set to continue with a warning, the step goes on without a report.

## A missing picture or field
- A picture the data names but that cannot be read prints as a box that says **Image not available** (or **No image**
  when the row names none), and the report is still made, with a warning such as "That image is not there, or not
  yours to read." or "Storage could not be reached for an image; try again." A report draws at most 500 pictures from
  its data.
- `'patient.name' is not in this data. Nothing is filled in for it: map the data, change the binding, or declare the
  field optional in the data contract.` A field the template uses is missing from the data: map it when you create the
  report, change the template, or mark the field optional.
- `'primary' is not a list in the data, so it cannot be counted or filtered.` A table or repeat expects a list and the
  data has one value: check the data the report was given.

## Too many reports at once
**The message:** `At most 30 generations a minute; try again in 12 s.`

**Why:** each person may generate up to 30 reports a minute. **Fix:** wait the seconds it says.

## Learn more
- Reports: [Report Studio at a glance](#rs-overview).
- Documents: [Upload documents and mail them in](#doc-intake) and [Review a document](#doc-review).

articles.title: Approvals
articles.summary: An approval rejected or expired, a rejection that needs a reason, a task that is overdue, your own request, and items bulk approve skipped.
articles.who: Approvers, and whoever follows the runs and requests that wait on them
articles.md:
A person's decision can stop a run or end a request, and a decision that never comes can too. These are the messages
you meet around approvals, and what each means.

## A rejected approval
**The message**, on the failed step and the run: `Rejected by Claire Martin (user 1054): Every line unmatched: the match
itself needs a look before approval.` The steps after it read "Skipped: step <name> was not approved.", and
**Runs › Failed** groups it as **Rejected by a reviewer**.

**Why:** an **Approval** step in the pipeline was rejected. The words after the name are the reviewer's own reason, or
"no reason given".

**Fix:** deal with what the reviewer asked (here, check the matching), then on the run's page **Retry from step N**
runs the Approval step again and asks for a new decision.

![A run stopped by a rejected approval](ts-rejected "The finance approver rejected the unmatched lines with a reason: the run failed and names who and why")

## An approval that expired
**The message:** `No decision by <time>: the approval request expired.`, with the time the request ran out.

**Why:** the Approval step's **Decide within (hours)** (1 to 720) passed with no decision. The run fails as if it had
been rejected.

**Fix:** retry from the step to ask again, and give the reviewers more time, or make sure someone is in the team the
step names (**Reviewers are** a role or a team).

## A rejection that needs a reason
**Why:** the workflow's step is set so that **A rejection needs a reason**. The comment box says so: "Comment: say why,
if you reject it (required)".

**Fix:** write the reason in the comment, then **Reject**. **Ask for changes** always needs a comment saying what should
change.

## Due soon and overdue
- "Due soon: <task>" and ""<title>" is still waiting for you, and is due on <date>." reach the approver before a task's
  due time.
- "Overdue, now yours: <task>" and ""<title>" passed its due time and has come to you." reach whoever the step sends an
  overdue task to (**When overdue, it goes to**, such as the requester's manager).
- In **Review › Approvals** an overdue task is marked **Overdue** ("Overdue · was due <time>"), and **Review › All
  waiting** lists overdue items first.

**Fix:** decide it, or **Pass on** it to a colleague with a note: the task moves to them and the request's history
records who passed it.

## Your own request
No one may approve their own request. In a workspace where nobody else could decide it, the note says so and points to
**Administration › Users** to add a person who can.

## Items bulk approve skipped
When you approve or reject several items at once, you first see what will happen to each. An item that cannot be
decided in bulk is skipped with its reason:

| Reason shown | What it means |
|---|---|
| Already decided | Someone decided it after the list was loaded |
| Not yours to decide | It waits for someone else |
| The pipeline requires individual review | The pipeline is set to be reviewed one by one: open and decide it on its own |
| Bulk approve is off in this workspace | The workspace's data policies keep runs or documents out of bulk approve |
| The document's rules fail, and the workspace policy keeps those out of bulk approve | Open the document and check the rules it fails |
| Changed since it was listed | Refresh the list and decide again |

## Learn more
See [Approval steps inside a run](#apr-approval-steps), [Decide many at once](#apr-bulk) and
[Who decides](#apr-who-decides). More questions:
[Frequently asked questions](#ts-faq).

articles.title: Frequently asked questions
articles.summary: About thirty questions people ask most, from a missing menu to a schedule that did not run, each with a short answer and where to read more.
articles.who: Everyone
articles.popular: Why can't I see a page or a menu?
articles.md:
Short answers to the questions people ask most. Each links the article that says more.

## Access and the menu

### Why can't I see the Billing menu?
Billing (Cost & usage, Analytics, Invoices and Billing documents) is for workspace administrators only; a member never
sees it, whatever their profile. Ask an administrator for what you need. See [Who sees what](#gs-who-sees-what).

### Why is a page missing from my menu, when a colleague has it?
A workspace member sees the pages their **Page access** profile opens; administrators see every page. Two people with
different profiles see different menus. See [Page access profiles](#adm-access-profiles).

### What does "… isn't part of your access" mean?
You opened a page your profile does not include, from a link or a bookmark. The page explains it and offers **Request
access**, which goes straight to your workspace administrators' notifications. A page for administrators only says
"This page isn't available to you" instead.

### Why does every change say "This workspace is managed by our team"?
Your workspace is run as a managed service: "This workspace is managed by our team, so this cannot be changed here.
Contact your account team to request the change." See [The managed service](#sec-managed).

### I lost the phone with my authenticator. How do I sign in?
Ask a workspace administrator: on **Administration › Users** they choose **Reset two-factor login** for you, and you set
it up again at your next sign-in. See [Two-factor sign-in](#gs-two-factor).

### Who may build pipelines?
Anyone whose profile includes Pipelines may read them; saving a pipeline is a workspace administrator's. See
[What a pipeline is](#pl-overview).

## Runs and schedules

### Why did my schedule not run?
Check, in this order:
1. The schedule is active, and its start date and time have come (and its end, if any, has not passed).
2. It runs **On a timetable**: a schedule set to **Only when started** runs only from **Run now** or a workflow.
3. Its last run had finished: a run due while the last one is still going is recorded as **Skip**.
4. The console was running: a run whose time passed while nothing was running to take it is recorded as **Missed**.

See [Run a pipeline on a timetable](#trg-schedules) and [Run statuses](#run-statuses).

### My cron schedule runs at the wrong hour. Why?
A cron expression is read in server time, Chicago, as the hint under the field says. `0 3 * * *` is 03:00 in Chicago.
See [Run a pipeline on a timetable](#trg-schedules).

### Why did my file not start the pipeline?
The schedule must have **A file arrives** ticked, and the file must land in the workspace inbox (Documents › Intake ›
File drop). A file that arrives while a run is going waits its turn. See [Start a pipeline when a file arrives](#trg-file).

### What is the difference between Retry from step N and Run again from the start?
**Retry from step N** runs the same run again from the failed step and reuses what the steps before it kept ("Reused
from attempt 1"). **Run again from the start** runs every step again. See [When a run or a step fails](#ts-runs--retry).

### How do I retry only the items that failed?
On the run's **Items** tab, choose **Retry failed items**: only the failed items run again, each from the step it
failed at. See [The Items view](#run-items).

### A run waits at "Waiting for approval". What now?
The pipeline has an Approval step: the run waits until a reviewer decides in **Review › Approvals**, or until the step's
time to decide runs out. See [Approval steps inside a run](#apr-approval-steps).

### Why was nothing done on a quiet day, and is it billed as a failure?
A scheduled read of only new files that finds none completes the run with no rows; it is not a failure. See
[Nothing new to do](#ts-runs--nothing-new-to-do).

### Where do I see what a run cost?
On the run's page, **What this run cost**. Administrators see every charge under **Billing › Cost & usage**. See
[What AI costs](#ai-costs).

### How long are a run's outputs kept?
The run's **Outputs** tab says, for each file, until when it is kept ("With the run · until …"). The workspace's
retention is set under **Administration › Data policies**. See [Retention](#sec-retention).

## Data, AI and privacy

### Can the console write to our database?
No. Database connections are read-only: pipelines read from them and write their results to files, buckets, reports,
webhooks and notifications. The Write Database step is listed in the Task Registry as unavailable. See
[Add a read-only database connection](#con-databases).

### Does the AI decide anything?
No. A model's answer is a draft for a person to check: pipelines mark it DRAFT, and a person approves or rejects it in
Review. A report is approved and signed by a person. See [AI in pipelines](#ai-steps).

### Which models may see our sensitive data?
That is the workspace's choice under **Administration › Data policies**. The Sensitive level starts as **Local only**:
only model connections your organisation runs itself may see it, until an administrator says otherwise. See
[Which models may see which data](#ai-data-levels).

### Does using the console make us compliant with HIPAA?
No product does that by itself. Meeting your organisation's privacy and regulatory obligations depends on how you
configure and use the console. See [Working with health data](#sec-health-data).

### Can someone outside our workspace fill in one of our forms?
Only through a link an administrator makes on purpose. Forms are shared inside the workspace, filled in by signed-in
members; **Share by link**, in the form's Settings, is off for the workspace until an administrator turns it on, and
each link has an expiry and may be limited to signed-in members. See [Share a form](#form-share).

## Approvals

### How do I give a colleague my approvals while I am away?
For one task, **Pass on** it in **Review › Approvals** to the person you pick. For a period, an **out of office** lets a
colleague decide your tasks, each decision recorded "for" you; the console has no page to set one yet. Sending approvals
to a team means anyone in it can decide. See [Out of office](#adm-out-of-office).

### Why can't I approve my own request or report?
No one may approve their own request, and a report version is approved by someone who did not generate it. Someone else
decides. See [Who decides](#apr-who-decides).

### Why did bulk approve skip some items?
Each skipped item says why, for example "The pipeline requires individual review": that pipeline's runs are decided one
by one. See [Items bulk approve skipped](#ts-approvals--items-bulk-approve-skipped).

### Why must I write a reason to reject?
The workflow's step asks for one (**A rejection needs a reason**), so the requester learns why. Asking for changes
always needs a comment. See [Approvals](#ts-approvals).

## Documents and reports

### I uploaded a document twice. Why is there only one?
The console keeps one document per file: the second upload says the file is already there and names the first. See
[The same document twice](#ts-documents--the-same-document-twice).

### Why was my report not made?
Most often it would have been longer than the workspace's page limit (300 pages unless set lower), or a field the
template needs is missing from the data. The message says which. See [A report over the page limit](#ts-documents--a-report-over-the-page-limit).

### How do I check that a PDF someone sent me is ours and unchanged?
On a report's page in **Reports › Library**, choose **Verify signature** and give it the file. See
[Discharge](#tour-discharge--check-the-signed-copy).

### Can I delete a report that was approved?
No. An approved report is a kept record: void the version, with a reason, or archive the report. A report never
approved can be deleted.

### A dashboard tile says "Nothing to read at …". Is the board broken?
No. The tile reads a file that is not there: "The connection worked, so check the path." Usually the pipeline that
writes it has not run yet. See [Where a board's data comes from](#dash-data-sources).

## Times and the API

### Which time zone are the times in?
The console uses a 24-hour clock. Where the zone matters it is named, as in "26 Oct 2026, 19:27 (Chicago)", and a cron
expression is read in server time (Chicago).

### Is the sandbox billed?
No. Test keys made under **API Clients › Sandbox** work only in the sandbox, and nothing there is billed. See
[The sandbox and test keys](#dev-sandbox).

whatsNew.text: A new patient's intake, typed in or scanned, checked in code, summarised by AI as a DRAFT, approved by a nurse and kept as a signed summary.

whatsNew.text: Give fields a section and the form shows them together under its heading.

whatsNew.title: Checkboxes field
whatsNew.text: A tick-all-that-apply question, with an optional least and most to tick.

whatsNew.title: Keep the decision as
whatsNew.text: Later workflow steps can use who approved, when and their comment, such as {{nurse.byName}}.

whatsNew.title: Quotes in Compute formulas
whatsNew.text: A value with a quote, such as O'Brien, stays one text inside a formula's quotes; write 'it''s' for a quote of your own.
